This paper introduces a new approach to designing spatial restrictions for motion planning within dynamic environments. Traditional motion planning methods typically define these restrictions as the union of obstacles and the trajectory path of a moving object. This study demonstrates that for optimal motion planning, it is more efficient to specify the restriction as the union and separation zones surrounding the object's trajectory, rather than simply including the object's trajectory itself. Furthermore, we establish that separation zones are indispensable for achieving an optimal trajectory, whereas union zones alone are insufficient. Finally, we propose a method for constructing union zones, proving that this strategy prevents a moving object from entering a restricted area. Numerical examples are provided to illustrate the efficacy of both the optimization-based approach and the spatial restriction formulation. Additionally, numerical examples and simulations are included to demonstrate the proposed restriction formulation in the context of optimal motion planning for two specific problems: a two-player pursuit-evasion game and a multi-agent rendezvous problem. These findings indicate that spatial restrictions formulated with union zones are particularly well-suited for applications involving two-player games and multi-agent rendezvous operations. The authors intend to explore the application of spatial restriction creation to other problems in future research. This paper introduces a new visual relocalization approach that integrates surfel maps with deep learning-based feature extraction to achieve robust 3D relocalization. Unlike traditional methods that rely on hand-crafted descriptors, our technique utilizes deep learning features to describe keypoints within an input image. By leveraging these features, we enable a more granular and detailed analysis of image content, which significantly enhances the accuracy of 2D-3D matching. Furthermore, we present an adaptive weighting mechanism that dynamically balances the contributions of deep features and surfel data during visual relocalization. This strategy optimizes the fusion of both information sources, thereby improving overall relocalization performance. Extensive experiments conducted on the TUM-VI and KITTI datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. The results confirm that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a 10.5% improvement in success rate at 2$\sigma$ and a 12.1% improvement at 1$\sigma$ on the TUM-VI dataset, while also delivering promising outcomes on the KITTI dataset. This study addresses the challenge of selecting a collaborative user group within a multiuser MIMO downlink network to achieve a specified target signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR). The selection process is modeled as a combinatorial optimization problem, which is subsequently approximated using a convex relaxation technique. Specifically, the Group LASSO method is employed to identify the optimal set of users for precoding. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed approach yields significant gains in power efficiency and computational complexity compared to conventional sequential user selection methods. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the resulting selection outcome is independent of the initial user set. Finally, the paper explores the relationship between the Group LASSO formulation and the maximum SINR formulation. The study concludes that both methods identify the same optimal user set, provided the Group LASSO uses an appropriate regularization parameter. Additionally, it is observed that the Group LASSO solution is generally robust against variations in the interference covariance matrix. However, when a diagonal approximation of the interference covariance matrix is utilized, the selected user set may exhibit a dependency on the specific channel realization. The paper also examines the link between Group LASSO and orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP), noting that the former can be viewed as a regularized variant of the latter. Finally, an efficient algorithm is proposed to determine the Group LASSO solution by iteratively solving a series of 2-norm minimization problems. This method is shown to be effective for identifying the optimal user set in most practical scenarios. To further enhance performance, a post-processing step is introduced to refine the user set selected by this method. The proposed post-processing is demonstrated to be more efficient than standard OMP. Simulation results confirm that the collaboration user set identified through this method achieves target SINR with lower transmit power than that required by the Group LASSO. We demonstrate that for any tropical curve, the collection of semifields generated by its theta functions constitutes a finite semifield that contains all rational functions expressible as logical functions of its theta functions. This result serves as a tropical analogue to a finding by Broersma, Broersma, and Vanstone. Our proof relies on the observation that rank subsemifields of the logical function semifield correspond to rank strata within the tropical curve. This relationship enables us to characterize rank subsemifields of the logical function semifield using the data provided by Abramovich, Chen, and Gross. Furthermore, we establish that the logical function semifield varies with the choice of polyhedral structure. However, we also prove that for any specific theta function, the semifields it generates remain consistent across all polyhedral structures. This finding offers a partial resolution to a question posed by Broersma, Broersma, and Vanstone. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between rational functions representable as logical functions of theta functions and those generated by such functions, revealing that while these sets are identical in dimension, they are not necessarily identical as semifields. Finally, we extend our findings to the context of tropical abelian varieties.

Keywords: tropical geometry, tropical abelian varieties, theta functions, semifields, logical functions, tropical curves, rank strata, tropical curves, tropical abelian varieties.

The study examines a two-player game where each participant selects a strategy from the unit interval, with payoffs determined by the product of their choices. We demonstrate that for any fixed payoff function satisfying a specific condition, the repeated application of best responses leads to the equilibrium at (1, 1). Furthermore, we establish that for a broad class of payoff functions, the best response dynamics converge to this Nash equilibrium from almost all initial states within the unit square. These findings extend our previous work, which was limited to payoff functions of the form $f(x)y$ where $f(x) = x^2 + 0.5x$. Additionally, we prove that for this particular case, the best response dynamics achieve a convergence rate of $\Omega(\log(n))$. Finally, we present a counterexample illustrating a scenario where the best response dynamics fail to converge to the Nash equilibrium. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/2D-Game-Theory. Our implementation is available here: https://github.com/ashwinbhat/2D-Game-Theory/blob/master/BestResponseDynamics.py. This research investigates the relationship between the Vassiliev characteristic of order three and the Fox-Hatcher characteristic. The characteristic of order three is defined as the sum of the three signs associated with the knot complement in $S^3$, as determined by the cohomology class in $H^2(M_\kappa, \mathbb{C})$ resulting from the representation $\rho: \pi_1(M_\kappa) \to SL_2(\mathbb{C})$. We calculate this characteristic for the Fox-Hatcher knots and demonstrate that it corresponds to the number of components in the knot when expressed as the connected sum of alternating knots. This result relies on the property that Fox-Hatcher knots maintain the same representation up to conjugacy as their constituent alternating knots. Additionally, we provide examples illustrating that these knots can possess multiple distinct representations, thereby exhibiting a non-vanishing characteristic of order three. Finally, we present examples of knots with a non-zero characteristic of order three that cannot be decomposed into the connected sum of two knots. Specifically, we examine the Stevedore knot, which has a characteristic of order three equal to 2, and the connected sum of the Stevedore knot with itself, which has a characteristic of order three equal to 4. We further generalize this finding to the connected sum of $n$ copies of the Stevedore knot, which yields a characteristic of order three equal to $n$. In each instance, we provide the explicit values for the second and third characteristic polynomials. It is worth noting that the second characteristic polynomial for the Stevedore knot was previously computed by J. Murakami in 1991. Our findings regarding the third characteristic polynomial align with those of J. Murakami. Finally, we explore the relationship between characteristic polynomials and finite type invariants, specifically demonstrating that the second finite type invariant is equal to the coefficient of the $t^2$ term in the second characteristic polynomial. We also present a calculation of the third finite type invariant for the connected sum of $n$ copies of the Stevedore knot, which is given by the formula $\frac{2^{n-1}(2^n - 1)}{3}$. This confirms that the third finite type invariant is non-zero. Furthermore, we establish that the third finite type invariant for any connected sum of $n$ copies of the Stevedore knot is precisely $\frac{2^{n-1}(2^n - 1)}{3}$.

The Nernst effect offers a valuable method for investigating quasi-two-dimensional (q2D) electronic systems, as it becomes significant near magnetic phase transitions and can detect the nematic phase in Fe-based superconductors. This study examines the Nernst effect in the Fe-based superconductor LiFeAs across both metallic and superconducting regimes. In the superconducting state, the Nernst signal is substantial, reaching approximately 100 \mu V/K at low temperatures and high magnetic fields. However, within the metallic regime, the Nernst effect is negligible, indicating that LiFeAs does not exhibit incipient nematicity. Furthermore, the nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) Knight shift data support a spin-density wave (SDW) ordering mechanism. Additionally, the temperature dependence of the in-plane resistivity in the metallic state aligns with the Mott law, a characteristic of q2D systems. These findings collectively suggest that LiFeAs possesses intrinsic q2D properties, yet its phase diagram lacks a magnetic phase transition or a nematic phase. Consequently, the nematic instability observed in other Fe-based superconductors is not a universal feature of q2D iron pnictides. Finally, the Nernst effect in LiFeAs is analyzed in the context of vortex dynamics. Specifically, the field dependence of the Nernst signal in the superconducting state is interpreted as evidence for a crossover from 3D to q2D vortex behavior. This interpretation is consistent with the temperature dependence of the Nernst signal, which exhibits a peak at a temperature corresponding to the crossover temperature between 3D and q2D vortex dynamics. Furthermore, the q2D nature of LiFeAs is corroborated by the weak temperature dependence of the Nernst signal in the superconducting state. Overall, the Nernst effect in LiFeAs provides compelling evidence for q2D vortex dynamics. The results are compared with data from other Fe-based superconductors, revealing that the field dependence of the Nernst signal in LiFeAs differs from that observed in FeSe. This distinction is attributed to the differing q2D characteristics of LiFeAs and FeSe. Finally, the field dependence of the Nernst signal in LiFeAs is compared with the vortex core size, demonstrating that the Nernst signal is limited by the vortex core size. This paper examines the Two Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM) in light of recent non-observation of new physics at the LHC and the measured 125 GeV Higgs boson properties. We evaluate two primary variants: the Type-II model, which extends the Standard Model (SM) to accommodate non-zero vacuum expectation values for both doublets, and the inert type-I model, where only one doublet acquires a vacuum expectation value while the other remains inert. The focus is on the lightest CP-even scalar $h$, which must align with current SM precision measurements. We present $h$-coupling contours for both models based on latest ATLAS and CMS data, incorporating uncertainties from the SM. Furthermore, we project future constraints from the High-Luminosity LHC and the Circular Electron Positron Collider (CEPC), which aims to measure Higgs couplings with approximately 1% precision. These projections will significantly refine our understanding of the $h$-ZZ and $h$-gg couplings, thereby narrowing the viable parameter space of the 2HDM. Additionally, we analyze the $h$-Z$\gamma$ coupling, which is crucial for interpreting ATLAS data at the 125 GeV resonance. Finally, we address the $h$-ggg coupling, which is sensitive to loop contributions from charged scalars and fermions, offering a valuable probe of the 2HDM parameter space. This analysis is complemented by constraints from the $h \to \gamma\gamma$ decay rate. In our study, we consider two scenarios for the CEPC: one with a Higgs factory design and another with a multi-purpose accelerator, both offering a factor of 10 improvement over current measurements. Our findings indicate that the $h$-ggg coupling will be precisely measured at the CEPC, providing a robust test of the 2HDM. We also consider the $h \to b\bar{b}$ decay rate, which is sensitive to loop effects from top quarks and bottom quarks, allowing for further exploration of the model's parameter space. This analysis is supported by constraints from the $h \to b\bar{b}$ decay rate. This study introduces a self-assembly method designed to generate novel neural network architectures tailored for solving problems within irregular geometric domains. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on standard architectures like the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), this method educates neural particles using geometric information encoded within the domain itself. By integrating these geometric data into the neural signals, the particles are capable of comprehending the domain's structure. Consequently, this enables the creation of non-trivial architectures capable of resolving problems in arbitrary geometric settings. The paper demonstrates the method's effectiveness by successfully solving a potential problem in a geometrically restricted region, such as the unit disk. Additionally, it applies the approach to simple self-replicating swarm robotics scenarios, illustrating the generation of neural networks where particles possess architectures adapted to their specific roles within the assembly process. Finally, the authors discuss how this approach can be extended to other scenarios, including other particle-based self-assembly problems and challenges involving irregularly shaped data clusters. We investigate robustness within chiral gauge theories, identifying a novel domain wall fermionization scheme. This approach enables the identification of robust anomalies in chiral gauge theories, distinguishing them from chiral spin models. This new scheme also clarifies the stages of chiral gauge theories, offering a systematic framework to categorize them based on their mass terms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both domain wall and twisted boundary conditions can induce this stage. These findings significantly advance the understanding of chiral gauge theories and assist in the construction of their lattice regularizations. Additionally, our results suggest that certain chiral spin models may be intrinsically inconsistent, a hypothesis we test by constructing a consistent 2+1 dimensional model that exhibits a robust anomaly. Finally, we explore the connection between stage and robust anomaly, revealing that this relationship can be interpreted as a lattice version of the index theorem. These insights may prove valuable for constructing consistent chiral spin models. Throughout this work, we employ lattice perturbation theory to analyze chiral gauge theories. We also examine the relationship between perturbation theory and the functional integral method, finding that the latter is more effective for investigating non-perturbative aspects. Consequently, we re-examine the relationship between robust and stage anomalies using the functional integral method. Our findings indicate that the relationship between these stages is more complex than previously understood through perturbation theory. To support this, we construct a consistent 2+1 dimensional chiral gauge theory featuring a robust anomaly and a stage, which is intrinsically inconsistent, utilizing the functional integral method. This construction confirms that the relationship between robust and stage anomalies is more intricate than the perturbation theory analysis suggested. Finally, we demonstrate that the relationship between robust and stage anomalies can be interpreted as a lattice version of the index theorem, providing a more comprehensive understanding of this relationship. We conclude that the functional integral method is more effective than perturbation theory for analyzing the relationship between these anomalies. This paper addresses the ill-posedness of the steady Navier-Stokes equations within critical Besov spaces. Our primary result demonstrates that for any given initial velocity field $u_0 \in B^{2}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ with $p>3$, there exists a sufficiently large magnitude $\lambda_0>0$ such that for all $\lambda>\lambda_0$, the corresponding Cauchy problem admits no solution. This finding extends and complements the work of Liang and Zhang (2019). Furthermore, we establish that the phenomenon of ill-posedness persists in homogeneous Besov spaces. Finally, utilizing counterexamples, we show that the ill-posedness result derived herein cannot be extended to the case where $p\leq 3$. These findings highlight the necessity of employing alternative analytical methods to extend the ill-posedness result to the critical Besov space $B^{2}_{3,1}(\mathbb{R}^3)$. Additionally, our approach utilizes a novel technique for estimating the commutator norm involving the Riesz potential. Finally, we note that the ill-posedness result for $\mathbb{R}^2$ presented in this paper is distinct from the one obtained by Liang and Zhang (2019). In summary, the ill-posedness phenomenon for the steady Navier-Stokes equations appears to be intrinsic to the critical Besov spaces under consideration. This study investigates the interaction between magnons and phonons in antiferromagnetic dielectrics. We demonstrate that phonons can trigger thermal compression, resulting in increased magnon density. Additionally, we reveal that magnon-phonon interactions induce both thermal expansion and nonlinear spectral displacement of magnons, which can be detected through thermal conductivity and spectroscopy. Furthermore, we establish that magnons can trigger thermal dilation, causing an expansion in magnon volume. These unexpected findings are validated by a detailed analysis of energy and momentum conservation laws. Our results offer a comprehensive framework for understanding the thermal behavior of magnons and their coupling with phonons. These insights are applicable to a wide range of magnetic materials, including ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, and multiferroics, as well as to various experimental techniques such as heat transport measurements, Raman spectroscopy, and ultrafast pump-probe methods. Our findings may also have significant implications for magnonics and magnon spintronics. Finally, we provide guidelines for future research aimed at exploring the complex dynamics of magnon-phonon interactions. Loidreau's code-based scheme relies on the general matrix product (MP) code framework, offering security comparable to McEliece but with significantly smaller key sizes. This paper introduces two modifications to enhance cryptsecurity: the first utilizes algebraic-geometric (AG) code components, while the second employs random code components. We demonstrate that the minimum distance of MP code under the first modification is $r$, which exceeds the distance $r-l+1$ found in the original system. Furthermore, we outline a generic information set decoding attack applicable to the first modification and utilize Magma software to evaluate the complexity of this attack against both systems. These experiments indicate that the original scheme and the second modification offer equivalent security levels, whereas the first modification provides superior security. Finally, we present two concrete instances for the first modification, with the first example exhibiting superior performance compared to existing schemes in both security and efficiency. Additionally, we illustrate that the second modification can be viewed as a specific instance of the first, thereby unifying these two approaches into a single framework. The proposed instances are available on GitHub. Our results suggest that the first modification outperforms the original system in all three metrics—key size, decoding complexity, and decryption time. However, regarding key size specifically, the second modification is only competitive with the original scheme when the parameter $l$ is small. Overall, the first modification represents the most promising approach, offering improvements across all three criteria. We conclude that the first modification is the most effective solution and provide a comprehensive comparison with current state-of-the-art systems. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research. This work was partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 61772002). The full version of this paper can be found in arXiv:1909.00019. This research was partially conducted while the second author was a visiting scholar at the Department of Computer Science, University of Texas at Dallas.

Language models (LMs) are now a cornerstone of numerous state-of-the-art machine learning applications. However, during both training and inference, LMs are prone to errors when encountering rare terms. This paper addresses this vulnerability by introducing a novel pre-training strategy called Dict-BERT, which incorporates a glossary to enhance performance. Specifically, we utilize a BERT-like architecture that integrates a glossary layer to process glossary tokens alongside regular tokens. This glossary layer functions as a lookup table that maps each glossary token to its corresponding entry in a provided glossary. Experimental results on various pre-training tasks demonstrate that pre-training LMs with Dict-BERT yields significant improvements, particularly for rare terms. Furthermore, we fine-tune the pre-trained model on a sentiment analysis task, achieving state-of-the-art results that outperform both BERT and BERT with WordPiece. Finally, we evaluate the model on a clinical text classification task, where it again surpasses BERT and BERT with WordPiece. Overall, these findings indicate that Dict-BERT effectively mitigates the issue of rare terms. The code and models are available at https://github.com/taehyungkim123/DictBERT.

This study examines a random complex $X$ formed by a random spatial point process within a $d$-dimensional compact domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, where $d \geq 2$. The spatial points are connected via an $l$-spannning acycle, defined as a $l$-dimensional subcomplex whose $l$-dimensional homology over a field $\mathbb{F}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{F}$. We demonstrate that if the components of the acycle are selected with equal probability, a typical acycle approximates the boundary of $\Omega$ in volume with high probability. Furthermore, for a random $2$-spanning acycle, we establish that its volume approximates $\Omega$ with probability approaching one as the number of spatial points increases. Additionally, we prove that for any $d$-dimensional compact domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and any $l$ where $d \leq l \leq 2d-1$, the components of an $l$-spannning acycle induce a continuity diagram that is homotopy equivalent to $\Omega$ over $\mathbb{Z}_2$. The findings for $k$-spannning acycles with $k > 2d-1$ remain an open question. These results hold significant implications for spatial point processes, including Poisson processes, as they provide the first existence proof for minimal spanning cycles and offer the first estimates for the volume of points enclosed by these cycles. The proofs rely on novel combinatorial and probabilistic techniques. Spatial point processes serve as fundamental models in various fields, such as biology, physics, and social sciences. A primary objective in this research is identifying the optimal subcomplexes that span the point process. This work introduces minimal spanning cycles and estimates the volume of points enclosed by them. The methodology is applicable to diverse point processes, with a specific focus on the Poisson point process. We derive explicit formulas for the expected volume of points enclosed by minimal spanning cycles as a function of the Poisson process's intensity. The results are also relevant to clustering, where identifying the optimal cluster structure is a critical challenge. We apply our findings to the $k$-means clustering problem, deriving upper and lower bounds for the number of clusters in the optimal solution. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-preserving framework where multiple data owners, each holding data from distinct dimensions, jointly train a machine learning model by aggregating their vertical data. This approach is particularly vital for sensitive domains like healthcare, enabling collaboration while safeguarding privacy. However, VFL faces inherent privacy risks due to data leakage across missing dimensions. This paper introduces the concept of Pragmatic Privacy Assaults (PPA) on VFL, a novel attack method that leverages external data to breach privacy. Unlike prior attacks, PPA utilizes external datasets that are not necessarily related to the target domain, provided they contain information from some unused VFL dimensions. This reflects real-world scenarios where external data sources are abundant and accessible. We demonstrate PPA's effectiveness through experiments on three benchmark datasets, showing that it can achieve high classification accuracy even when using external data from only a single domain. Furthermore, we propose a countermeasure to mitigate PPA, which reduces the model's test accuracy by 10% to 20% across all experimental settings. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi1997/VFL_Privacy.

We calculate the $B$-meson to baryon form factors using QCD light-cone sum rules, incorporating both twist-3 and chiral contributions. Utilizing these form factors, we investigate the $B\to \bar{p}\bar{n}$ process within the dark baryon model, which extends the dark sector framework by introducing dark baryons. Our findings indicate that the two-body $B\to \bar{p}\bar{n}$ decay is feasible if the dark baryon masses are sufficiently low, specifically $m_{\bar{p}}+m_{\bar{n}}<m_B$. We derive the following numerical results for the relevant hadronic parameters: $|\xi_1(0)|=0.32\pm0.04$, $|\xi_2(0)|=0.30\pm0.04$, $|\eta_1(0)|=0.25\pm0.03$, and $|\eta_2(0)|=0.24\pm0.03$. Furthermore, we determine the branching ratio for the $B\to \bar{p}\bar{n}$ channel, finding $\mathcal{B}(B\to \bar{p}\bar{n}) = 1.0\times10^{-3}$ under the assumption of $m_{\bar{p}}+m_{\bar{n}}=1.0\ GeV$. Additionally, we examine the impact of baryon masses on this decay and explore the potential for detecting dark antibaryons through missing energy measurements at the LHC. We conclude that the dark antibaryon mass must be very small, approximately $m_{\bar{p}}+m_{\bar{n}}\sim 1.0\ GeV$, to ensure detectability. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the dark baryon model. This work is dedicated to Professor Shouhuang Xu on the occasion of his 60th birthday. Intelligent Urban Defense (IUD) represents a growing field focused on safeguarding cities through the integration of artificial intelligence, advanced defense strategies, and urban infrastructure. This domain encompasses both adversarial and cooperative interactions among diverse entities, including human and robotic agents, military and civilian organizations, as well as local and national authorities. These interactions occur across spatial, temporal, and functional dimensions within dynamic urban environments. This paper introduces the Intelligent Urban Defense Game (IUDG), a novel multi-agent framework designed to model adversarial scenarios within urban settings. The IUDG is intended to facilitate research into resource management, defense planning, and the development of intelligent agents. Furthermore, it aims to support the training of city protection systems and enable the simulation of diverse urban defense scenarios. We provide a comprehensive overview of the game, including its theoretical foundations, formalization, and specific use cases. Additionally, we outline the user interface and various methods for interacting with the system. The IUDG is accessible at https://iudg.org. We anticipate that this tool will significantly contribute to research in resource management, defense strategy, and artificial intelligence within the context of urban defense.

This study examines a specific class of black stars confined within a cavity, demonstrating that they can undergo Hawking--Page phase transitions. These transitions correspond to the intersections between the thermal equation of state and the energy conservation relation, with the resulting black stars possessing low entropy relative to their cavity radius. Furthermore, by selecting an appropriate equation of state, the analysis reveals the coexistence of multiple phases and first-order phase transitions. This framework extends the traditional Hawking--Page transition, which involves conventional AdS black holes, to encompass black holes with equations of state similar to those of baryonic compact stars. Consequently, this research offers valuable insights into black holes with low entropy and large masses. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings for the black hole information paradox. The theoretical framework utilized is detailed in Section 2.1.1. Additionally, the results presented in Sections 2.1.2 and 2.1.3 are derived from calculations performed by other researchers. Given the significant implications of these findings for the information paradox, it is essential to clarify the origin of these results. Their response confirms that the results in our work were derived from their own computations. We apologize for any confusion this may have caused and have revised the manuscript to ensure a more accurate presentation of the results. In machine learning, ranking algorithms are designed to identify the most probable labels for items within a batch. However, when noise is present in the labeled data, these algorithms may produce erroneous outputs. To address this challenge, we propose a new method called bag sampling and group-based loss (BSGL). This approach is designed to mitigate the impact of noisy data retrieval. We evaluated BSGL across various ranking algorithms and compared its performance against the standard KNN algorithm, which lacks noise-resilience. Our proposed method demonstrates a significant reduction in both false positive and false negative rates. Furthermore, we conducted extensive experiments on the IMDB dataset to validate the effectiveness of BSGL. These results confirm that BSGL enables data retrieval algorithms to withstand noise in labeled datasets. Additionally, the method is computationally efficient, making it suitable for real-time applications. Finally, BSGL is applicable to a broad spectrum of data items, including but not limited to images, videos, text, and objects. To demonstrate this versatility, we also applied BSGL to a new dataset comprising labeled images of various fruits. This example illustrates that BSGL can effectively handle diverse data types, such as objects and scenes. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ahmedmohamed1999/label-noisy-data-ranking. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Label scarcity remains a critical challenge in graph classification. While recent semi-supervised learning approaches have attempted to address this by generating pseudo-labels, they often produce unreliable tags for minor classes, leading to biased graph neural networks. To overcome this limitation, we introduce p2t-GNN, a novel framework designed to learn accurate pseudo-tags and robust representations even with very limited labeled data. Our approach employs a self-play mechanism to generate self-refined tags and utilizes an auxiliary meta-GNN to model the conditional distribution of these tags. Furthermore, we integrate a self-distillation mechanism to ensure consistent tag generation across different models. Extensive experiments across various datasets demonstrate that p2t-GNN outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised baselines. This study investigates the stability of electron bunches undergoing betatron oscillations as they propagate through a high-intensity, fixed-focusing proton driver beam, a mechanism intended to generate novel beam radiation for physics research. We present a comprehensive radiation hydrodynamics code designed to model the co-evolution of radiation hydrodynamics and charged particle dynamics. This framework incorporates the complex interplay of electromagnetic fields, space charge effects, radiation hydrodynamics forces, and self-induced currents. We demonstrate the simulation of radiation hydrodynamics force chains and analyze the stability of intense electron bunches accelerating within a proton driver. Furthermore, we estimate the intensity and spectrum of emitted radiation, specifically focusing on X-ray and gamma-ray ranges, with particular attention to the impact of radiation damping and radiation pressure. Finally, we outline a specific experimental setup for detecting betatron radiation during the upcoming AWAKE Run 2 phase. These findings are intended to guide future experimental efforts to observe and characterize this radiation. Additionally, the developed code is made available for the broader scientific community.

This study introduces a series of algorithms for distributed decision tree learning that adhere to differential privacy principles. These methods utilize the noisy counting query mechanism, where the degree of noise added is governed by a privacy parameter $\varepsilon$. The core challenge in distributed privacy is ensuring that data distribution remains sufficiently noisy to prevent information leakage. We propose a unified framework for these noisy counting query mechanisms, enabling the integration of various distribution strategies to enhance privacy. Specifically, we demonstrate that the exponential mechanism can be applied to the loss function of decision tree splitting to construct algorithms that offer both exponential utility privacy and $\varepsilon$-differential privacy. Furthermore, we develop a privacy accounting method based on advanced composition to establish the exact privacy guarantees of our distributed privacy algorithm. Finally, experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate the theoretical analysis and illustrate the trade-off between model accuracy and privacy levels. Chain event networks are gaining popularity for modeling the interdependent choices people make across a series of sequential decisions. While previous research has focused on either network estimation or framework selection, this study introduces a Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo approach to framework selection. We apply this methodology to a simulated dataset and an eye movement tracking study to demonstrate its effectiveness. The findings indicate that the proposed Bayesian framework selection method performs well, offering a robust solution for choosing between different framework types in chain event networks. This approach enables researchers to identify the most suitable network structure for their specific data and subsequently estimate structure-specific parameters. The method is implemented in the python-package `CHAINR` and is accessible at https://github.com/chainr/CHAINR. Keywords: Chain event networks, framework selection, Bayesian model selection, Markov chain Monte Carlo.

We introduce a robust asymptotic framework to analyze a specific inertial dynamics system, which incorporates a Tikhonov regularization term that diminishes over time. As time progresses toward infinity, this regularization effect becomes minimal. Within the minimization context, this approach is recognized as dynamic regularization. Our analysis demonstrates that the asymptotic inertial trajectory of the inertial system converges to the minimizer of the objective function with the smallest norm. Furthermore, under appropriate assumptions, we establish that the trajectory remains stable and provides a convergence rate for this process. These findings are supported by numerical experiments on a large-scale quadratic problem. Additionally, our results offer a fresh perspective on the equivalence between two prominent continuous-time models for global minimization: the heavy-ball method and gradient flow. Specifically, we illustrate that the trajectory generated by the heavy-ball method can be interpreted as a regularized trajectory, with a time-varying Tikhonov regularization parameter that decreases as iterations advance. This insight enables us to derive novel convergence results for the heavy-ball method that are robust to initial conditions. Finally, we extend our theoretical results to a non-quadratic setting, proving convergence to a stationary point and stability, while also providing theoretical justification for numerical experiments on a large-scale non-quadratic problem. The paper concludes with a discussion on potential future research directions. This work extends our previous study (arXiv:2101.01300). For clarity, we have incorporated several new theoretical results, such as those concerning local convergence to a stationary point, and have expanded the experimental section to include additional numerical tests. This survey examines a surface curvature-driven motion defined as the average of mean and Willmore curvatures, alongside its long-time behavior and asymptotic limits. We provide a comprehensive presentation of the short-time existence theorem, long-time convergence results, asymptotic behavior, and the asymptotic energy estimate that underpins the proof of global regularity. Additionally, we outline a continuum limit result for small mean curvatures, which serves as the asymptotic version of the previously mentioned global regularity result. This paper is primarily intended for mathematicians interested in geometric evolution equations, surface motion, and related asymptotic phenomena. In the final section, we address surface diffusion, a widely studied motion characterized by a purely mean curvature dependence, providing a concise overview of its long-time behavior and asymptotic limits. Given the extensive literature on this topic, our discussion is necessarily selective. We conclude by presenting an open problem. Throughout this survey, references are provided to the extensive literature on the subject. While efforts have been made to ensure accuracy, the author welcomes any corrections or suggestions. This work serves as an expanded and refined version of the author's plenary lecture delivered at the 2019 conference "Asymptotic Behavior of Geometric Flows" in Beijing.

This study introduces GrowSpace, a novel indoor environment designed to discover and execute morphological plant controls. The system integrates a three-dimensional light tower with closed-loop plant growth monitoring and control capabilities. We demonstrate the system's capacity to perform simultaneous morphological and physiological optimizations on a *Brassica rapa* subspecies. These results validate the effectiveness of evolutionary methods in creating complex plant structures and highlight the potential of combining such methods with advanced actuation and sensing technologies to automate the design of plant morphologies for applications including art, architecture, and manufacturing. We establish a conformal gluing theorem for semi-infinite directed correlation functions defined on quantum disks with conformal boundary fields. Leveraging this theorem, we demonstrate the domain Markov property and construct the random line known as Schram-Loewner exploration (SLE) within quantum disks. This approach offers an alternative proof of the existence of the SLE cycle on random surfaces with Liouville Quantum Gravity (LQG) as developed in [DGMS21], alongside providing a concise and self-contained proof. Additionally, we present a novel construction of the space of quantum gravity points on such surfaces. By employing quantum wedge and disk conformal boundary fields, we elucidate the relationship between the SLE cycle and the quantum gravity point. Finally, we offer a new demonstration of the coupling between the uniform measure on the SLE cycle and the uniform measure on the LQG area exponentiated to the LQG parameter $\gamma^2-2$. This specific coupling was previously utilized in [DGMS21] to demonstrate the non-degeneracy of the LQG area. Furthermore, we prove the consistency of the SLE cycle across nested quantum disks under quantum cone measures. These findings extend the framework of [DGMS21] to settings involving Liouville Quantum Gravity with boundary. Throughout the study, we maintain the conformal boundary field formulation for LQG, as introduced in [DS20]. The concepts of conformal boundary fields and their associated correlation functions are essential for advancing the theory of LQG and its interplay with Liouville Conformal Field Theory. Consequently, this paper may serve as a foundation for future research into LQG structures on surfaces with boundary. To facilitate this, we have compiled a collection of technical results within the work. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive exposition of the theory of quantum surfaces with conformal boundary, which is integral to this research. This exposition is designed to be self-contained and accessible to a broad audience. It serves as a valuable resource for understanding the theory and can function as supplementary material for courses or research projects focused on LQG and its connections to Liouville Conformal Field Theory. Specifically, it may be utilized as a textbook for a graduate course on LQG. The material is structured to facilitate a one-semester course, with exercises included to reinforce key concepts. This study investigates $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction off the nucleon, analyzing the recently observed $S_{01}$ and $P_{01}$ partial wave resonances. The analysis employs the relativistic isobar model, which incorporates the N*N*, N*N*dec, and NN*dec channels. To identify the nature of these new resonances, we vary the function of the N*N* dibaryon resonance, a key component in the isobar model. By adjusting the N*N* mass width, we examine the resulting effects on the $S_{01}$ and $S_{01}$ amplitudes. Furthermore, we explore the possibility that these resonances arise from the N*K* and N*K*dec channels. Finally, we compare our findings with experimental data to determine the characteristics of the N*N* parameters that best describe the new $S_{01}$ and $P_{01}$ resonances. Our results indicate that the $S_{01}$ resonance is primarily single-particle in nature, whereas the $P_{01}$ resonance is likely dominated by the N*K* and N*K*dec channels. Additionally, the mass width of the K* and K*dec dibaryons is found to be approximately 100 MeV. These findings offer a viable approach for future analyses of new baryon resonances. We evaluated various OpenCV pre-treatment techniques, including face detection, alignment, cropping, and resizing, applied to 10,000 images from the MORPH-II database. This study examines the distribution of face detection rates and the impact of pre-treatment on the quality of the resulting face images. Furthermore, we explore the challenges associated with applying these pre-treatments to real-world datasets and suggest potential solutions. Finally, the paper analyzes how different pre-treatment methods affect subsequent face recognition systems. Our results indicate that face detection yields a 20% improvement in accuracy, while face alignment provides a 10% boost. Additionally, we recommend that face cropping be omitted, as it does not enhance recognition performance. Our primary contribution lies in establishing a baseline for face detection and alignment using OpenCV on the MORPH-II dataset, offering a reference point for evaluating alternative pre-treatment approaches. This work is especially pertinent for researchers dealing with real-world data, where factors such as poor lighting, occlusions, and image degradation are inevitable. Ultimately, we demonstrate that OpenCV is a highly effective tool for implementing face detection and alignment. The accompanying repository contains our face detection and alignment code, which utilizes OpenCV. While the toolkit offers numerous other pre-treatment options, such as face blurring, we did not evaluate them here due to the absence of specific requirements for their application. It is a well-known phenomenon that including multiplicative features in a linear model results in additive terms within the logistic loss function. This paper examines the inverse scenario, where specific constraints are applied to the linear model to prevent interaction effects in the loss function. We demonstrate that this optimization problem can be transformed into a convex formulation that retains a closed-form solution for the resulting linear model and offers intuitive geometric insights. Furthermore, we extend these ideas to a regularized variant, proving that under $\ell_1$ regularization, the method can be solved efficiently using the proximal gradient method. We also explore the connections between this approach and the "switching model" from piecewise linear modeling. Finally, we validate the method's effectiveness through simulations and case studies focused on gene expression data. A Python implementation is available at https://github.com/akshaykumar1992/avoiding_interaction. The findings presented here originate from a master's thesis by Akshay Kumar.

Headlines serve as concise summaries of news articles, typically positioned at the top of online publications. While manual headline creation is costly, automated systems offer a solution; however, these systems often generate outputs that lack naturalness or fail to align with user expectations. To enhance the evaluation of such automated headline generation, this study introduces a new dataset comprising 1.5 million news articles paired with their corresponding headlines. We train a transformer-based model to classify articles as having human-created or machine-created headlines. This classifier aims to facilitate more accurate assessment of headline generation models, thereby improving user satisfaction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms all baselines, achieving a test accuracy of 90.1%. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/taehyungkim2000/AHEAD. Future research will focus on developing evaluation metrics that correlate more strongly with human judgments. The source code for the experiments can be found at https://github.com/taehyungkim2000/AHEAD. This work was presented at the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. Keywords: Natural Language Generation, News Headline Generation, Automatic Evaluation Metrics.

We present a classical spin model that incorporates both ferromagnetic and frustrated interactions, capable of describing a wide range of magnetic configurations in real materials. By employing Monte Carlo simulations, we identify a unique amorphous state that exhibits nearly perfect chiral order and supports a deconfined chiral spin fluid phase at elevated temperatures. This phase transition is confirmed through the divergence of the magnetic susceptibility and the emergence of a power-law behavior in the two-point correlation function. Furthermore, we observe that reducing the system's dimensionality from 3D to 2D results in a significantly broader paramagnetic regime. Finally, we demonstrate that this paramagnetic phase can be reached within the polycrystalline phase diagram, which contains a first-order transition between a ferromagnetic state and a spin glass characterized by non-zero chirality. These findings suggest that our model offers a viable framework for investigating chiral paramagnetism in frustrated materials. Additionally, the presence of chiral order in the ferromagnetic phase implies that these materials may serve as promising candidates for applications in chiral devices. Our results also highlight the critical role of disorder in shaping the phase diagram and underscore the necessity of considering both quenched and annealed disorder when analyzing the magnetic properties of these systems. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this model to higher-order multipole interactions. Such an extension could offer a unified description of the magnetic phase diagrams for both the frustrated pyrochlore and spinel families of materials. In this scenario, the ferromagnetic phase would evolve into a ferromagnetic quantum spin liquid, while the chiral paramagnetic phase would become a deconfined chiral spin fluid. This latter phase is expected to play a crucial role in the paramagnetic region of the phase diagram, particularly in the presence of disorder. Consequently, the phase diagram would be divided into two distinct regimes: a weak-disorder regime dominated by a ferromagnetic quantum spin liquid, and a strong-disorder regime dominated by a deconfined chiral spin fluid. In the latter case, the transition would be first-order, separating a ferromagnetic state from a spin glass with non-zero chirality. We anticipate that these insights will offer valuable guidance for future experimental investigations into the magnetic properties of these systems. Finally, we note that the phase diagram of the frustrated magnet Tb$_2$Ti$_2$O$_7$ exhibits a striking resemblance to the phase diagram predicted by our model. This paper introduces a calibration strategy designed for wide-field imaging at large-N radio interferometers, such as the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) and the Square Kilometre Array (SKA1). The method's computational complexity scales as $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ for every visibility measurement, where $N$ represents the number of antennas per array. This efficiency is achieved by exploiting the regular arrangement of baselines on a 2D grid, which allows visibilities to be computed in a single pass. The approach is demonstrated using MWA data from the MWA SKA Pathfinder (MWA-SP) experiment. The primary application of the method involves self-calibration, where visibilities are formed between a small subset of antennas, resulting in a computational cost of $\mathcal{O}(K\log{K} \times N_a)$ per visibility. Here, $K$ denotes the number of baselines and $N_a$ is the number of antennas in the selected subset. The study confirms that self-calibration effectively corrects for gain fluctuations in MWA-SP data. Additionally, the paper outlines a roadmap for implementing this strategy in future wide-field radio interferometers. Given that the number of baselines in these upcoming instruments will likely exceed $10^6$, the proposed algorithm is essential for enabling real-time imaging. Furthermore, it can be readily adapted to calibrate polarization leakage and other instrumental effects. The code is accessible at https://github.com/astro-berkeley/calibration. A primary objective of investment portfolio management is risk diversification, which can be achieved by combining assets with low correlation. However, identifying assets with sufficiently low correlations is difficult because correlation is a local metric that fluctuates over time. This challenge is exacerbated in the cryptocurrency market, where the number of assets is large and correlations are volatile. To address this, we introduce a new approach to portfolio diversification utilizing a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). This method involves training a GAN to replicate the joint distribution of multivariate time series based on their individual components. Subsequently, a conditional GAN is employed to generate synthetic data for assets that are conditionally independent. Empirical results demonstrate that this technique effectively identifies assets with low correlation and successfully constructs a portfolio that outperforms the S&P500 index. Furthermore, this proposed method surpasses existing portfolio allocation strategies. Notably, the approach is fully automated, eliminating the need for human intervention. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/akshaykumar12345/ACGAN-Investment-Portfolio. This study introduces a novel Bayesian framework utilizing a neural network to categorize gamma-ray quasars based on their spectral parameters. Such a classifier is essential for future research on the gamma-ray quasar population, which is vital for understanding the evolution of supermassive black holes. We trained a Bayesian multi-layer perceptron to assign quasars to FRB1, FRB2, or no-peak classes, relying on data from the Fermi-LAT catalog. The model's weights are modeled as probability distributions, providing confidence intervals for its predictions. Our findings indicate that this approach outperforms the standard Fermi-LAT catalog classifier, achieving an accuracy of 82.5% with confidence intervals of ±1.5%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Bayesian multi-layer perceptron can effectively identify outliers, such as blazars, within the gamma-ray quasar sample. These results suggest that Bayesian multi-layer perceptrons are highly effective tools for the classification of supermassive black holes. Social media has become a primary channel for disseminating information and connecting with friends and family. For many Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) individuals, these platforms are essential for social interaction and professional advancement. However, current interfaces are primarily designed for able-bodied users, creating significant usability barriers for people with disabilities. This study addresses the specific challenges Deaf and HHH users encounter when creating content, such as posts, photos, and events. By analyzing existing literature and conducting interviews with Deaf and HHH participants, we identified key obstacles and suggested design opportunities to enhance the content creation process. Additionally, we proposed three potential improvements for interface designers and researchers to facilitate greater access to content creation for this demographic. We validated the insights gained from our interview analysis by comparing them with the perspectives of Deaf and HHH practitioners. Finally, we discussed how our findings can inform future research and content creation interfaces, aiming to support more accessible participation on social media. This work represents an initial step toward developing user-centered, accessible content creation tools for Deaf and HHH users. We believe that by integrating their needs into the design process, the broader community can create more inclusive digital environments. To support this, we have made our interview data available to researchers on GitHub. We introduce a unified statistical framework that integrates patient recruitment patterns with longitudinal modeling, offering a comprehensive approach to address variability arising from both patient heterogeneity and the order of their inclusion. Results indicate that the model offers a straightforward and efficient means to characterize the time-dependent effects of gantenerumab on cognitive function. The identification of action landscapes and the pathways connecting critical points along the most probable transition routes are essential for deciphering the mechanisms behind dynamical events. While the instanton method has been widely used to map these landscapes and routes, it suffers from a significant limitation: its findings are highly sensitive to the initial guess of the transition path. This study demonstrates that the global enhancement technique, originally developed for Monte Carlo simulations, can be applied to instanton calculations. The resulting approach, a global-enhancement-instanton method, is shown to be highly effective in revealing the free-energy landscape and the most probable transition routes of dynamical events. Furthermore, the method successfully identifies the critical saddles that define these transition paths. The study also introduces a straightforward criterion for determining the optimal reaction coordinate for describing the transition route. The robustness of this new method is validated by its successful application to two well-known dynamical events: the escape of a pendulum from a metastable state and the phase transition of a Lennard-Jones cluster. Finally, a potential challenge for this method is addressed, demonstrating that it remains effective even in scenarios where the reaction coordinate is not uniquely defined. The proposed method is anticipated to be broadly applicable to various dynamical events. Additionally, the framework is expected to facilitate the discovery of new reaction paths in quantum field theory and chemical reactions. This paper demonstrates that the $L^{\infty}$ approximation utilizing convex envelopes of viscosity solutions for parabolic complex Monge-Ampère and Hessian equations yields approximations for the corresponding very weak viscosity solutions. Consequently, this approach enables the derivation of parabolic Monge-Ampère and Hessian equations as limits of elliptic equations, provided suitable initial and boundary conditions are imposed on the resulting approximations. Furthermore, we establish that the Monge-Ampère and Hessian measures emerging from these limits are independent of the specific choice of $L^{\infty}$ approximations. Finally, we illustrate the application of this method to solve a specific Dirichlet problem within the framework of parabolic complex Monge-Ampère equations. Notably, the derived solution is a very weak viscosity solution that is not necessarily a true weak solution. Additionally, we observe that our methodology is applicable to a broader class of equations beyond just parabolic complex Monge-Ampère and Hessian types. To facilitate these findings, we have also developed a collection of technical tools applicable to various $F$-type equations. These tools are detailed in the current work and a related paper [1].

This paper introduces the concepts of the standard structure space and the standard prime spectrum for groups, which are defined as specific collections of standard subprimenesses. We establish structural properties for this set and provide a characterization based on algebraic conditions. Furthermore, we examine the topology induced by this collection and demonstrate that it forms a Hausdorff space. Additionally, we explore the relationship between this topology and the Jacobson topology, noting that the Jacobson topology is coarser than the proposed structure space topology. The study also presents various examples of groups, their corresponding standard structure spaces, and the sets of J-irreducible closed sets within their Jacobson topology. Finally, we derive the Hausdorff structure theorem for groups, which serves as an analog to the classical Hausdorff theorem for rings. The results indicate that the standard structure spaces of groups are not necessarily Noetherian, although the sets of J-irreducible closed sets in the Jacobson topology possess the Noetherian property. The paper concludes with several open problems. This work serves as a group-theoretic extension of the classical structure spaces and prime spectra of rings.

Keywords: Groups, Standard Structure Space, Standard Prime Spectrum, J-topology, Quasi-Artinian Groups.

Cross-domain text-to-SQL is a widely researched area that has seen limited improvement due to the difficulty of handling both natural language and SQL simultaneously. To address this, we introduce a novel end-to-end cross-domain text-to-SQL model that leverages a supportive task to guide main task performance. This approach employs a meaningful parser to incorporate semantic features into the encoder, ensuring that critical information is retained throughout the process. Additionally, a supportive code generation task, which utilizes semantic features to predict query structures, is introduced. The internal connections between this supportive task and the primary task create a regularizer that enhances the performance of both. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches on both public datasets. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenChen1997/CTSTSQ.

This study addresses secure navigation within multi-robot systems by introducing a risk-averse management approach designed to mitigate collision risks during coordinated movements. The proposed framework utilizes data-driven multi-objective optimization to simultaneously pursue two key goals: minimizing collision probability and reducing navigation time. Specifically, it employs multi-objective optimization to generate a Pareto-optimal set of control inputs, from which the most suitable input is selected for execution. This risk-averse strategy ensures secure navigation while enhancing the flexibility of control input selection. The proposed method's efficacy is validated through simulations of multi-robot scenarios. Results demonstrate that the approach successfully navigates robots to their destinations without collisions and outperforms existing risk-averse methods in terms of both security and agility. Furthermore, the approach is flexible, allowing for the integration of various collision risk estimation techniques. Finally, the method exhibits robustness, maintaining its effectiveness even when collision risk estimates are noisy. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SeongJinKim123/MO-MPC.

We report the detection of a dwarf galaxy within the Andromeda group, designated Andromeda XXV (And XXV), characterized by a notably low central dark matter density. This discovery stems from a deep, wide-field survey of the Andromeda group utilizing the Subaru HSC. We determined the galaxy's distance to be 770.8 ± 1.2 kpc, derived from the distance modulus of its brightest member star. By integrating proper motion data with our distance measurement, we calculated the galaxy's transverse velocity to be 100.0 ± 1.2 km/s. Furthermore, we determined its total mass to be 1.1 × 10⁸ solar masses, yielding a mass-to-light ratio of 1.1 × 10³. Given that the galaxy's luminosity is 1.0 × 10³ solar luminosities, this low mass-to-light ratio implies a minimal dark matter content. Additionally, we determined the galaxy's age to be 10.5 ± 0.2 billion years. We also examined the galaxy's metallicity, finding it to be [Fe/H] = -0.9 ± 0.2. Finally, we analyzed the galaxy's kinematics, noting that its peculiar velocity is 100.0 ± 1.2 km/s, indicating a peculiar velocity of 28.0 ± 1.2 km/s relative to Andromeda. These findings suggest that And XXV is a dwarf galaxy with a low dark matter density, potentially having been tidally stripped by Andromeda. We conclude that And XXV is likely a member of the Andromeda group. This object represents the most metal-poor dwarf galaxy identified in the Andromeda group to date. The identification of And XXV is significant for understanding the formation and evolution of dwarf galaxies. Grant-free non-orthogonal pattern design for massive connectivity scenarios aims to enhance the trade-off between detection reliability and system capacity. This paper introduces a dual-stage genetic algorithm to generate large-scale, low-redundancy, and balanced sets of non-orthogonal patterns. The first stage employs a genetic procedure to create a robust pool of patterns, which the subsequent stage utilizes to design corresponding decoding matrices. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed dual-stage genetic approach yields grant-free non-orthogonal patterns that outperform the best-known state-of-the-art sets. Furthermore, these new patterns enable the detection of up to 1000 users while maintaining a performance comparable to that of theoretically optimal orthogonal patterns. Additionally, the algorithm is highly efficient, capable of producing these patterns in under 10 seconds on a standard laptop. The resulting patterns are particularly well-suited for massive Internet of Things applications. A MATLAB implementation is available for researchers to facilitate the replication of the results.

This study examines the Ma and Bexon (2009) approximation for simulating humid air. While this method offers significant computational efficiency, it lacks thermodynamic coherence. The analysis explores various modifications to achieve thermodynamic coherence, with each variant also demonstrating computational efficiency. Although all variants are thermodynamically consistent, none are thermodynamically coherent. The paper concludes by proposing an ideal approximation for modeling humid air. Additionally, an extension of the thermodynamically coherent variants is developed to simulate three-component liquid mixtures. The work includes detailed discussions on multi-phase systems and liquid mixtures. Furthermore, the author presents a comprehensive collection of exercises and exercises accompanied by solutions, designed to aid learners in acquiring a deep understanding of approximations for humid air and liquid mixtures. These resources are also intended to assist educators in teaching these subjects. The paper is structured into 10 sections, with Section 1 providing an introduction, Section 2 reviewing background information, and the remainder of the document focusing on the analysis of Ma and Bexon's approximation and its thermodynamically coherent variants. The analysis spans various levels of approximation, ranging from those involving only algebraic operations to those incorporating transcendental functions. Exercises and their solutions are presented at the conclusion of each section. The final section of the paper addresses exercises and solutions related to multicomponent liquids. The author intends to expand this work in the future to include exercises and solutions concerning multiphase mixtures. The concept of the "sum" of matroids on a common ground set is extended to a broader framework termed "outer algebra" that encompasses both matroid sums and free sums. This new construction offers a matroidal structure that integrates elements of sums and inflations while providing greater flexibility. Specifically, it enables the definition of homomorphisms between outer algebras, the inflation of such homomorphisms, and a formulation of the strong rank function applicable to outer algebras. Furthermore, this work introduces a formulation of minor-closedness for outer algebras and a corresponding version of the Strengthened Rota's Conjecture. Finally, the paper concludes with several illustrative examples. Keywords: Matroid, Outer algebra, Strong rank function, Minor-closed property, Strengthened Rota's conjecture. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05B35.

This paper introduces a new method for dialogue state tracking that models speech recognition uncertainty using a finite-state representation of ASR uncertainty, specifically the word confusion network (wcn). We demonstrate how to efficiently extract probability scores for potential words from these networks and show that incorporating these scores into an HMM-based tracking framework yields substantial performance gains. Furthermore, we extend the integration of wcn scores into a deep neural network-based tracker, achieving significant improvements in monitored dialogue systems that utilize both an HMM and a deep neural network as state trackers. Finally, experimental results are reported for two real-world conversational systems: a restaurant domain system and a home appliance booking system. In both cases, the proposed method achieves significant state tracking performance gains. Additionally, we observe that the deep neural network tracker is more sensitive to hedges than the HMM tracker, leading to a greater performance improvement from the wcn approach in the deep neural network scenario. Overall, our results indicate that modeling ASR uncertainty via word confusion network scores is a highly effective strategy for enhancing dialogue state tracking performance. To our knowledge, this work represents the first effort to integrate word confusion network scores with neural network-based dialogue state tracking. Our code will be made available upon publication. \footnote{https://github.com/abhishekgupta1995/ASR-uncertainty-for-dsT} \end{footnote}

We demonstrate that the count of $\mu$-stable sheaves on a genus $g$ curve with fixed rank and Euler characteristic can be expressed as the count of $\mu$-stable sheaves on an appropriate genus $g-1$ curve. This count for the reduced curve can subsequently be calculated using the Euler characteristics of certain cohomology groups on the curve, thereby offering a novel approach to enumerating these sheaves. These findings offer a conceptual framework for verifying the author's conjectures regarding the enumeration of sheaves on curves of genus 2 and 3, and they confirm a conjecture by Chen and Guo concerning the enumeration of sheaves on a rational curve. Furthermore, we establish a recursive formula for the count of sheaves on a hyperelliptic curve of genus $g$, which enables an inductive verification of a conjecture by Guo and Li concerning the enumeration of sheaves on a curve of genus $g-1$. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for the count of sheaves on a curve of genus 3. Finally, we provide a conjecture that encapsulates the behavior of our primary theorem. In conclusion, we demonstrate that our conjecture is verified on genus 0 curves and that it offers a comprehensive explanation for the established results concerning the enumeration of sheaves on curves of genus 1 and 2. This framework also clarifies the structure of the expected results for sheaves on a curve of genus $g+1$, given the known results for the curve of genus $g$. Specifically, it predicts the necessary components required to formulate a recursive formula for the count of $\mu$-stable sheaves on a curve of genus $g+1$, assuming the count for genus $g$ can be represented via the Euler characteristics of the cohomology of a complex of vector bundles. We conjecture that this framework will elucidate the structure of the recursive formula for the count of $\mu$-stable sheaves on a curve of genus $g+1$. Consequently, we have developed a computer program to generate the recursive formula for the count of $\mu$-stable sheaves on a curve of genus $g$, contingent upon the count for genus $g-1$. This program will serve as a valuable tool for verifying conjectures and understanding the recursive formula for the count of $\mu$-stable sheaves on a curve of genus $g$, given the count for genus $g-1$. The introduction of novel frameworks for the universal quantum mechanical evolution of systems is examined through the lens of intricacy, a measure that quantifies the complexity of a state's description. A key finding is that the universal intricacy of universal entry is infinite. This conclusion stems from the necessity to manage an uncountably infinite set of possible initial conditions when computing the universal state, which requires addressing the concept of "the intricacy of a set of states." It is demonstrated that the total intricacy of a set of states is finite only if the set is countable. Consequently, the universal algorithm for entry must be formulated as a co-algorithm, consisting of two components: one that generates a countable set of initial conditions and another that manages the remainder. This duality implies that the co-algorithm is inherently distributed. Furthermore, the co-algorithm for entry is shown to be the logical complement of a co-algorithm for rejection. The impossibility of concentrating all initial conditions into a single trajectory indicates that the distribution of pre-images is a fundamental property of the universal map, rather than a specific characteristic of any single distribution. Finally, the co-algorithm for rejection is demonstrated to be equivalent to the universal rejection algorithm proposed by Alberti and Prandini. These outcomes suggest that the rejection principle is an intrinsic feature of the universal quantum mechanical evolution of systems. Additionally, it is established that the universal state describing rejection is independent of the initial condition. Finally, the rejection principle is linked to the non-contraction principle, which asserts that the intricacy of a system never decreases over time. The significance of these principles in the context of the universal quantum mechanical evolution of systems is also explored. (Univ. Access to Local Resources) (Univ. We introduce a general framework for optimally inferring entanglement within arbitrary quantum optical systems. This approach relies on two key components: first, a method to construct the entanglement witness corresponding to any chosen type of quantum entanglement; and second, an optimal measurement strategy for that witness in the input space of a quantum channel. We demonstrate that for most relevant cases, optimal measurements are achieved through standard homodyne detection. Furthermore, we illustrate that this formalism enables the optimal verification of entanglement in non-Gaussian continuous-variable quantum systems. This is a significant advancement over previous protocols, which were limited to detecting only specific forms of entanglement. Our results pave the way for new experimental investigations into the entanglement of continuous-variable quantum systems. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package that implements this theory, allowing researchers to design optimal strategies for entanglement assessment in their specific systems. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of this formalism to other types of resource state assessments. Our findings are particularly pertinent to the emerging field of continuous-variable quantum networking, where resource states play a crucial role. We anticipate that this formalism will facilitate the optimal certification of entanglement and other quantum resources within the photonic channels essential for quantum communication. Specifically, we highlight the continuous-variable quantum internet as a prime example of a resource where this method can be applied. We demonstrate that this approach enables the optimal certification of entanglement in various continuous-variable resources, including Gaussian channels, Gaussian states, and Gaussian unitaries. Moreover, we show that this formalism can optimally certify the entanglement of non-Gaussian channels, states, and unitaries—capabilities that were previously unattainable. These findings underscore the value of our method for advancing the continuous-variable quantum internet and similar quantum communication infrastructures. We also note that our theory can be adapted to optimize the certification of other quantum resources, such as non-Gaussianity and magic. Finally, we emphasize that our approach is applicable to the optimal certification of resources in any specific quantum channel, state, or gate. To facilitate this, we have made our theory accessible through an open-source Python package, which includes examples for optimizing the certification of resources in specific quantum channels, states, and gates. These resources are selected based on their relevance to the continuous-variable quantum internet. We conclude by discussing how this formalism can be extended to other scenarios beyond the ones we have explicitly detailed. Our work is especially relevant to the continuous-variable quantum internet, a resource that our theory can optimize

This study presents a detailed analysis of the characteristics and dynamics of ELM-free plasma discharges on the JET tokamak, utilizing data from over 100,000 discharges. Through systematic comparisons of time-resolved diagnostics, we identify the presence of quasi-coherent, high-frequency ($f\sim$100Hz) oscillations in the edge current profile, which we term "Palm Tree Modes" due to their visual resemblance to palm tree fronds. These modes are observed exclusively in high-performance discharges, appearing either naturally or via lower hybrid current drive (LHCD). They are absent in discharges utilizing Ohmic heating or Neutral Beam Injection (NBI). The Palm Tree Modes exhibit a strong correlation with enhanced edge transport, manifesting as fluctuation amplitudes roughly ten times greater than those in standard discharges. Additionally, they are linked to a significant reduction in the radial width of the edge current profile. We demonstrate that LHCD-induced Palm Tree Modes arise from the resonant interaction between the edge current profile and the fast waveguide mode, which is driven by the non-inductive current deposited by the fast wave. This mechanism is supported by NBI/LHCD switching experiments and current profile reconstructions. We show that LHCD-induced Palm Tree Modes can be suppressed by detuning the edge current profile from the fundamental fast waveguide mode. Furthermore, we establish a quantitative relationship between LHCD power, edge current profile, and Palm Tree Mode frequency. Finally, we propose a model linking Palm Tree Modes to the edge transport barrier and the pedestal structure. These findings offer a potential explanation for the origin of ultra-high-performance discharges in current-profile shaped tokamaks.
