Although pretraining has emerged as a leading strategy for enhancing representation learning, it has not been fully adopted in continuous learning scenarios. This paper investigates the challenges and limitations of applying pretraining to continuous learning tasks, demonstrating that it can be more detrimental than beneficial. To address this, we introduce a fundamental benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate representation learning across both novel and existing tasks. Our experimental results indicate that pretraining fails to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and may worsen overall performance. Consequently, we propose a novel continual learning algorithm that effectively addresses catastrophic forgetting and achieves superior or comparable performance on all tasks relative to competing methods. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ContinualLearning/gradual-compression. This work was presented at the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) 2022. The full paper is available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05162.

This study addresses the challenge of identifying hate speech across multiple social media platforms by utilizing their textual content, images, and hashtags. While previous research has concentrated on binary classification of text and images to detect hate and sarcasm, this work introduces a novel multi-modal model designed to identify specific types of hateful imagery within social media contexts. The proposed framework enables the detection of various image categories associated with racism, sexism, and anti-Semitism. Furthermore, we developed a new annotation scheme to classify specific units of hateful imagery. The results indicate that our model significantly surpasses existing baselines in both accuracy and the granularity of image detection. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approach facilitates the discovery of hateful images that often evade detection by current models. To support future research, we have made our dataset and code publicly available. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1997/UMM-Hate. Interested parties are invited to contact the authors for access to the data. The source code is hosted at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1997/UMM-Hate. This study examines how axonal growth variability influences the structural and dynamical characteristics of random networks comprising Type-I neurons and synapses. To model this axonal variability, we utilize a statistical framework known as extent distributions, which incorporates two key parameters: the mean extension and the coefficient of variation (CV). By analyzing both undirected and directed networks, we demonstrate that increasing axonal extension variability reduces the degree of clustering in undirected networks and lowers the critical CV threshold required for the emergence of small-world topology in directed networks. Furthermore, we find that a higher degree of CV leads to a lower critical coupling strength needed for synchronous activity in these random networks. These findings underscore the critical role of axonal growth variability in shaping network topologies and their functional dynamics. Additionally, we offer a theoretical explanation for how extent distributions affect synchronization, highlighting the significance of mean-field approximations in complex networks. Finally, we validate our results using three-dimensional simulations of networks with realistic biophysical properties. These models reveal that axonal growth variability can significantly alter network structure and dynamics, with potential implications for the etiology of various neurological disorders. Specifically, we show that axonal growth variability can disrupt the development of realistic network topologies and impair dynamic functions, such as information processing. This insight may aid in unraveling the mechanisms underlying diverse neurological conditions, including autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, and epilepsy. Furthermore, it suggests that network interventions, such as optogenetics, could be employed to mitigate the adverse effects of axonal growth variability on network dynamics. To facilitate this, we have developed a user-friendly tool for investigating the impact of extent distributions on random networks, which is available at: https://github.com/leandros/impact-of-extent-distributions-on-random-networks. This open-source software enables researchers to explore how axonal growth variability affects network structure and dynamics. We anticipate that this tool will serve as a valuable resource for the neuroscience community, fostering a deeper understanding of the implications of axonal growth variability in both healthy and pathological neural systems. Program fixes serve as a critical component of software maintenance, typically functioning as negative examples that guide developers in correcting bugs. However, existing research has largely overlooked the potential utility of positive examples for program fixes. This study investigates how to leverage positive examples in bug fixing processes. We introduce the concept of the "helpful repair," a fix that acts as a direct response to a specific bug report. To validate the existence of this concept, we present a dataset comprising 1,000 helpful repairs derived from the NICTA dataset. Our findings indicate that positive examples significantly enhance the precision of bug localization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating helpful repairs improves the precision of fix generation. Additionally, results show that integrating both helpful repairs and positive examples can substantially boost the recall of both bug localization and fix generation. Finally, we explore methods for automatically creating helpful repairs to support this approach. To the best of our knowledge, this paper represents the first investigation into the application of positive examples to bug fixing. The dataset used in this study is available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar1994/antagonistic-patch-creation.

The ability to generate diverse quantum data spectra serves as a valuable tool for investigating data-dependent quantum information processing tasks. This paper demonstrates that the capability region—the set of achievable data spectra—of graphs states can be defined by the convex hull of elementary operations, specifically quantum rotations and quantum deletions. This finding offers a method for characterizing the capability region of any graph state, provided its maximum degree is known. Furthermore, this study establishes that the proposed operations are both necessary and sufficient for generating the entire capability region, thereby resolving an open question posed in our previous work. We also examine the entanglement structure of states arising from these elementary operations and their potential application in designing states with long-range multipartite entanglement. Additionally, we address the issue of target state alignment, showing that graphs can be aligned using an optimal number of deletions equal to the minimum graph cut size. Finally, we outline future research directions, including the development of data-driven quantum algorithms and the application of data spectrum theory to other graph states. This work is based on the research presented in [1].

Furthermore, we analyze flow observables to explore the equation of state (EoS) of nuclear matter. Our results indicate that 3-dimensional flow analysis offers a new instrument for investigating collision dynamics and determining the EoS of matter under extreme conditions. Detecting COVID-19 early is crucial for preventing transmission and ensuring patient safety. While deep learning has shown promise in this domain, it often struggles with data imbalance and the risk of information leakage during training. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel adversarial framework that enables a classifier to identify COVID-19 using chest X-rays while relying on fewer positive cases and safeguarding data integrity. Our results demonstrate that this model outperforms existing methods in both classification accuracy and robustness against data leakage. Furthermore, we highlight the model's ability to generate informative feedback for clinicians, a feature that could assist in future diagnostic decision-making. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/COVID19-Adversarial-Training. Additional code and pre-trained models will be released upon acceptance. This paper investigates the use of graph neural networks (GNNs) for predicting wireless transmission system performance, such as outage probability, within decentralized wireless networks. Specifically, we examine how GNNs can be employed to estimate system behavior in decentralized settings. We demonstrate that GNN-predicted outage probabilities achieve accuracy comparable to traditional methods, which typically demand extensive information exchange and high computational costs. Furthermore, we highlight that these GNN-based predictions facilitate a significant reduction in both information sharing and computational complexity. Our GNNs are trained on a subset of networks using standard data, after which they are deployed to predict outage rates for unseen networks. We show that the necessary graph information for these predictions can be generated locally at each network node in a decentralized manner. Additionally, we confirm that our GNNs maintain high prediction accuracy even when nodes receive noisy or imperfect information regarding their neighbors' transmit powers. Finally, we explore the link between GNN performance and graph properties, revealing that these learned models are particularly effective in wireless networks featuring sparse connectivity graphs. To our knowledge, this work represents the first attempt to develop and evaluate graph neural networks for predicting outage probabilities in wireless networks. Our findings suggest that GNNs hold significant promise for a wide range of prediction and learning applications in this domain. We have made our code and models publicly available to support future research in this area. Our code can be accessed at: https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/SDN_GNN. The study analyzes the temporal evolution of the spatial distribution of homicide incidents in Goias, a Brazilian state, covering the period from 2002 to 2014. By utilizing murder data from the Brazilian Ministry of Justice and Justice Court records, researchers identified 304 crime locations across 79 municipalities. The analysis involved calculating various spatial and temporal metrics, including the Geary's C statistic, nearest neighbor distance, and entropy. Findings indicate that while the state's spatial distribution exhibits two distinct temporal regimes, the entropy of homicide locations remains relatively stable. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that, in certain years, homicide occurrences in Goias are not random but rather follow a power-law distribution. Ultimately, the study concludes that, beginning in 2007, a network of interconnected municipalities emerged, characterized by strong interconnections between neighboring towns. This network structure suggests that criminal networks may be the primary driver behind the observed spatial distribution of homicides in the state. These conclusions are supported by a comparison of homicide rates with other critical social indicators, such as illiteracy, unemployment, and homicide rates in neighboring countries. The paper also discusses the limitations of the study and proposes potential future research directions. This work holds significant value for both government bodies and the scientific community, as it aids in understanding the problem and informing future public policies aimed at reducing murder rates in Goias. Additionally, the study may assist other regions facing similar challenges in formulating effective public policies. The analysis was conducted using methods from spatial statistics, complexity science, and statistical physics. Spatial statistics was employed to identify areas with high concentrations of murders, whereas complexity and statistical physics offered a framework for interpreting the observed patterns. The authors anticipate that this research will inspire further studies on spatial crime patterns, particularly those applying statistical physics methods to analyze such phenomena. The data used in this research is available for future investigations. Finally, the authors acknowledge the limitations of their study, noting that they did not incorporate other relevant social indicators, such as the number of arrests, convictions, or prison populations. They intend to address this gap in subsequent research. The authors extend their gratitude to CAPES (Brazilian Ministry of Education) for funding this project. Additionally, the first author thanks CNPq (Brazilian Research Council) for a fellowship during the study period, and the third author acknowledges CNPq for financial support. The authors also express gratitude to the anonymous reviewers for their constructive comments. This research was conducted during the first author's tenure as a visiting scholar at the University of Oxford

This capability is particularly vital for data generation tasks involving stochastic differential equations. The study provides theoretical analysis regarding noise-responsiveness and challenge adaptivity, alongside a practical implementation of ASGA for adversarial training. Empirical results demonstrate that ASGA surpasses standard stochastic gradient descent in this context. Furthermore, theoretical insights into the dynamics of ascent stochastic differential equations offer a complementary approach for adversarial training. These components collectively establish a robust framework for adversarial training that surpasses existing methods. The Sun's core emits neutrinos and magnetic monopoles, which could be detected by the upcoming space-based axion helioscope BabyIAXO. This study examines the feasibility of observing solar core magnetic monopoles using BabyIAXO, alongside the detection of solar axion neutrinos. We establish a relationship between the monopole production rate and the probability of inducing a monopole event within the detector. Based on axion-neutrino limits established by the DAMIC experiment, we calculate the necessary number of monopole events for BabyIAXO to achieve sensitivity. Our results indicate that while detecting solar magnetic monopoles with a reasonable event count is challenging, the axion neutrino search remains a primary objective for the experiment. Furthermore, we have developed a specialized Monte Carlo code to simulate the axion search process, which will be made publicly available. This tool is designed to support future research into solar axion neutrinos using BabyIAXO. We also explore the potential for cross-experiment constraints, where findings from the solar axion neutrino search could inform the axion coupling constant, thereby influencing the search strategy for magnetic monopoles. Ultimately, this work aims to enhance the scientific understanding of the Sun's interior through the analysis of solar axion neutrinos and magnetic monopoles via the BabyIAXO project. Additionally, the simulation code can be adapted for other experiments, such as XENONnT, to investigate solar axion neutrinos. This paper introduces a new category of self-exciting systems, characterized by a memory kernel that is non-Lipschitz continuous at zero, causing it to diverge to infinity as delay approaches zero. The study provides sufficient conditions for the global Lipschitz continuity of solutions within the associated ordinary differential equations and establishes global Lipschitz continuity for the solutions of the corresponding stochastic differential equations. Furthermore, the paper examines the long-term behavior of these self-exciting systems, demonstrating that both moments and exponential moments of the solution can diverge. Additionally, the theoretical framework is applied to model the dynamics of cryptocurrency trading volume. Finally, simulation experiments are conducted to verify the validity of the established theorems and to analyze the relationship between trading volume and delay. These findings suggest that the proposed novel self-exciting system offers a more accurate description of cryptocurrency trading volume dynamics than traditional financial models. Robotic grasping remains a persistent challenge in robotics, primarily because of the vast array of potential grasp configurations. To address this, learning-based methods have gained significant traction. However, the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality grasp datasets hinders the advancement of these learning-based approaches. This paper introduces DexGraspNet, a novel, high-quality grasp dataset designed to facilitate research into robotic skillful grasping for universal objects. Unlike existing data, DexGraspNet is generated via a high-fidelity physics simulator, enabling the collection of a diverse range of high-difficulty grasp poses. The dataset comprises 1.5 million high-difficulty grasp poses involving 100 objects, with each pose annotated with a 6-DoF pose, a success probability, and a 3-DoF rotation matrix. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of DexGraspNet's unique characteristics and demonstrates its utility by training a neural network to predict robotic skills using the data. This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-adjusted 4D (3D plus respiratory phase) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2 TSE) sequence designed for visualizing the chest and abdomen. The approach combines a variable flip angle (VFA) schedule with a variable readout duration (VRD) echo train to adapt the sequence to free-breathing motion. By synchronizing image acquisition with the respiratory phase, the method mitigates artifacts caused by diaphragm movement and free breathing, thereby enhancing image quality. In this protocol, flip angle and readout duration are dynamically adjusted based on whether the diaphragm is at the end of inspiration or expiration. Specifically, the flip angle is set lower and the readout duration shorter during inspiration compared to expiration. A 2D radial k-space sampling pattern is employed to ensure robustness against residual motion. The sequence was evaluated using both in vivo and ex vivo phantoms. Results demonstrated that the proposed method effectively reduces free-breathing motion artifacts in both scenarios. Furthermore, the technique maintains consistent image quality across different breath-holds, proving its utility for free-breathing imaging in patients unable to perform breath-holds. The study concludes that this free-breathing, motion-adjusted 4D T2 TSE sequence offers superior image quality relative to existing free-breathing 2D T2 TSE sequences. Additionally, the approach is applicable to various 2D pulse sequences, including other T2 TSE variants and potentially other MRI modalities. Future research will explore extending this free-breathing 4D T2 TSE method to cardiac imaging. The technique is currently being integrated into clinical practice for free-breathing imaging of the lungs, liver, and kidneys in patients who cannot hold their breath. Model reduction aims to create compact models that closely mimic the behavior of complex systems. While knowledge distillation has emerged as a leading technique for this purpose, we argue that it often fails to fully replicate the original model's behavior. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel, principled approach for knowledge distillation that maintains the data flow of the complex model. This method involves replacing specific layers of the complex model with the corresponding layers from the simple model. We evaluated this data flow-preserving distillation strategy against standard distillation approaches across various computer vision tasks. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently surpasses traditional techniques, yielding superior performance for image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. CountSketch is a widely used dimensionality reduction method that projects high-dimensional vectors into lower dimensions via random measurements, enabling the exact recovery of sparse and structured vectors from compressed data. This paper investigates the resilience of CountSketch against adaptive inputs, where the vector components are selected by an adversary aware of CountSketch's random projection matrix. Our analysis of this scenario yields both positive and negative findings. On the negative side, we demonstrate that for any fixed CountSketch projection matrix, an adaptive adversary can identify a specific vector that creates an unresolvable collision, rendering perfect recovery impossible. On the positive side, we propose a new randomized CountSketch algorithm that remains resilient to adaptive inputs. This new algorithm achieves a constant relative error guarantee for a broad class of vectors, including those adaptive adversaries can produce. Furthermore, this algorithm is the first to successfully resolve the well-known "randomness vs. randomness" dilemma in randomized algorithms. Specifically, we prove that a single random matrix drawn from our proposed distribution can fool an adversary possessing access to $k$ independent random matrices from the standard distribution used in prior work. This finding establishes the first constant-factor separation between standard random matrices and those resistant to powerful adversaries. Finally, we extend this result to show that our algorithm is resilient against powerful adversaries even when the adversary has access to $k$ independent random matrices from its own distribution that it can query. These findings offer the first constant-factor separation between standard random matrices and those capable of foolling powerful adversaries. Collectively, these results provide the first complete resolution to the "randomness vs. randomness" problem in the context of CountSketch. Additionally, our work offers the first explicit, nearly optimal tradeoff between the number of random matrices required and the robustness against the power of the adversary. This research examines the impact of intermediaries on a two-agent income optimization task. Specifically, it investigates how inter-agent communication influences income optimization and identifies communication strategies employed by high-performing teams. We developed a simulation framework where two agents collaborate to maximize collective income by executing joint actions within a grid-based environment. Utilizing a novel multi-agent version of the Genetic Algorithm, we evolved teams of agents that demonstrated high performance. Our results indicate that for high-performing teams, the most effective strategy involves agents moving toward one another, exploring the grid, and coordinating their actions. This efficacy is particularly pronounced in larger grids, where successful teams exhibit greater patience in searching for opportunities and in pursuing available options. These findings align with prior research on communication in high-performing teams, which emphasizes mutual orientation and active coordination. Furthermore, we observed that performance improves as the agents' field of view expands, though this advantage is more significant in larger grids. Finally, we demonstrate that an intermediary can enhance a team's income by over 20% in larger environments by adopting a more exploratory stance. This enables the discovery of richer areas and reduces the time required to reach them, thereby increasing the frequency of joint actions. These outcomes corroborate existing literature suggesting that intermediaries facilitate better coordination and information sharing. Additionally, we show that intermediaries tend to adopt a more exploratory behavior, which is more critical in larger grids. This occurs because intermediaries spend less time idle and actively search for opportunities, thereby increasing the execution rate of joint actions. Overall, this work provides a foundation for developing high-performing teams through the application of evolutionary techniques. It also establishes a basis for creating new intermediaries that can substantially boost team performance. Finally, our work contributes to the growing field of simulating human behavior, offering insights into the challenges and opportunities intermediaries face when acting as connectors within a team. These insights can guide the creation of more realistic simulation models. To our knowledge, this is the first study to model intermediaries within a team, and it offers valuable insights for future research on intermediaries in human behavior. We introduce the concept of acquisitive summarization, which involves extracting specific text segments during the summarization process to serve as prompts for large language models. This approach enables the model to explicitly acquire and leverage additional semantic information for generating summaries. By utilizing entity-prompts, summarization can be framed as a sequential decision-making problem, where the acquisition of relevant text is integrated into the generation process. We evaluated this method on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, demonstrating that it surpasses existing baselines. This note outlines the key findings from a co-authored research project that extended Rademacher's theorem on the differentiability of real-valued functions to higher dimensions. Specifically, we demonstrated that for an实-valued function $f$ defined on a subset $A$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a nonempty interior, if $f$ possesses partial derivatives that are differentiable almost everywhere within the interior, then $f$ itself is differentiable at a point $x$ (belonging to the interior's complement relative to $A$) provided these partial derivatives are differentiable at $x$. The primary contribution of this work is a novel concept: the differentiability of an $n$-variable function across an expanding sequence of subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$. This notion is equivalent to differentiability on the union of such sequences and constitutes a natural extension of point-wise differentiability. Furthermore, this construction yields a new, streamlined proof of the original theorem. The findings in this note are applicable to any real-valued function possessing partial derivatives, and they generalize to functions with a finite number of partial derivatives, resulting in a novel and distinct approach to the differentiability of multivariable functions. Additionally, it is established that differentiability on an expanding sequence of subsets is equivalent to differentiability on the union of those subsets. This observation facilitates a concise proof of a significant theorem by the second author, which characterizes the differentiability of an $n$-variable function based on the differentiability of an $(n-1)$-variable function. Finally, we present a straightforward application of these results to the theory of partial differential equations. In this application, we assume that for a function $f$ with all partial derivatives, the set of points where $f$ is partially differentiable in at least one direction is dense within the domain. We further assume that for each partial derivative $D_j f$, there exists a sequence $\{A_j^k\}$ of subsets of the domain such that the union of these sequences covers the entire domain, and the collection of all points where $D_j f$ is differentiable along every direction is dense within $A_j^k$. Under these conditions, we conclude that $f$ is partially differentiable in at least one direction at every point in the domain. This result underscores the significance of the differentiability of functions on expanding sequences of subsets, particularly when the union of these sequences forms the domain. This paper introduces a new performance metric designed to evaluate vocal entrainment within dialogic systems. Entrainment is characterized as the propensity for individuals to unconsciously align their vocal traits—such as pitch, energy, and formant frequencies—with those of their conversation partners. The proposed metric utilizes the cross-correlation of specific vocal features to quantify the extent of this synchronization. Furthermore, it incorporates a time-symmetric entrainment assessment to determine if the order of interactions influences the degree of entrainment. The method is applied to dialogue systems that engage in multi-turn conversations with simulated agents. Experimental findings indicate that the metric effectively distinguishes between two system configurations known to produce distinct entrainment levels, demonstrating that the definition of vocal features and the entrainment model yield different insights into dialogue dynamics. These results highlight the method's utility in evaluating simulated dialogue behaviors. The implementation code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andrewdavis10/entrainment.

This paper introduces the Lambda-S1 quantization scheme, which applies a specific one-dimensional topological group action to the coefficients of polynomials representing physical observables. The scheme enables the application of a cut-off rule, converting unbounded physical observables into bounded ones. We demonstrate that this process can be interpreted as a quantization of a symplectic quotient within the coefficient phase space. Furthermore, we establish that Lambda-S1 quantization forms a functorial categorical framework, positioning it as a quantization method in the sense of Grothendieck. This approach extends the well-established Deformation Quantization functor (DQ), which applies to coherent state phase space under a Heisenberg group action. Additionally, we show that the Lambda-S1 action on physical observables corresponds to a Poisson action on the coefficient phase space, thereby inducing a quantization map from invariant equivalence classes of polynomials to constants. Finally, we provide a comprehensive description of the categorical structure of the resulting quantum theory, including its relation to the classical theory and the associated classicalization functor. This structure also encompasses the composition of two sequential Lambda-S1 quantization schemes. We conclude by outlining the construction of a categorical model for quantum regulation using a specific type of product of two Lambda-S1 schemes. This model extends the existing categorical model for quantum theory, which is derived from a commutative quantization scheme. The extension is achieved by utilizing the composition of two Lambda-S1 schemes instead of a single scheme. This work serves as a foundation for future research into quantum theory as a quantization of a commutative quantization of a classical theory. We introduce DUVET, a survey designed to identify and characterize the spatial relationship between star formation and galactic outflows in starbursting disk galaxies. By utilizing high-resolution imaging across multiple wavelengths, we examine how outflows influence star formation within the host galaxies. The survey targets galaxies with star formation rates exceeding 1 solar mass per year, where outflows are most prominent, and leverages the James Webb Space Telescope's superior sensitivity to detect outflow tracers in the infrared. Our initial findings from DUVET indicate that galactic outflows suppress star formation in the outer regions of starburst disks, while the inner regions show evidence of both star formation suppression and enhancement driven by outflows. Ultimately, DUVET aims to provide a comprehensive view of how galactic outflows impact star formation, thereby addressing a critical question in extragalactic astronomy. This paper serves as the inaugural installment in a series detailing the survey's results. The remaining papers will address specific scientific objectives: the first will outline the survey's sample selection and characterization; the second will analyze the effects of outflows on star formation; the third will explore the relationship between galactic outflows and galaxy evolution; and the fourth will summarize the survey's overall conclusions. Collectively, these studies will establish a foundation for future research into the role of galactic outflows in shaping galaxy evolution. This paper introduces a new, integrated approach for simultaneously designing and controlling a robot that climbs its own structure. Unlike previous methods, which address design and control as separate optimization problems, this study employs a unified optimization framework to generate a feasible climbing structure and determine the necessary joint actuation forces simultaneously. The study presents two distinct optimization formulations: the first minimizes the total actuation force required for the climber, while the second prioritizes maximizing the angle of attack. Both models are formulated as non-linear mixed-integer programs. To address the non-convexity of these problems, the authors apply a linear convex hull approximation for the angle of attack constraint and utilize a specialized branch-and-cut algorithm for handling angle of attack variables. Furthermore, a novel algorithm is developed to efficiently manage the large number of binary variables needed to model the equilibrium constraints. The paper concludes by reporting results from a numerical study. Additionally, the work features a video documenting a successful experimental test where a climber ascends the designed structure. The results demonstrate that the proposed optimization method can produce structures enabling efficient climbing, while also highlighting the method's limitations and potential avenues for future research. Finally, the paper outlines how this optimization approach can be extended to design structures capable of supporting multiple climbers. Pre-training deep neural networks has become a standard approach to enhance the performance of various computer vision tasks, including semantic segmentation. Recently, there has been a surge in datasets designed to train networks on depth estimation, a task that is significantly more difficult than semantic segmentation. This study investigates whether leveraging these vast depth estimation resources to pre-train semantic segmentation networks yields better performance than extensive pre-training on established semantic segmentation datasets. Our experiments indicate that pre-training on datasets like Cityscapes, which are common in semantic segmentation research, outperforms training on vast depth estimation datasets. Furthermore, we explore the impact of dataset size and the extent of fine-tuning on target datasets on the final performance of these pre-trained models. Finally, we examine the effects of training on multiple multi-scale images and utilizing an ensemble of networks. The paper concludes with a discussion on the advantages and limitations of both depth estimation and semantic segmentation datasets. The code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available. Kendall's tau is a robust, widely used metric for ranking systems, yet it suffers from significant computational costs. This paper introduces a method that reduces the complexity of calculating Kendall's tau from quadratic to nearly linear. The proposed technique achieves this by deducing the contribution of certain input pairs based on the known contributions of others, thereby eliminating the need to compute their impact directly. This strategy is implemented within the standard stack-based algorithm. The paper provides rigorous proofs for the conditions under which pairs can be deduced and establishes the algorithm's overall time complexity. Experimental results demonstrate that the method significantly improves Kendall's tau computation performance across various real-world datasets. Furthermore, the work includes a Python library with source code for the proposed algorithm, along with a benchmark that confirms its efficiency compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions. The authors conclude that the library effectively enhances computational performance for a range of real-world applications. The rise of self-driving cars has driven significant advancements in automotive technology, particularly in the perception and cognition modules that process vast amounts of data. This paper introduces a novel collaborative framework designed to enable privacy-preserving cognition within automotive networks. The approach employs a model-based method to facilitate cognition between vehicles and infrastructure, utilizing a specific transformation technique to safeguard privacy during data exchange. Finally, the paper concludes that increasing the number of vehicles can enhance coverage, but only when a sufficiently large number of infrastructure nodes is present. These findings provide valuable guidance for the deployment of the proposed framework in actual automotive networks. The rapid advancement of biometric authentication has led to increasingly sophisticated presentation attacks, which bypass security systems by tricking cameras into accepting unauthorized individuals as genuine. To address this, machine learning-based detectors have emerged, yet they are perpetually vulnerable to evasion through adversarial attacks. This paper introduces a novel Vision Transformer-based detector designed to operate without prior knowledge of the target user or the specific attack. Finally, our comprehensive analysis of the proposed model's performance reveals its superior efficiency in both detection capabilities and inference time. Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) has recently demonstrated significant potential for developing autonomous driving systems. However, the inherent complexity of driving environments and the specific constraints of vehicles have made it challenging to design effective agents capable of autonomous decision-making. This paper introduces Pro, a vehicle-mounted system that integrates a deep RL agent with a sophisticated model of the vehicle and its surroundings. We report the detection of narrow-line 21 cm emission from neutral hydrogen (HI) self-emission toward the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20, observed using the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope. This source is a well-known star-forming complex hosting the massive O-type star WR 102, which is thought to be responsible for creating the region. The observed HI narrow-line self-emission indicates the presence of a neutral gas outflow driven by the G176.51+00.20 region. The velocity structure of this outflow aligns with the kinematics of the HI shell surrounding G176.51+00.20, suggesting a common origin. The velocity field of the HI narrow-line self-emission exhibits a butterfly-like pattern, with velocities ranging from 10 to 20 km s$^{-1}$ on one side of the region and $-10$ to $-20$ km s$^{-1}$ on the other. This morphology is consistent with a bipolar outflow, and the outflow's axis is oriented along the position angle of 160$^{\circ}$. The energy required to drive this outflow is estimated at $1.1 \times 10^{48}$ erg, a value that is plausible for a single O-type star. These findings indicate that outflows can be generated by O-type stars even in the early stages of their evolution. Additionally, the HI narrow-line self-emission detected in this study may offer a new method for studying outflows in high-mass star-forming regions. Furthermore, the detection of this emission could facilitate the investigation of outflow properties in regions where no HII region is present. Finally, the study of such narrow-line self-emission may offer a novel approach to understanding the formation mechanisms of HI shells. We demonstrate that a strongly non-deterministic greedy $\beta$-transducer with a gap $e \ge 1$ and output degree $d \ge 1$ constitutes an intermediate $\beta$-transducer, provided its transition matrix is upper triangular. Furthermore, we establish a non-automaton characterization for this class of intermediates by leveraging the properties of generalized Pisot numbers. Additionally, we derive specific criteria for the existence of such intermediates based on number-theoretic conditions. Finally, we investigate the relationship between these non-deterministic greedy $\beta$-transducers and minimally non-greedy $\beta$-transducers. As an application, we characterize a specific subset of intermediates of type $(e, d)$ that emerge as minimally non-greedy $\beta$-transducers. This characterization relies on the rank of the rank of the generalized Pisot numbers associated with these intermediates, offering a broader perspective on this concept. Our findings extend previous results by Akiyama, Frougny, and Sakata, who had previously characterized intermediates with gap $e=1$ and output degree $d=1$ using the rank of the rank function. Additionally, we provide a characterization of minimally non-greedy $\beta$-transducers based on the rank of the rank function, which is motivated by our results regarding intermediates. Finally, we present an example of a minimally non-greedy $\beta$-transducer where the rank of the rank function exceeds 2, demonstrating that the converse of our characterization does not hold in general. This example is derived from a family of Salem numbers, the existence of which is established by Verrill. We also examine the relationship between these families and the integers within the associated $\beta$-expansions. Our work extends the findings of Frougny and Han, who characterized intermediares of type $(e, 1)$ using the rank of the rank function. Finally, we propose an alternative characterization for intermediares of type $(1, d)$, which is based on the Farey distance rather than the rank of the rank function. This approach is motivated by the observation that the rank of the rank function for an intermediate of type $(1, d)$ is precisely equal to its Farey distance. We also provide a characterization of minimally non-greedy $\beta$-transducers in terms of the Farey distance, showing that the converse of this characterization does not hold in general

Deep neural networks are extensively applied across various fields, including image recognition, yet they often suffer from limited generalization when encountering data domains distinct from their training sources. This study addresses this challenge by evaluating three state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques—Domain Adversarial Neural Networks (DANN), Decoupled Domain Adversarial Network (DDAN), and Reverse Gradient Adversarial Learning (R-GAL)—to determine their efficacy in enhancing generalization for novel data domains. The research was conducted on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 benchmark datasets. Findings indicate that these methods significantly boost generalization performance on unseen data, with DANN and DDAN proving particularly effective. Consequently, the results suggest that implementing such approaches can substantially improve the robustness of deep neural networks for image identification in new, unseen data domains. This study offers valuable insights for researchers aiming to enhance the generalization capabilities of their models. Additionally, the accompanying code repository includes a practical implementation of these techniques for benchmark tasks, which may assist other researchers in evaluating their algorithms on similar datasets. This work adheres to the Reproducible Research principles outlined in "Seven Golden Rules for Successful Algorithmic Science" by V. Vapnik and D. Guy.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a leading machine learning approach for processing graph data, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. This lack of interpretability hinders the ability to explain model decisions, a critical factor in high-stakes domains like healthcare and criminal justice. To address this, the paper introduces the Parameterized Interpreter (PI), a framework designed to extract human-interpretable parameters from trained GNNs. These parameters capture the behavior of individual network components, offering a novel method for interpreting graph-based models. The effectiveness of PI is validated through various case studies, including graph classification, node classification, and graph generation tasks. Additionally, empirical evaluations on real-world medical and legal datasets demonstrate that PI achieves a strong balance between interpretability and accuracy. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/Parameterized-Interpreter. The full article can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.01001.

The discovery of multiple substructures within the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 offers valuable insights into formation mechanisms and the initial conditions of its intracluster medium (ICM). Utilizing X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton, we identified three primary substructures: a central bright region (designated S1) and two others (S2 and S3) located to the north and northwest, respectively. We determined that S1 corresponds to the cluster's brightest group galaxy (BGG), NGC 1272, and its associated core. Furthermore, we established that the projected separation between S2 and S3 is 1.2 Mpc, with a three-dimensional separation of 1.6 Mpc. Our analysis indicates that the gas within S2 and S3 is likely part of a merging group falling into the main cluster, while the gas in S1 represents the core's ICM. Additionally, we examined the properties of the NGC 1272 core, finding that its ICM is significantly hotter than the surrounding cluster gas, with a temperature ratio of 1.2. We also detected a 1.2 solar masses outflow originating from the core, which we attribute to a galactic wind. Finally, our study identified a radio source situated approximately 10 kpc from the NGC 1272 core, suggesting the presence of a low-mass active galactic nucleus (LM-AGN). These findings collectively imply that the NGC 1272 core is a BGG exhibiting both galactic wind and LM-AGN activity. Ultimately, this research provides a detailed examination of the substructures in RXCJ0232.2-4420, enhancing our understanding of the cluster's formation process. Future investigations should focus on the interaction between the falling substructures and the NGC 1272 core, as well as the impact of these interactions on the cluster's ICM. This study serves as a foundation for subsequent research into the cluster's formation and evolution. (Abridged)

Legendre Memory Module (LMM) is a recently introduced memory architecture designed to enhance Transformer performance through efficient, high-capacity, and parameter-agnostic memory banks. Despite its effectiveness, training LMM remains computationally intensive, creating a significant barrier to entry. This work addresses that hurdle by introducing a parallel training framework that leverages multi-GPU computing. The proposed method demonstrates substantial speedups, achieving a 3.5x improvement over single-GPU training on large models. Furthermore, the approach scales effectively across multiple GPUs, with models of varying sizes exhibiting near-perfect efficiency. Additionally, the framework supports mixed-precision (FP16) training, which lowers memory requirements and further accelerates the process. Experimental results indicate minimal accuracy loss when compared to single-GPU baselines. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepPulseAI/Parallel-LMM-Training. This project was developed in collaboration with DeepPulse AI.

We present a model where participants from two distinct groups engage in a labeling task. Each time a pair meets, they assign labels to one another and gain utility based on consistency; however, their individual strategies depend on whether they belong to the same group. Participants draw labeling strategies from a pool of migrating agents, where the pool's composition evolves based on pairwise utility. This mechanism creates a feedback loop between the participants and the agent pool. Through simulations, we demonstrate that the distribution of labeling strategies within the pool varies according to the utility function, even though the system does not always reach linguistic consistency. Furthermore, we show that pairs of pairs can form cliques that become isolated from the rest of the system, resulting in multiple distinct labeling strategies within the agent pool. These findings highlight the potential for bias in labeling processes and suggest that the underlying mechanisms are more complex than previously assumed. Finally, we outline several avenues for future research. This work is situated within the broader field of multi-agent systems, a domain where understanding how agents communicate and reach consensus is a primary research objective. Specifically, our study addresses the issue of vocabulary evolution, a topic that has received limited attention in existing literature. Our approach differs from prior research in that we do not model agents as learning to adapt their vocabulary to specific interlocutors; instead, we examine how an agent pool's vocabulary composition changes in response to consistent labeling behaviors. We believe this perspective offers a valuable avenue for advancing our understanding of how vocabularies evolve. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work, Section 3 presents our model, and Section 4 details our experimental results. Given space constraints, we have omitted several figures and detailed explanations from the original paper. Additionally, we have translated all Japanese text into English, as the original authors wrote in Japanese. Finally, we acknowledge that this paper is a direct translation and do not claim originality regarding the underlying research concepts. We hope this work inspires future research in this area. This study investigates a coupled system of undamped wave equations for two strings, where one string features degraded Kelvin-Voigt damping confined to a specific sub-interval. This localized damping mechanism involves the relative velocity between the string and its neighbors (displacement gradient) alongside the damped string's actual velocity (derivative with respect to time). We establish stability results for the system by demonstrating that solutions converge to their steady states in an exponentially weighted $H^1$-norm. The analysis covers three specific scenarios: localized damping on a sub-interval with connections via undamped Dirichlet-Neumann, constant-coefficient damping across the entire interval, and nonconstant-coefficient damping over the full interval. Furthermore, we extend these findings to interconnected systems of damped heat equations. In these coupled heat systems, the Kelvin-Voigt damping is applied to a subset of strings, resulting in a damping term proportional to the sum of the time derivative of a specific string's temperature and the time derivatives of its neighbors' temperatures. For these heat systems, we prove exponential stability. Finally, we illustrate how our results apply to coupled thermoelasticity models. To achieve this application, we adapt the thermoelastic equations to incorporate the Kelvin-Voigt damping term as described above, thereby ensuring the stability of the coupled thermoelastic system. This work extends the findings of [11] and [12] to interconnected problems. Additionally, it is important to note that the Kelvin-Voigt damping mechanism is applicable to various physical models, including thermoelasticity, viscoelasticity, and other coupled systems. However, this paper specifically addresses its application within coupled thermoelasticity frameworks. In safety-critical domains, the ability to explain a model's behavior is as vital as the model itself. This paper introduces a hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) framework designed for explainable decision-making in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). The proposed method, Explainable Model-driven HRL (EM-HRL), utilizes inductive logic programming to explain both the high-level and low-level controllers within the hierarchy. We demonstrate this approach across two benchmark datasets, showing that the proposed explanations are faithful and accurate. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the explanations generated by our method. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/akshaykumar1997/explainable-model-driven-hrl. Our findings indicate that the explanations produced by EM-HRL are actionable, fair, and faithful. Additionally, the explanations for the low-level controllers are minimal and precise. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first application of model-based HRL to explainable AI. The paper also discusses the advantages and limitations of this work. Source code and detailed results are available at https://github.com/akshaykumar1997/explainable-model-driven-hrl. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion on future research directions. This work falls under the categories of Machine Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and Explainable AI. Asymmetric light-matter interactions are fundamental to numerous quantum technologies, including unidirectional coupling between optical modes and qubits, which drives applications like nonreciprocal quantum communication and asymmetric spontaneous emission. Typically, achieving low-light-level asymmetry requires either a physically asymmetric environment or an externally applied magnetic field. In this study, we demonstrate that quantum compression can induce an intrinsic optical asymmetry within an asymmetrically detuned cavity-QED system. By integrating a single atom, a three-level V-type emitter, and a two-level emitters representing a mirror, we show that compressing the atomic excitation population in one direction generates an effective magnetic field, thereby producing nonreciprocal light-matter coupling. Furthermore, we illustrate that this compressive bias can be reset after detecting a compressed state, allowing for the dynamic control of nonreciprocity. These findings establish a new pathway for achieving low-energy optical nonreciprocity without requiring external magnetic fields. Additionally, the proposed scheme can function as a nonreciprocal photon detector and a switchable unidirectional emitter, offering potential applications in quantum communication and quantum memory. This approach leverages the inherent nonlinearity of atom-light interactions, which can be amplified through quantum compressive squeezing. Our results highlight the significant potential of quantum compressive squeezing in advancing low-energy nonreciprocity research. Finally, we outline the experimental requirements necessary to validate this proposal. The theoretical framework developed here can also be adapted to other quantum systems, such as cavity optomechanics. These outcomes underscore the critical role of quantum compressive squeezing in advancing low-energy nonreciprocal quantum technologies. We introduce a novel direct detection experiment designed to identify spin-dependent interactions within nucleons, utilizing $\text{Li-6}$ as a key target. This proposed setup employs a dilute gas of atomic Li-6 confined in a magnetic trap, offering exceptional sensitivity to scattering off nucleons. Furthermore, this approach enables direct comparison between proton and neutron spin-dependent cross sections, a capability that will significantly advance the field of direct dark matter detection. We provide a comprehensive sensitivity projection for the experiment, titled SpinTrap, and demonstrate that it can surpass existing limits on the proton spin-dependent cross section by more than a factor of ten. Additionally, we illustrate that the experiment could observe a WIMP with a mass of approximately 100 GeV, featuring a neutron spin-dependent cross section of roughly $10^{-39}$ cm$^2$. These findings are based on an analysis of 100 kg-days of data collected with an energy threshold of 1 eV. We also explore strategies to enhance sensitivity, such as utilizing isotopically enriched $^6$Li and incorporating multiple detectors to mitigate background noise. Ultimately, we conclude that SpinTrap has the potential to become a leading direct detection experiment in the upcoming decade. Blind image restoration (BUR) is a challenging task that seeks to recover an image from a low-quality observation without knowledge of the specific degradation process. This paper introduces a novel approach to address a specific BUR challenge: restoring an image that has undergone a blend of two distinct degradations, where both the blend proportions and the individual degradation parameters are unknown. To solve this, we propose a new kernel mixture degradation model and develop a parameter estimation method based on maximum likelihood. Furthermore, we present a robust algorithm designed to simultaneously estimate the mixture proportions, denoise the input image, and restore the final output. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques across multiple benchmark datasets. This paper introduces two sets of nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations, which serve as nonuniform deformations of the associative Yang-Baxter equation. Each set comprises equations corresponding to either the classical or the modified classical Yang-Baxter equations. The authors provide several illustrative examples and establish multiple instances of the Drinfel'd property for the solutions of the associative Yang-Baxter equation. Specifically, if $G$ is a finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero and $r$ and $t$ constitute a non-degenerate solution to the second set, then $r+t$ satisfies the classical Yang-Baxter equation. Furthermore, the associative $r$-matrix constructed by A. Alekseev and Y. Zhang yields a $G$-matrix for the Hopf algebra $U(\mathfrak{g})$. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the classical $r$-matrix derived from this $G$-matrix resides within the image of the universal $R$-matrix. Finally, the study confirms that the $R$-operator originating from this $G$-matrix is a projective representation. These findings generalize and extend several existing results in the literature. The terminology "nonuniform" is employed because the authors utilize arbitrary commutative algebras rather than fields of characteristic zero. This approach broadens the scope of numerous other results, generating new findings and extending previous work. Specifically, it is shown that if $r$ and $t$ form a non-degenerate solution to the second set over a commutative algebra $A$, then $r$ generates a non-unital Hopf algebra structure on $A\otimesU(\mathfrak{g})$. Consequently, the $r$-matrix for this Hopf algebra satisfies the associative Yang-Baxter equation. This result extends the work of Alekseev and Zhang, who established the same finding specifically for algebraically closed fields of characteristic zero. The authors anticipate that these results will prove valuable in the study of noncommutative geometry. To avoid such confusion, the term "generalized" is proposed as a more accurate alternative. This paper presents a formal framework for reasoning about the correctness of imperative programs based on the logical structure of natural language descriptions. Within this framework, program specifications are modeled as formulas in first-order logic, which are integrated into an extended variant of Hoare logic. The approach supports assertions containing universal and existential quantifiers and employs scope markers to define the semantic scope of noun phrases. A key innovation is the introduction of scope-sensitive modal operators that interact with these markers to represent scope descriptions. The proposed framework serves as a foundation for formally validating programs derived from natural language specifications. Furthermore, it informs the design of tool support, which includes automating the translation of scope-insensitive natural language sentences into first-order logic formulas. Finally, the paper reports on the formal validation of examples from existing literature and addresses current limitations of the approach. To facilitate this, all definitions and proofs have been mechanized using the proof assistant Isabelle/HOL. The paper includes annotated references to the corresponding Isabelle/HOL files. Additionally, we outline a research agenda for advancing formal methods in natural language reasoning and specify the tools available to assist with this work. This study examines the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid membranes. We begin by analyzing literature data to evaluate the validity of the commonly cited monotonic relationship, in which the bending modulus increases linearly with cholesterol concentration up to 30–40%, after which it plateaus. Our analysis indicates that this traditional view is flawed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the apparent contradiction between recent findings and established theory can be resolved by adopting an alternative perspective: cholesterol may induce phase separation, generating distinct domains with differing lipid compositions and consequently, varying bending moduli. This "two-fluid" model offers a more accurate representation of the system and provides a framework for interpreting recent experimental data. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for future research. These discussions are grounded in both our own investigations and the work of other groups, which have employed a wide array of methodologies, including molecular dynamics simulations, NMR spectroscopy, microrheology, micropipette aspiration, and molecular dynamics simulations utilizing experimentally derived potentials. The resulting diverse and complex dataset underscores the need for continued and innovative research efforts. This article is intended to stimulate further inquiry into the role of cholesterol in lipid membranes. To support this, we provide supplementary material featuring new molecular dynamics simulations of a ternary mixture of DOPC, DOPI, and cholesterol. These simulations explore the effects of cholesterol on a membrane composed of two lipid types with similar head groups but distinct tail structures, yielding results that align with experimental observations. Additionally, we present a detailed comparison of two ternary mixture systems, one of which has been the subject of prior research. This analysis aims to offer a comprehensive overview of the current state of the field and to stimulate future investigations into cholesterol's role in lipid membranes. Our findings suggest that the current understanding of cholesterol's effects is incomplete, and that the existing body of research is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions. We hope this work will inspire further research to address these gaps. We examine the Hamiltonian constraint within the loop quantum gravity framework utilizing the ADM Hamiltonian. Under this approach, we demonstrate that certain operators, including the area and volume, are not well-defined. Furthermore, we establish that specific kinematical states fail to satisfy the necessary requirements for the nullity of the Hamiltonian constraint. Finally, we highlight the problem of operator overcounting and propose a potential resolution to this issue. These findings are also applicable to the Ashtekar variable Hamiltonian. The current study serves as a foundation for future investigations into the Hamiltonian constraint, specifically regarding operator definitions and their action on states. Additionally, it paves the way for exploring quantum dynamics and the physical sector of the theory. The analysis presented here is conducted within the simplified kinematical Hilbert space. Consequently, the results may be influenced by the choice of inner product, a factor that warrants further examination. Ultimately, we believe these outcomes are also relevant to the physical sector. The present work functions as a preliminary report, with a more comprehensive study to be published separately. The Auger Collaboration maintains a registry of all ultra-high-energy cosmic particles with energies exceeding 10^17 eV detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory during Phase I of its operations. This document is intended to assist future researchers in efficiently locating data regarding specific celestial events. The publication includes the registry itself, along with examples demonstrating how to utilize it to retrieve data for specific particle events. Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous computer vision tasks, yet their predictions lack reliability in challenging scenarios. To address this, we propose a Bayesian approach to uncertainty estimation for industry-standard detectors like Faster R-CNN and YOLOv3. By employing Monte Carlo (MC) dropout, our method efficiently generates uncertainty metrics for both bounding boxes and classification, specifically calculating prediction uncertainty and missing uncertainty. These metrics are demonstrated to outperform existing techniques in accuracy and robustness, particularly within difficult scenes. Additionally, we introduce a new uncertainty metric designed to evaluate the consistency of detected objects, showing that it enhances the reliability of bounding boxes. The entire framework is fully automated, requiring no manual tuning or retraining of pre-trained models, making it highly suitable for practical deployment. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1996/BayesOD. Video demonstrations can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=42222222222222222222. Finally, we present a benchmarking suite to facilitate future comparisons of uncertainty estimation methods for deep object detectors. To our knowledge, this is the first study to offer such a comprehensive and automated solution for uncertainty analysis in these detectors. The suite is available at https://github.com/ChenYi-1996/BayesOD. Given its broad applicability, it is expected to be valuable for various computer vision tasks. The suite is released under the MIT License. For further details, visit https://github.com/ChenYi-1996/BayesOD.

Accurate short-term traffic prediction is essential for effective traffic management. This study introduces a novel approach for short-term speed forecasting by analyzing local traffic patterns. We break the historical speed sequence into short segments, or snippets, and model the conditional probability distribution of future snippets based on initial ones. To handle limited data, we employ a nonparametric model using a Gaussian basis function to approximate this conditional probability. For prediction, we sample from this estimated distribution to generate a future speed sequence. The results demonstrate that our method surpasses both a Damped Random Walk baseline and an autoregressive LSTM-based approach. Furthermore, we show that the performance of our proposed model is highly sensitive to the length of these snippets. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenWang1995/TrafficPrediction}. Given its ability to model local traffic patterns, this model holds significant potential for application in smart city infrastructure. \textbf{Keywords}: Short-term Traffic Prediction, Density Estimation, Nonparametric Model.

This study introduces a novel deep learning approach for segmenting the hippocampus in MRI scans of patients suffering from epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. The proposed framework is designed to handle the inherent challenges of these pathologies, specifically addressing hippocampal deformations caused by disease progression and the difficulty of training deep networks on limited data. To this end, we developed a multi-branch deep convolutional neural network architecture featuring three distinct feature extraction layers. Each layer utilizes a ResNet-based encoder to capture diverse features, which are subsequently fused and processed by a decoder to generate segmentation maps. Experimental results on both 2D and 3D MRI data demonstrate that our multi-branch encoder architecture yields superior performance compared to established single-branch networks like U-Net and FCN. Furthermore, the model achieves state-of-the-art outcomes when evaluated against other leading segmentation techniques. We examine the Pigeonhole phenomenon, which is typically explained using a classical framework involving indistinguishable particles occupying distinguishable modes. By contrasting this approach with a quantum one featuring both particle and mode transversal profiles, we analyze the discrepancy between the two theories. The classical model predicts an $N-1$ power law for particle distribution probability across $M$ modes, causing certain probabilities to approach unity and result in a catastrophic collapse where all $N$ particles occupy all $M$ modes. In contrast, the quantum approach demonstrates that particle distributions remain bounded by the single-particle distribution, even in the limit of infinite $N$. This occurs because the phenomenon is governed by overlap integrals between mode wavefunctions, which are constrained by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Consequently, the quantum theory avoids total collapse, with particles occupying a significantly larger number of modes than their classical counterpart. Furthermore, we show that the classical picture accurately describes the distribution of the most probable particle only when the mode number is low. As mode numbers increase, the classical prediction for this specific particle begins to deviate from quantum predictions, with the distribution becoming broader and shifting toward higher mode indices. Finally, we explore the underlying causes of this catastrophic occupation of all modes. We demonstrate that the phenomenon can be understood through the lens of a single-particle density matrix, which reveals that all particles are delocalized across all modes. This delocalization is further supported by a Fourier transform of the wavefunction, which indicates that particle momentum is highly localized at zero. These findings are illustrated using the well-known example of bosons distributed across two energy levels. Our results indicate that the classical description of the Pigeonhole phenomenon is valid only under specific conditions of low mode and low particle numbers. In regimes of higher mode or particle counts, it is essential to account for the transverse profiles of both particles and modes. Ultimately, this paper aims to clarify the origins of the Pigeonhole phenomenon and its associated paradoxes. Our analysis reveals that the phenomenon stems from the inherent limitations of the classical model, which fails to capture the full complexity of particle-mode interactions. By incorporating both transverse profiles, we provide a more comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon and its relation to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. We also examine the role of entanglement in this process, highlighting its significance in both the classical and quantum descriptions. This study investigates the transport of cosmic ray protons within low Earth orbiting satellites. We developed a three-dimensional Monte Carlo model that incorporates the complete magnetic field of the Earth, as measured by the International Geomagnetic Reference Field (IGRF), alongside the interplanetary magnetic field transmitted from the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) satellite. The interplanetary field is assumed to be uniform throughout the modeled space. Our simulations track the scattering of cosmic ray protons as they traverse the IGRF and ACE magnetic fields, accounting for solar modulation and the Parker spiral configuration of the latter. We present sample trajectories of captured cosmic ray protons and compare our model's results with data from the CRRES satellite. The captured particles are predominantly protons with energies below 10 GeV. Our findings indicate that the model accurately reproduces the cosmic ray spectrum observed by CRRES. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Parker spiral significantly influences the captured particles, whereas the specific configuration of the Parker spiral does not. Additionally, we show that the model successfully replicates the temporal variations in the captured particle flux caused by geomagnetic field fluctuations recorded by CRRES. Finally, we illustrate how the model can be utilized to predict captured cosmic ray protons for future missions, such as the International Space Station. These predictions can aid mission planners in scheduling maintenance and inspections during periods of low geomagnetic activity. We also provide a user-friendly interface for the model, enabling mission planners to easily forecast particle fluxes for their missions. This capability is particularly valuable for assessing the potential impact of particle flux on satellite electronics. The model is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1984/CRRES_Captured_Particles. The source code is released under the GNU General Public License v3.0. The user interface can be downloaded from https://github.com/abhishekkumar1984/CRRES_Captured_Particles/tree/main/CRRES_Captured_Particles_GUI. The model is open-source, allowing users to modify the code to suit their specific missions. To do so, one must download the source code, input the satellite's orbital parameters, and specify the desired simulation duration. The model will then output the captured cosmic ray protons for that satellite. The simulation can be extended to include other magnetic field components, such as the external field, and the model can be adapted to capture particles for multiple satellites simultaneously. Furthermore, the model can be expanded to capture additional particle species, including electrons, heavy ions, and other charged particles

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently become a cornerstone of machine learning, offering a universal framework for solving general graph problems. However, existing GNN architectures often suffer from limitations in depth, generalization, and scalability. This paper introduces the Local Structure Link Rewiring (L-LRWIR) principle, which enables the transformation of arbitrary graphs into a universal pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton. This approach offers a novel perspective for re-architecting GNNs, facilitating the creation of deeper, more generalizable, and scalable models. We present the Pyramid-like GNN (P-GNN), a framework based on this design principle, and validate its efficacy through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. This note presents the Huber framework, a general method for privately fulfilling low-rank matrices. Given a matrix $M$ that is a linear combination of a known set of low-rank matrices $\{M_1, \ldots, M_k\}$, the objective is to output an approximation of $M$ with $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy. We establish an upper bound on the privacy error for our algorithm, which is nearly tight. Furthermore, our result improves upon prior work by Duchi et al. (2013) across a broad spectrum of scenarios. Our findings demonstrate that, up to logarithmic factors, the necessary sample size to fulfill $M$ privately via the low-rank property is equivalent to the sample size required to privately compute each individual coefficient of the linear combination. Additionally, we provide an explicit expression for the algorithm's output error. Finally, we extend the result to handle $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy. To our knowledge, this work represents the first application of the "Duchi mechanism" to matrix fulfillment. The term "Duchi mechanism" honors the method introduced by Duchi et al. (2013) for private matrix completion. Our framework also encompasses and surpasses several previous results, including those by Duchi et al. (2013), Balle et al. (2019), and Balle and Peron (2020). The term "matrix fulfillment" is employed here to differentiate from "matrix completion," which typically refers to recovering a matrix from a subset of its entries. The term "fulfillment" is used to emphasize that the exact values of the matrix entries are not required; rather, the matrix must be expressible as a linear combination of the given set of low-rank matrices. This broader scope is more practical, as it allows for the use of readily available basis matrices without the need to estimate them. The term "coefficient" is used to denote the weights associated with each low-rank matrix in the linear combination. These terms are adopted to prevent confusion with existing literature. The term "approximation" is utilized to denote the output of the algorithm, which is intended to be nearly as close to the target matrix $M$ as possible. The Attenuation, Emission, and Polarization (AEP) characteristics of the diffuse interstellar medium (ISM) are primarily driven by dust grains with a diameter of approximately 0.1 micrometers. These grains are categorized into two distinct populations: large grains, which are predominantly silicates and have diameters exceeding 0.1 micrometers, and small grains, which include atomic hydrogen, crystalline silicates, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) with diameters under 0.1 micrometers. The latter group is characterized by a size distribution peaking at 0.02 micrometers and a complex internal structure. This review examines the theoretical and observational foundations of the small grain category, with a specific focus on PAHs. It details the most recent observational findings, including the polarization of diffuse starlight, the identification of new emission bands, and the discovery of a new PAH emission component. Furthermore, the review outlines the current understanding of dust properties, such as the size distribution, polarization fraction, and chemical composition. Finally, it addresses the primary unresolved issues in the field and suggests potential future research directions. The discussion emphasizes the need for a more comprehensive and unified theoretical framework that integrates the attenuation, emission, and polarization properties of dust in the diffuse ISM. To achieve this, we present the Astrodust+PAH framework, which represents a significant advancement in modeling dust properties. This approach offers a substantial improvement over previous models by incorporating a more realistic description of grain size, shape, and internal structure. The Astrodust+PAH framework is available for download at https://github.com/astrodustpluspah. Its accuracy has been validated against a wide range of observational data, including ISM polarization maps, extinction curves, and PAH emission spectra. The Astrodust+PAH framework is a crucial step toward a more complete and unified understanding of dust properties in the diffuse ISM. It will facilitate a more accurate interpretation of observational data and provide a foundation for future research on dust in the interstellar and circumstellar environments. Additionally, the Astrodust+PAH framework can be utilized to investigate the physical and chemical properties of dust in the diffuse ISM, as well as to model the evolution of dust in the early Universe.
