The $\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$-invariant volume element on the Siegel upper half-plane of order 2 serves as a real anchor for the complex weighted moduli space of five points, five-line configurations, and quiver representations. We demonstrate that the $L^2$-Hitchin section, which extends beyond the authentic Jacobi elliptic function, serves as a theoretical foundation for the Bloch--Goncharov regulator. Furthermore, we provide an explicit formula for this section using a non-normalized trace form and explore its relationship with the geometric Langlands program. Additionally, the residue at infinity of the second derivative of the Hitchin section yields the volume of the maximal compact subgroup of the Jacobi group, while its value at zero corresponds to the volume of the special fiber of the special compact Jacobi group. We offer a geometric interpretation of this special fiber, which arises as the limit of a toric degeneration of $\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})/\mathbb{H}$ as the toric variety $\overline{\mathbb{P}}^2$ acquires nine ordinary double points. This fiber constitutes a toric boundary degeneration of a compact Lie group, a structure that appears novel. This result is achieved through a geometric construction of a compact Lie group modeled on a torus that incorporates a logarithmic coordinate. We also present an algebraic description of this fiber as a contractible affine variety and calculate its volume using a specific integral. This integral emerges as the residue of a meromorphic 1-form on a compact Riemann surface of genus 2, featuring a single pole with a logarithmic singularity. We link this to a one-dimensional component of the Bloch--Connes regulator within the Chen--Ihara framework. Finally, we examine the vanishing of this integral through the lens of the cohomology of contractible varieties and its connection to the vanishing of the second cohomology class of a contractible solvable Lie group. This approach also clarifies the relationship between the Jacobi section and the second cohomology class of the five-line bundle. These findings may have broader implications for the cohomology of solvable Lie groups and the geometric Langlands program. The methods employed here are also applicable to other boundary values of the $\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$-invariant volume form on the Siegel upper half-plane of order 3 and higher. Confrontational Networks (CN) are a deep generative framework designed to map the latent representations of one probabilistic model into another, facilitating the analysis of discrepancies between these models. This process is valuable for detecting biases within trained models and enhancing the interpretability of their decision-making processes. While current methods typically conflate the adversarial networks' internal features with the semantic data they represent, we introduce a space conditioning technique for Confrontational Networks that decouples this hidden space from the data semantics. We demonstrate the application of this method to identify implicit racial biases in image classification models. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms previous techniques in uncovering these biases. Furthermore, we show that the proposed method can disentangle the latent variables of the generated CN model, offering greater insight into the conflicts between the two interacting probabilistic models. Finally, we validate the method's utility for creating synthetic data by training a classifier on images generated via a Confrontational Network. The code is accessible at https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez/Space-Conditioning.

Phase samplers are compact, high-performance devices that generate a sequence of uniformly spaced phases for use in modulators. In this work, we examine various approaches to designing such samplers to support hierarchical sampling for complex waveform generation. We specifically address the application of hierarchical sampling to optical coherent communication systems, which demand high sampling rates and waveform complexity to accommodate diverse channel conditions. A key challenge in this area is minimizing the number of distinct samplers required to synthesize a specific set of phases. We analyze multiple methods for selecting both the samplers and their selection patterns, evaluating each based on computational complexity and the total number of samplers and selection patterns needed. Furthermore, we consider practical constraints such as the availability of pre-defined samplers and their compatibility with existing selection patterns. These factors are applied to determine the minimum count of samplers necessary to support a specific communication system. The proposed methods are benchmarked against a greedy approach, demonstrating that our techniques achieve a reduction of at least 20% in the required number of samplers. Additionally, we explore the trade-off between the number of samplers and the length of the selection pattern, noting that longer patterns can further decrease the sampler count. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this work, including the development of more sophisticated samplers and the application of these methods to broader contexts beyond coherent communication. The methods described in this paper are available as open-source software at https://github.com/andrewjg/phase-sampler-generator. We present a resilient tagging scheme for a fixed class of planar graphs that enables any subset of vertices to calculate their distances to all other vertices, even in the presence of a polynomial number of faulty processors. This approach relies on a polynomial-sized set of tags, where each tag is $O(\log n)$ bits long and stored within the processor at each vertex. We demonstrate that these tags facilitate the distance computation for every pair of vertices using $O(\log n)$ bits of communication between any two vertices. Furthermore, we establish that this tag size is nearly optimal, as a lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$ bits is required for any scheme capable of determining distances for a subset of vertices under the same fault conditions. Additionally, we introduce a resilient method for identifying a vertex subset that allows each vertex to assign itself a tag of $O(1)$ bits. This method remains robust against a polynomial number of failures, provided that the number of vertices in the resulting tagged subset does not exceed $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$. We also discuss a straightforward adaptation of our resilient tagging approach to support vertex sorting. Our primary contributions are the development of resilient tagging schemes for vertex subsets and sorted subsets, which are essential components for constructing a resilient algorithm to compute the complete distance matrix for all pairs of vertices in the graph. We propose a resilient algorithm for the distance matrix that operates with $O(1)$-bit communication between vertex pairs. The algorithm's complexity is $O(n^2)$, which is optimal, and it successfully tolerates a polynomial number of failures. To our knowledge, this represents the first resilient algorithm for the distance matrix problem in planar graphs that achieves both optimal complexity and $O(1)$-bit communication. We also examine the model of resilient communication complexity, which is relevant to the broader field of distributed computing. In this framework, distributed computation is viewed as a black box that functions correctly as long as a polynomial number of processors do not halt. We illustrate that this model is more general than the model of distributed resilience, which has been extensively studied in recent literature. We provide a resilient solution to a specific problem within this model and prove that this solution is optimal. Finally, we extend our analysis to resilient communication complexity, a concept with significant implications for distributed computing. We show that our resilient tagging scheme for vertex subsets can be adapted to support set membership testing. This study examines an entangled Bose-Hubbard system where each bosonic site is coupled to a distinct bath of harmonic oscillators. These bath oscillators are subjected to a combined influence of thermal equilibrium and external driving forces. We demonstrate that two-entity correlations within the bosonic modes can be analyzed using correlation functions in the oscillatory mode space, achievable through a moment-based entanglement criterion. Furthermore, we show that the spectrum-domain scattering matrix of the bosonic subsystem can be retrieved from the oscillatory mode space correlation function, provided the scattering matrix is Hermitian. Finally, we illustrate how both the correlation of bosonic modes and the spectrum-domain scattering matrix are impacted by the thermal and dynamical properties of the bath oscillators. These findings suggest that the proposed bosonic system could serve as a viable platform for quantum information processing. Additionally, the methodologies employed can be extended to investigate correlations in other bosonic and fermionic systems. The theoretical framework is supported by numerical evidence. These results are derived from the analytical exact solution of the model, which is also presented. The code used for numerical calculations is available at [1].

This study introduces a general framework for out-of-domain detection within Gaussian process (GP) models. By integrating a Gaussian mixture prior with GP regression, we derive a novel framework for identifying out-of-sample observations. We demonstrate that applying this general approach to classification tasks yields a new method for detecting out-of-domain labels in Gaussian process classifiers (GPCs). Furthermore, we show that existing techniques for limiting overfitting in GPs, such as Gaussian process discriminative covariance, can be derived from this approach. The framework is also extended to support batch out-of-domain detection. Through synthetic and real-world experiments, we illustrate the benefits of our framework for out-of-domain detection and evaluate its performance against current state-of-the-art methods. Our results indicate that this general framework outperforms existing methods, while our specific implementations for both in- and out-of-domain detection are competitive with current literature. Additionally, we provide a Python implementation of the framework, which is available on GitHub. Finally, we examine the framework's performance in the context of domain adaptation, showing that it surpasses other approaches in this area. Our findings suggest that GP models combined with a Gaussian mixture prior are highly effective for both out-of-domain detection and domain adaptation. Periodically driven quantum systems can exhibit non-equilibrium steady states that avoid heating, a phenomenon known as prethermalization. This study investigates the prethermal behavior of a one-dimensional open quantum system featuring two sites, where a two-photon drive couples each pair of adjacent vibrational bands. We demonstrate that, under specific driving conditions, a non-Hermitian skin effect emerges due to open boundary interactions, resulting in a prethermal state where excitation amplitudes are localized at the open ends. Furthermore, we show that this non-Hermitian prethermal state can be utilized to achieve the quantum aggregation of bosons. This work establishes a framework for engineering prethermal states in open driven systems and for quantum aggregation using open boundary conditions. Additionally, our findings offer a pathway to observe prethermalization in driven systems where periodic driving induces complex eigenvalues. Finally, we highlight the potential applications of these prethermal states in quantum sensing and the simulation of non-Hermitian topological phases. Non-repetitive optical clocks are rapidly advancing technologies that are anticipated to soon surpass the capabilities of their current microwave-based counterparts. A defining attribute of these optical clocks is their exceptional long-term stability, which enables precise monitoring of their frequency evolution over extended periods. This study introduces a statistical framework designed to analyze the time-domain characteristics of general non-repetitive clocks. We demonstrate that the full conditional distribution of clock times can be effectively modeled using a finite-order non-linear autoregressive model with exogenous inputs (NARX). This approach facilitates the long-term monitoring of clock drift and short-term noise, while also allowing for the prediction of future clock behavior. The proposed methodology is validated through an analysis of an existing dataset from a state-of-the-art optical lattice clock. The findings indicate that this specific clock exhibits a long-term drift rate of $-1.1(1)\times 10^{-16}\,\mathrm{day}^{-1}$ and a white frequency noise level of $1.1(1)\times 10^{-16}$. These results align with independent measurements of the hyperfine transition in $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}^{+}$ and the systematic uncertainty of the Al$^+$ clock used as the microwave reference. Furthermore, we establish that the drift rate of the optical clock is independent of its loading, suggesting that the drift is primarily caused by the microwave reference. Additionally, we examine the potential for predicting clock performance and discuss the broader implications of this methodology for timekeeping research. We contend that investigating the long-term behavior of non-repetitive optical clocks is essential for fully exploiting their stability and for optimizing the design of future clock experiments. Consequently, we argue that characterizing the long-term behavior of any new optical clock is a fundamental prerequisite for its development. We provide a practical guide for analyzing clock time series data and for determining the optimal loading for future experiments. This methodology is implemented in the open-source Python package `optclock`, which is made available to the scientific community. We demonstrate that `optclock` can be utilized to extract the drift and white frequency noise of any optical clock, as well as to predict its future performance. We also outline how the package can be adapted to identify the optimal loading for a specific experimental setup. We illustrate this by analyzing a dataset from a novel nuclear clock candidate, $^{229}$Th$^{+}$. The code is accessible at https://github.com/QuantumOpticsGroup/optclock. This study introduces a fog-assisted software-defined network (SDN) framework designed to address Service Function Chains (SFC) in critical, real-time applications within fog environments. The system dynamically manages network resources, including switches, servers, and links, to recover from failures, mitigate faults, and optimize energy usage for asset deployment. By integrating these capabilities, the proposed solution ensures high availability, performance, and energy efficiency for time-sensitive services. Simulation results demonstrate that the approach achieves a 99.99% availability rate with minimal service delay, while also reducing both the number of servers and switches deployed in the network. Furthermore, the research offers valuable insights for designing SFCs in future fog-assisted SDN architectures. This paper investigates how altering gradients during training influences model behavior when using different loss functions. Our results indicate that models trained with modified gradients exhibit distinct characteristics, such as altered generalization capabilities and increased robustness against adversarial attacks. Specifically, we observe that minimizing the $l_1$ norm of gradients produces networks that generalize more effectively, are more resilient to adversarial examples, and demonstrate greater robustness to input noise. Furthermore, we note that the sensitive and insensitive regions of adversarial examples generated by these models are more balanced. These findings hold true across various architectures, including ResNet, VGGNet, and MobileNet, as well as different datasets like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. Additionally, we explore the impact of combining gradient manipulation with label smoothing and establish a link between the two approaches. We introduce and analyze a novel holographic error correction protocol, the Hyper-INvariant MERA (HIMERA), which extends the established holographic code framework. This code is defined by a pure, power-law correlated error correction ensemble. HIMERA maintains the essential characteristics of a holographic code, including the existence of a dual gravity theory, the ability to correct errors up to a critical threshold, and the emergence of a geometric structure from error correction operations. Notably, the error correction processes in HIMERA are invariant under time translations. We demonstrate that, unlike the standard HaPPY diagram, the boundary of a generic HIMERA configuration does not necessarily form a regular polygon. Furthermore, we establish that the minimal surface area in this geometry is proportional to the entanglement entropy of the corresponding quantum state. Finally, we outline potential applications of HIMERA in modeling non-equilibrium dynamics and simulating topological quantum matter. These findings suggest that holographic error correction schemes can be derived from any pure state exhibiting power-law correlations. Consequently, this research expands the domain of holographic physics to include non-geometric systems and provides a theoretical framework for investigating non-equilibrium phenomena within holographic models. Additionally, it offers a method for constructing non-equilibrium holographic models that are difficult to analyze using conventional methods. As a specific application, we examine the quench dynamics of a free fermion model, showing that HIMERA can accurately reproduce the relevant physical observables. This study investigates the three-dimensional distance distribution among Galactic Core (GC) fibers, utilizing the recently released FEROS-SDSS-IV Galactic Center (GC8) dataset. By employing the Voronoi tessellation method, we calculate distances between fibers within the GC8 sample. Our analysis reveals that fiber distances in this region are not randomly distributed; instead, they follow a log-normal distribution characterized by a mean of $\mu=0.12$ and a standard deviation of $\sigma=0.25$. This distribution is well-described by a Gaussian function in the logarithmic domain. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fibers within the GC8 sample are significantly overdense compared to the surrounding Galactic disk. These findings suggest that the fibers are gravitationally bound and constitute a dynamically distinct structure within the Milky Way. Additionally, the observed overdensity and log-normal distance distribution align with the Poisson clumping law, a principle applicable to self-gravitating systems. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the nature of the Galactic Center bar. These conclusions are supported by Appendix A, which details the data processing methodology, and Appendix B, which presents a Monte Carlo simulation of fiber distance distributions. This research was conducted using the FEROS-SDSS-IV Galactic Center (GC8) sample. This paper introduces an ideal conservation voltage reduction (ICVR) scheme designed for primary-secondary distribution networks, which encompass both overhead and underground lines. Unlike traditional DVR-based approaches, this new method eliminates the need for multiple DVR units, thereby lowering costs and simplifying maintenance. By leveraging the availability of voltage and power data from utility intelligent electronic devices (IEDs), the proposed ICVR strategy identifies critical nodes where voltage sags occur and retrofits ideal DVRs at these specific locations. The DVR control strategy aims to maintain node voltages at a reduced level to minimize real power losses in radial feeders, while ensuring that all non-sagging nodes stay within acceptable limits. To achieve this, a distributed optimization framework utilizing alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is developed. This approach enables each critical node to independently determine the optimal DVR output to maximize voltage set-point reductions, without requiring communication with neighboring nodes. Simulation results on a 13.8 kV feeder demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed ICVR and its distributed solution. Furthermore, the study addresses the communication requirements for utility IEDs, evaluating the system's robustness against data loss and delays. Finally, the advantages of this distributed approach are contrasted with those of a centralized solution. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. This study examines a non-stationary stochastic bandit framework featuring arm-dependent lags, where the efficacy of an arm is influenced by its own prior pulls. We demonstrate that standard stochastic bandit algorithms fail in this environment, even when applied to a simplified variant with uniform lags. Furthermore, we prove that existing non-stationary stochastic bandit algorithms also falter within this specific setup. Finally, we introduce a specialized bandit model designed for this scenario and develop a corresponding algorithm that guarantees a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(T^{1/2})$. This performance matches the bounds of our simpler special-case version and is only marginally worse than the ideal stochastic bandit regret limit, thereby confirming near-optimality. This paper presents the results of our participation in the LEATHER challenge, which focused on enhancing textual generation within a conversational setting. Our approach involves a two-stage pipeline: first, we extract user information from the conversation history to construct a user profile, and second, we produce text based on this profile and the ongoing dialogue. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the challenge's scoring metrics, offering insights to guide future research in automatic conversational generation. This document, which serves as a contribution to the proceedings of the International Conference Lattice 2021, has been translated and edited by the Lattice QCD at Finite Temperature and Density Working Group. It provides a comprehensive overview of significant Lattice QCD research conducted over the past several years under non-vanishing temperature and density conditions. Furthermore, it highlights anticipated future findings resulting from enhanced computational capabilities and sophisticated theoretical methodologies. Lattice QCD, grounded in first principles, plays a crucial role in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) by providing a quantitative framework for understanding the strong interaction between quarks and gluons. By utilizing space-time lattices to represent QCD variables, it enables a non-perturbative numerical investigation of QCD's non-Abelian gauge theory. This approach is particularly valuable for exploring the non-perturbative aspects of the QCD vacuum and the phenomena arising from the dynamical generation of mass. Furthermore, it facilitates a systematic analysis of QCD's phase diagram under varying temperature and density. Given that many nuclear physics scenarios involve non-vanishing temperature and/or density, lattice QCD calculations are essential for advancing our understanding of the nuclear medium. This text specifically examines QCD thermodynamics and baryon spectroscopy at finite temperature and density, with a focus on light quark masses. Additionally, it addresses recent advancements in computing the QCD phase diagram, including recent breakthroughs in direct simulations at finite baryon chemical potential. The discussion also encompasses lattice QCD applications to heavy quark systems at finite temperature, such as charmonium and bottomonium, as well as open heavy quark systems, before concluding with an examination of the heavy quark effective theory. Finally, it outlines future research directions and potential findings, supported by recent numerical results. The primary objective of this work is to provide an accessible introduction to lattice QCD for a broad audience, while also presenting a selection of recent numerical findings. Consequently, this document is intended for a wide readership, including graduate students and early-career researchers. While it does not cover all facets of lattice QCD, it emphasizes topics directly relevant to finite temperature and density conditions. The text is structured to be self-contained, requiring no prior knowledge of lattice QCD. **Background:** Accurately forecasting the long-term statistical behavior of offshore wind-turbine (WT) loads is essential for optimizing WT design and siting. However, current state-of-the-art probabilistic modeling methods are often too computationally intensive for practical application. **Objectives:** This study introduces a novel modeling framework for probabilistic proxy modeling of offshore WT stresses and their derived loads. The approach combines linked Gaussian process (GP) models to represent the joint distribution of stress components, thereby eliminating the need for error-prone post-processing steps like de-correlation and re-normalization. **Methods:** The proposed linked GPs are trained on detailed, high-fidelity finite element method (FEM) simulations of a generic WT subjected to realistic environmental conditions. The framework's performance is evaluated using probabilistic distributions of stress and load components from an offshore WT located in the North Sea. **Results:** The linked GP proxy model effectively replicates the statistical characteristics of the high-fidelity WT model, specifically accurately predicting the marginal distributions of turbine loads. **Conclusions:** The findings indicate that linked Gaussian process models serve as a highly efficient probabilistic proxy for offshore wind-turbine loads, offering a viable alternative to current state-of-the-art modeling techniques. The 2010 earthquake in Izmir, Turkey, caused extensive damage and loss of life. This study examines Twitter data from the initial phase of the disaster to analyze user activity, detect trends, and monitor sentiment. The findings reveal that, despite the scale of the destruction, the number of Twitter users in the affected region was too low to generate statistically significant data for reliable analysis. Additionally, the research demonstrates that sentiment analysis is highly sensitive to the selection of training data, a crucial factor for future applications. Given these limitations, the paper concludes that Twitter data is not currently suitable for monitoring such disasters. However, it emphasizes that this conclusion may change as social media adoption grows in developing countries. The study also highlights that Twitter could be more effective for disaster monitoring in developed nations, where higher user penetration is likely to yield more significant results. To advance future research in this area, the paper recommends developing sentiment analysis methods that are less dependent on specific training datasets. The accompanying code is available at: https://github.com/ozgurkaya/twitter-quake. Keywords: Twitter data, examination, sentiment analysis, trend analysis, earthquake monitoring.

Time-resolved spectroscopy is a powerful method for probing dynamic processes in chemical and biological systems. However, extracting information about evolving properties from these experiments is difficult because the data is typically noisy, sparse, and limited to short durations. This challenge is exacerbated by the fact that the mechanisms generating time-dependent signals are often poorly understood. To address this, we introduce a forward-optimization method that is robust against data imperfections and independent of prior knowledge regarding the underlying dynamics. This approach is implemented within a generalized path framework, where the inverse problem is solved using the adjoint method. We validate the technique's efficacy by reconstructing time-resolved structural information from simulated noisy and sparse data using time-resolved X-ray scattering. Furthermore, we examine the method's connections to other reconstruction strategies found in the literature. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed approach is highly effective for recovering time-resolved information from experimental data. The code is accessible at https://github.com/maartensw/FOBO. Furthermore, we explore how the reflected entropy inequality can be utilized to investigate the nature of BCFT and ICFT. Finally, we establish that the reflected entropy between intervals $A$ and $B$ exhibits symmetry under the exchange of $A$ and $B$, thereby extending the concept of reflected entropy to BCFTs and ICFTs. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of entanglement properties in the presence of defects. This method enables the investigation of entanglement structure in holographic CFTs that are not dual to gravity in AdS$_3$. This work examines the stability of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons within nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometries. We demonstrate that, in contrast to the rigid behavior observed in the $\mathrm{G}_2$ setting, the existence and moduli space of these instantons are highly sensitive to the specific geometry of the underlying nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ structure. Specifically, we establish both existence and non-existence results for certain abelian instantons, as well as for general instantons possessing a non-trivial one-dimensional moduli space. These findings rely on a newly identified family of non-abelian instantons, which are the first of their kind to be found in a nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometry. Additionally, we investigate the existence of instantons on the seven-dimensional Heisenberg manifold. Our results indicate that while no $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons exist in this case, non-trivial abelian and general instantons do exist, with their presence contingent upon the choice of connection metric. Finally, we explore the relationship between these instantons and the holonomy group of the associated connection.

This approach utilizes energy measurements from quantum sensors, such as cameras, to train a classifier. We validate this method using a quantum aperture code, a recently proposed quantum image format, to demonstrate its efficacy. This paper introduces a new tool for synthesizing provable code within the ACL2 theorem prover. Currently, many verification efforts rely on external code checkers, such as translating C programs to formal specifications and then proving their correctness. This process is often laborious and prone to errors. Our approach instead employs a "self-contained" method, where both code synthesis and correctness proofs occur directly inside ACL2. To achieve this, we utilize a superficial embedding of C into ACL2, recently developed by the fourth author, which allows for a straightforward and efficient translation of C programs into ACL2. This technique enables the direct translation of programs verifiable using conventional checkers into provable ACL2 code. The resulting code generator produces provable ACL2 code from standard checkers with minimal effort. Experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully generates provable code for C programs that are typical subjects of traditional code checking. We establish the circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory, specifically under the complex representation $V=\mathbb{C}^n$, for the $T=\mathbb{C}^*$-space $X=\mathrm{CP}(V)$. This is achieved by defining a new homotopy theory, $[\mathrm{PT}]\mathrm{Top}_*$, which incorporates a pretopology on spheres. This pretopology is defined as the collection of all $T$-invariant maps originating from spheres. Consequently, circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology emerges as a specific instance of generalized equivariant cohomology within this novel framework. Furthermore, our findings regarding $[\mathrm{PT}]\mathrm{Top}_*$ hold a formal resemblance to equivariant K-theory of $\mathrm{CP}(V)$ under $GL_n(\mathbb{C})$ symmetry. This similarity arises because the representation ring of $GL_n(\mathbb{C})$ is isomorphic to that of the circle. Finally, we demonstrate that circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology for $\mathrm{CP}(V)$ is equivalent to the circle-equivariant theory for $\mathrm{S}^n$ (the sphere associated with $V$) augmented by the circle-equivariant cohomology of a point. This last equivalence aligns with the relationship between the K-theory of $\mathrm{CP}(V)$ under $GL_n(\mathbb{C})$ symmetry and that of the representation ring of the circle under $SO(n)$ symmetry. These parallels suggest that a deeper connection exists between our proposed homotopy theory and $G$-linear cohomology. Additionally, we provide an alternative approach to calculating the circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of a point, which yields the same outcome as the circle cohomology of a point. This technique also produces a $G$-linear cohomology theory for $G=SO(n)$ that is equivalent to circle-equivariant cohomology of a point, thereby reinforcing the link between $G$-linear and circle-equivariant theories. This study investigates $J/\psi$ angular distributions for the processes $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c$ and $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$ (where $J=1,2$) at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV, incorporating both initial- and final-state QCD corrections. The analysis reveals that next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD corrections significantly influence the coefficients of the $P_{2}$ and $P_{4}$ Wigner $d$-function elements ($d_{mm'2}$ and $d_{mm'4}$) in the helicity frame, as well as $d_{02}$ and $d_{04}$ in the production frame. Furthermore, the ratios $P_{2}/P_{0}$ and $P_{4}/P_{0}$ are found to be sensitive to NLO corrections. However, in the chosen helicity frame, the $P_{1}$ distribution remains insensitive to these corrections at NLO. Additionally, the study confirms that the previously observed "turning point" in the $P_{4}/P_{0}$ ratio near $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV persists after including NLO QCD corrections. Finally, the angular distribution $P_{0}$ is examined to explore potential violations of the QCD factorization hypothesis at NLO. These findings are intended to aid future experimental efforts in testing the QCD helicity rule and the gluon spin contribution to the proton spin.

Although the Signal app is designed to be user-friendly, it mandates PINs, group codes, and joining pins as barriers to entry that conflict with its core usability goals. This study investigates how these requirements affect non-technical, enthusiastic Signal users. Through in-depth interviews with 15 participants, we examined their approaches to creating, remembering, and managing these PINs, as well as their strategies for handling forgotten codes. Our findings reveal that users often lack clear understanding of the purpose behind these PINs, leading to ad-hoc, inconsistent methods for implementation and memory retention. Additionally, we identified various user-generated workarounds for overcoming these obstacles. These results offer valuable insights for Signal's designers and provide a foundation for future research into the trade-offs between usability and security in messaging applications. Ultimately, our work underscores the necessity of designing for end-users and highlights the complex balance between usability and security in such apps. By presenting user perspectives on PINs, we aim to inspire designers to create more intuitive, user-centric security measures. This study introduces an efficient numerical approach for calculating integrals of the form $\int_0^T f(t)dt$, where the weight function is determined by the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a stochastic process. We apply this solar-weighted quadrature method to integrate the irradiance CDF across various locations and times, thereby precisely quantifying the temporal availability of solar energy. This high-precision integral computation is essential for rigorously evaluating solar generation statistics, such as the mean and variance, which are critical for solar energy planning. Our findings indicate that the irradiance CDF adheres closely to a beta distribution, enabling the application of Gauss quadrature to achieve accurate results. We demonstrate that this method achieves high accuracy with a minimal number of evaluation points, offering significant computational advantages. Furthermore, we show that the irradiance CDF can be derived from a single clear-sky day, eliminating the need for extensive historical data. Finally, we apply the solar-weighted quadrature to derive statistics for solar energy availability. We observe that solar irradiance exhibits strong non-stationarity, with the irradiance CDF varying significantly over time. Consequently, we propose a practical method to characterize this non-stationarity using a single clear-sky day and a limited number of additional historical data points. Ultimately, we illustrate that solar energy availability is highly intermittent, with the mean daily fraction of time a location experiences zero irradiance reaching up to 80%. These insights are valuable for solar energy planning, particularly in designing storage systems and assessing the potential for utilizing solar irradiance data to enhance the efficiency of other intermittent energy sources. This study examines the low-dimensional structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton (GN) matrix in the vicinity of a solution, a property known to enable the curvature method's superior local convergence. By employing the parameterization of manifold optimization, we demonstrate that the generalized GN matrix, when restricted to the tangent space of the manifold, exhibits the same low-rank characteristic as the manifold's curvature operator, a property referred to as the "curvature entry." We further illustrate that the search direction produced by the tangent space-based generalized L-BFGS method is equivalent to that of the conjugate gradient method, thereby confirming the equivalence between the Variational Inequality Variational Technique (ViVT) and the Conjugate Gradient Method applied to the tangent space-based curvature entry. Additionally, an error analysis is conducted to quantify the rank deficiency of the generalized GN matrix's projection onto the tangent space relative to the manifold's curvature operator. Finally, a numerical experiment is presented to validate the theoretical equivalence between ViVT and the tangent space curvature entry within conjugate gradient methods, as well as to assess the performance of ViVT against other state-of-the-art algorithms. This study examines how gendered nouns are represented within a multilingual Transformer model trained on a gender-labeling language. We introduce a dataset comprising 100,000 pairs of German nouns and their corresponding gender labels, sourced from the German Wikipedia. Our findings indicate that the model encodes gender information in its n-gram representations, a capability that emerges in the model's intermediate layers. This effect is most pronounced in the 2-3 most frequent male and female nouns, where the model consistently assigns the correct gender in over 90% of cases. Additionally, we analyze the semantic categories of these high-frequency nouns and their associated gender priming effects. We conclude that the model's ability to represent gender is rooted in the gender-priming properties inherent in the training data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon is specific to gender-priming languages, such as German, and does not occur in languages lacking this trait, like English. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for gender bias in neural networks. The dataset is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/robinhauer/gendered-nouns}. The source code can be found at \url{https://github.com/robinhauer/gendered-nouns-analysis}. Both the data and code are released under a permissive license. We establish that countable discrete torsion-free arithmetic hyperbolic groups are charmable, meaning they possess stem amenable wreath products. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both properties are hereditary under taking index-one subgroups and direct limits. Our findings also include the rigidity of torsion-free arithmetic $p$-adic semisimple groups and their charmability. Additionally, we prove that torsion-free arithmetic $p$-adic semisimple groups with $\mathrm{rank}\geq 2$ exhibit property $\mathcal{Q}$, a property closely related to property $(T)$. Specifically, we show that such a group $\Gamma$ exhibits property $\mathcal{Q}$ if and only if every infinite index-one subgroup $\Gamma'\leq \Gamma$ contains an infinite Fuchsian subgroup as a finite index subgroup. Finally, we confirm that torsion-free arithmetic subgroups of $\mathrm{SO}(n,1)$ are not property charm, indicating that charmability is strictly weaker than property $\mathcal{F}$. These results extend to broader classes of arithmetic groups. Our findings have significant implications for the study of property $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ within arithmetic hyperbolic groups. In this context, we identify a sufficient condition for a hyperbolic group $\Gamma$ to be charm, based on the property $\mathcal{F}$ of its surface subgroups. We also derive necessary conditions for $\Gamma$ to be non-charm, which are satisfied by groups containing infinitely many Fuchsian subgroups of sufficiently large rank. These findings lead to the conclusion that torsion-free arithmetic subgroups of $\mathrm{SO}(5,1)$ are charm, whereas those of $\mathrm{SO}(n,1)$ with $n\geq 7$ are not. Zero-shot object localization involves estimating an object's position within an image without prior training data, a capability essential for processing newly introduced classes in dynamic, zero-shot open-set environments. Current research typically relies on image-level supervision, where images are marked as containing or excluding a specific class, often resulting in suboptimal performance. This paper introduces a method that leverages class-level supervision to enhance object position estimation. By integrating a class-level supervision module with a position estimation network, the approach generates high-confidence bounding boxes for all instances of the target class within each image. Evaluated across multiple datasets, the proposed method demonstrates significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, it is designed to be computationally efficient, requiring no additional training once the model is initialized. Experimental results indicate that the method can identify and estimate the positions of multiple object instances within a single image. Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for traffic management, planning, and control. While deep learning models have been widely applied to this domain, they typically depend on extensive traffic data and precise location details, rendering them unsuitable for scenarios where data is scarce and locations are private. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel deep learning model designed for prediction tasks involving extensive traffic data and sparse traffic volumes. Our approach leverages the similarity between road segments to forecast traffic for specific roads. To validate the efficacy of this method, we applied it to predict traffic for Los Angeles, utilizing extensive traffic data collected from a previous study. The results demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms existing approaches in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Real-time observation of the dynamic Universe has been a longstanding objective in radio astronomy. The Irish LOFAR facility, established in 2018, has been equipped with REAL-time Transient Capture (REALTA) since its inception. This system is designed to identify, record, and archive radio transients in real-time for subsequent analysis. The project aims to enhance our understanding of the Universe's most energetic events, such as Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), and to enable new research areas like data mining and automated machine learning. The system operates by continuously monitoring the entire LOFAR array, flagging significant events, and storing them for later study. Additionally, it publishes metadata for all events to facilitate data mining efforts. This paper details the REALTA system's initial performance, including its capture rate of LOFAR's most intense events, such as FRBs and terrestrial interference. Furthermore, we present a novel method for flagging FRBs using LOFAR data, which leverages the system's ability to detect transients across all frequencies simultaneously. This approach offers a new means of characterizing FRBs and their dispersion measures. Finally, we discuss the REALTA project's future development and its potential contributions to the growing fields of data mining and automated machine learning. This study examines how current film datasets are influenced by the inclusion of pre-released features, such as actor trailers and critical reviews. Current data limitations stem from the absence of these recently introduced variables. To address this, we introduce a novel dataset built upon the KDD 2016 Freenomics Film dataset, which incorporates these additional features. By analyzing the impact of these new variables, we demonstrate that they significantly enhance the predictive capabilities of models designed to forecast a film's gross revenue. Furthermore, we compare various machine learning algorithms to identify the most effective model for revenue prediction. Our findings indicate that the XGBoost algorithm performs optimally, achieving an R² score of 0.811 on the test set. This represents a substantial improvement over the baseline Freenomics model, which scored an R² of 0.612 without these pre-released features. Consequently, our results prove that integrating these new features leads to a significant increase in model performance. The processed dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/ML-Data-Processed. This study introduces a model for a power grid incorporating auxiliary frequency regulation, where voltage levels adjust in response to altered operating frequencies. Such adjustments are crucial for grid operators to implement new frequency setpoints gradually, thereby minimizing disruptions to sensitive power consumers. The proposed system is represented as a nonlinear dynamical system, for which we derive conditions ensuring the uniqueness of the steady state and the local stability of the operating point. Additionally, we propose simple diagonal controllers capable of local stability compensation, demonstrating stable and sufficiently rapid voltage behavior. These findings are validated through simulations of a detailed European power grid model. The research is supported by the German Research Foundation (DFG) under grant WA 2868/10-1.

The advancement of cyberphysical systems has driven the need for a broader, more general framework to describe networks of systems that can perceive, reason, and act cognitively. This paper introduces the concept of cybercognitive systems, which integrate traditional cyberphysical systems with cognitive capabilities. We outline the foundational principles of this field and propose a unified framework for such systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that a common model for their cybercognitive components can be derived from existing literature. Furthermore, we illustrate how networked cybercognitive systems can be designed to achieve distributed decision-making and control. The paper concludes by discussing key research challenges and potential applications within this emerging domain. Ultimately, we argue that cybercognitive systems represent a vital and promising field for the future of cyberphysical systems. Additionally, we identify cognitive computing and brain-inspired computing as essential research areas within computer science to support the development of this field. Finally, we suggest that the design of networked cybercognitive systems should be approached as a control problem, thereby extending the principles of distributed decision-making and control to these systems. By integrating the principles of cybercognitive systems with core computer science disciplines, we can advance this field and enable the creation of intelligent, networked environments. Specifically, we show that a control-theoretic approach to networked cybercognitive systems can be established by leveraging foundational cybercognitive principles and effectively applying established control techniques. This control-theoretic perspective offers a systematic method for designing, analyzing, and controlling these systems, while also providing a clear, unified language for their description. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that cybercognitive systems serve as a foundational element for the future of cyberphysical systems and highlights the critical role of computing research in advancing this field. By integrating principles of cybercognitive systems with fundamental computer science areas, we can foster the growth of this field and facilitate the realization of intelligent, networked spaces. In summary, cybercognitive systems are an essential component of the future of cyberphysical systems, and computer science research plays a pivotal role in their development. Furthermore, a control-theoretic approach to networked cybercognitive systems enables the application of established control techniques, providing a systematic design methodology and a clear, unified language for their implementation. Additionally, computer science research is fundamental to the advancement of this field, as it underpins the theoretical and practical foundations of cybercognitive systems. The control-theoretic approach to networked cybercognitive systems facilitates the use of established control techniques, offering a systematic design methodology and a cohesive language for their application.

The origin of the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra remains a debated topic, with two primary hypotheses: thermal emission from the broad-line region (BLR) or non-thermal radiation from the jet's X-ray component. This study investigates the latter scenario by applying the fully developed partially polarized Monte-Carlo code (MAPPIES) to a sample of 12 blazars. The analysis incorporates relativistic effects, scattering geometry, and the anisotropy of the photon field. Results indicate that the non-thermal BLR hypothesis can successfully reproduce the observed spectra of these 12 sources. Furthermore, the derived electron distribution parameters align with findings from other blazar models, and the results are consistent with the scenario of thermal emission originating from the BLR. Finally, the study examines the potential for distinguishing between these two hypotheses through future polarimetric observations. Specifically, it calculates the required number of photons to achieve a statistical error of 10% on the polarization degree, showing that this threshold is achievable with approximately 100 photons. Additionally, the necessary exposure time for the upcoming CTA observatory to collect this quantity of photons is estimated to be less than 10 hours. These estimates are contingent upon the accuracy of the MAPPIES model, which is further validated by comparing its predictions against the most recent relativistic Monte-Carlo simulations. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that a fully developed, fully polarized Monte-Carlo code is essential for analyzing the non-thermal BLR hypothesis. The generated code will be made publicly available. We present a method for creating an analytic extension of Cauchy's integral formula for a function defined on the complex plane, utilizing the sample data of its analytic continuation. This approach is implemented through a robust algorithm that operates on complex digital surfaces, enabling high-precision evaluation and symbolic tracking of rounding errors. The resulting algorithm is both precise and efficient, with performance that is nearly independent of the number of samples. Furthermore, it supports parallel execution across any digital surface, including complex ones, making it ideal for high-performance computing environments. We have developed a C++ library featuring core functions that facilitate the construction of analytic extensions over complex terrains. This library includes a function to compute the Cauchy kernel for a surface and another to evaluate the extension at arbitrary points. We demonstrate the library's utility by applying it to extend the magnitude of a complex signal, specifically the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), beyond the DFT grid. This capability allows for the precise determination of local maxima in the DFT spectrum. The implementation supports arbitrary dimensions and includes a symbol for the complex number zero to enable exact tracking of rounding errors. Additionally, the library features a function to identify locations of local maxima on the extended signal. We have applied this tool to analyze the extended Fourier spectrum of a periodic quasi-crystal signal, successfully pinpointing the quasi-crystal's periodicity. Finally, we have utilized the library to perform a Fourier analysis of a signal originating from a chaotic Lorenz attractor. In this case, we observed that while the extension of the Fourier magnitude decays polynomially outside the core frequencies, it remains non-zero at large distances from the grid. This finding indicates that the chaotic signal lacks periodicity, consistent with established theory. The magnitude and location of the local maxima in the extended spectrum were determined using the library. These results highlight the library's utility in analyzing periodic and aperiodic signals, as well as the underlying characteristics of the sources generating them. Baryon production is investigated through the quantized splintering of a helical string within a QCD phase diagram featuring strong helical color fields. In this framework, a splintering process generates a fermion-antifermion pair, with the resulting baryon captured by the receding string core. This mechanism aligns with the concept of string breaking, where vacuum fluctuations in the presence of a strong color field create baryon-antibaryon pairs, leading to string breaking and string-meson formation. Furthermore, this process is complementary to the coalescence of antifermions with the string core, which reduces entropy and contributes to baryon enhancement. The production rate of baryons and antibaryons is derived from the probability of this splintering event, contingent upon specific parameters of the string and color field. Additionally, the model elucidates the origin of the helical structure observed in high-transverse momentum antibaryons at LHC energies. Ultimately, this model offers a novel perspective on the origin of the baryon anomaly.

Solar active regions generate significant magnetic fields and associated currents that drive the Sun's magnetic dynamo. These currents are believed to influence solar oscillations, which in turn affect helioseismic travel-time measurements. This study examines the relationship between currents within active regions and variations in helioseismic travel times. We analyze high-resolution Doppler and magnetogram data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) to calculate horizontal currents around active regions. Simultaneously, we derive horizontal currents from horizontal travel-time perturbations. Our results indicate that currents within active regions contribute substantially to horizontal travel-time changes, which aligns with the hypothesis that active regions are the primary drivers of solar magnetic activity. Consequently, this suggests that the solar magnetic cycle is fundamentally rooted in the magnetic fields of active regions. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that horizontal currents in active regions are essential for explaining the observed north-south hemispheric differences in travel-time variations. This insight is crucial for understanding the solar dynamo and the origin of solar magnetic activity. Additionally, we show that the correlation between currents in active regions and helioseismic travel-time variations peaks at a time lag of approximately 10 days, indicating a strong link between active regions and solar activity. This correlation is vital for space weather forecasting, as active regions are key drivers of solar activity. Finally, we explore the implications of our results for solar dynamo models and space weather prediction. Our results suggest that active regions play a critical role in the solar magnetic cycle, and that incorporating currents within active regions is essential for accurately modeling solar magnetic activity and forecasting space weather. We conclude that future space weather models should integrate the effects of currents within active regions to improve prediction accuracy. This research underscores the significance of active regions in solar physics and their potential impact on space weather forecasting. By understanding the role of currents within active regions, we can better predict solar activity and its effects on Earth and other planets. This study investigates the detection of gravitational wave background signals generated by stochastic magnetic fields within neutron star populations. While prior research has primarily focused on the pulsar gravitational wave background, this work extends the analysis to include pulsar timing spectrum bands. We derive the theoretical expression for the gravitational wave strain amplitude and conduct a comprehensive simulation of the gravitational wave background. Our findings indicate that a 10 kHz bandwidth offers the optimal balance between signal strength and noise levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the pulsar timing spectrum band holds significant potential for detecting gravitational waves. Finally, we identify the key parameters governing the gravitational wave background signal, including the neutron star formation rate, the magnetic field power spectral density index, and the range of magnetic field energy within neutron stars. These results may inform future observational strategies for conducting gravitational wave background searches using pulsars. This study introduces a learning-driven approach for compressing light field (LF) scenes, utilizing a disparity-aware model to enhance compression efficiency. By integrating disparity information into both entropy modeling and bitstream decoding, the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to traditional techniques. Specifically, the disparity-aware model calculates scene depth to generate disparity data, which is then fused with tensor-based prediction and transform techniques to build an effective entropy model. This model enables precise probability estimation for pixel values across multiple views. Additionally, the entropy model facilitates bitstream decoding, allowing for the recovery of pixel values and disparity maps. Experimental results demonstrate that, relative to state-of-the-art compression methods, this approach delivers significant improvements in entropy modeling and compression efficiency. Furthermore, the method supports variable resolution decoding, offering greater flexibility for diverse application needs. Ultimately, the proposed solution outperforms existing techniques in PSNR, SSIM, and compression efficiency. Finally, the method's practicality is validated through its application to compressed LF images captured by real-world light field cameras. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/LF-Compression. Keywords: Light Field, Image Compression, Learning-Driven, Disparity-Aware Model.

Interactive and non-interactive methods represent the two primary paradigms in cross-language information retrieval (CLIR). While recent research has focused on the advantages of incorporating user feedback within interactive systems, this study evaluates the potential of such feedback to enhance non-interactive approaches. We introduce a query expansion technique designed for CLIR that optimizes the relevance and precision of retrieved documents by leveraging user input. This approach is applied across multiple languages and compared against standard baseline methods. Furthermore, we investigate the performance of our proposed query expansion across various CLIREVAL tasks, contrasting it with traditional monolingual relevance expansion and a random baseline. Our findings indicate that user feedback can significantly boost the performance of both frameworks, yielding substantial improvements over baselines. Additionally, our approach demonstrates superior results compared to monolingual expansion methods in the CLIR domain. Finally, we examine the robustness of this query expansion method when applied to low-resource languages. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1996/CLIR-Query-Expansion. This study introduces two estimation techniques to generate reliable health metrics from sparse data, with a specific focus on the 2017 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey (EHS). The first approach utilizes small-region modeling to estimate fertility and under-five mortality rates, while the second employs a region-level spatial clustering method to derive fertility rates. Both strategies calculate period under-five mortality rates and fertility rates for the 2017 EHS, which includes data for 50 woredas. These estimates are subsequently compared against the survey's published fertility and mortality figures. The results indicate that both methods yield estimates for fertility and under-five mortality that align closely with the published national-level data. Furthermore, the spatial clustering method successfully identified neighboring woredas with similar fertility rates, whereas the small-region modeling approach failed to detect any spatial correlation in under-five mortality. Ultimately, both methods offer robust solutions for generating credible estimates when faced with limited resources. However, the spatial clustering approach is noted for its ability to leverage the spatial interdependence of regions, a feature absent in the small-region modeling technique. Additionally, the spatial clustering method proved more straightforward to implement. Given these advantages, the spatial clustering approach is recommended for future applications. The findings also highlight a critical need for enhanced capacity to analyze complex survey designs in Ethiopia and other low- and middle-income countries. Finally, the study underscores the necessity of strengthening the health information system in Ethiopia, which is currently hindered by a lack of data on key indicators such as under-five mortality. We propose an approach to arbitrary quantum cloning that frames the task as a series of repeated bets on the outcomes of measurements performed on the source. In this framework, the bettor adheres to the Kelly criterion, aiming to maximize the exponential growth of their bankroll. By modeling the measurement process as a series of bets with unfavorable odds, we demonstrate an apparent paradox: although the bettor loses money in each individual step, their cloned copy gains wealth at every stage. This phenomenon is resolved by recognizing that different sets of measurements are bet against in each step, meaning the losses are not independent. We prove that this method is mathematically equivalent to treating the cloning task as a sequence of bets with unfavorable odds, thereby eliminating the paradox. Furthermore, we show that for the specific case of cloning a set of equiprobable symbols, our approach yields the same optimal measurement series as established previous results. Finally, we apply this scheme to the broader task of quantum wagering, where the source is an arbitrary quantum state rather than a set of discrete symbols. In this more general context, we derive the optimal evolution of the bankroll and determine the complete set of measurements required to optimally extract information from the source. While an analytical solution for these measurements remains elusive for arbitrary states, we have obtained them numerically for several specific cases. Additionally, we calculate the optimal bankroll growth rate as a function of the source's von Neumann entropy. This formulation offers a new perspective on the fundamental limits of quantum information extraction and may prove useful in other quantum information applications. Ultimately, we believe this paper provides a novel and valuable framework for analyzing the fundamental limits of quantum cloning.

Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have garnered significant interest for their exceptional excitonic properties. However, the recently introduced class of materials, transition metal diatomides (MA$_2$Z$_4$), offers an additional atom that enables precise tuning of quasiparticle energy alignments. This study examines the quasiparticle energy levels of MA$_2$Z$_4$ using the GW approximation. The findings indicate that these energy alignments are contingent upon the specific atom selected, with the quasiparticle energy gaps for transition metal silicides (MSi$_2$Z$_4$) being approximately 0.5 eV lower than those of the corresponding phosphides and arsenides. Furthermore, the energy alignments remain consistent across hetero- and homostructures formed by these materials, suggesting the presence of a stacking-independent exciton. These results offer valuable insights for future experimental investigations into these emerging materials. Additionally, the study addresses the previously debated energy alignment between the conduction band minimum (CBM) and valence band maximum (VBM) in MSi$_2$Z$_4$, confirming that the CBM and VBM are indeed aligned. This alignment is independent of the specific metal used and persists even when considering multi-layer configurations. Consequently, this suggests that a one-dimensional exciton could be realized in these materials. Finally, the research explores the potential for constructing both direct and indirect excitons through the heterostructure of these compounds. Specifically, the indirect exciton is predicted to exhibit a large separation between CBM and VBM, a feature particularly promising for optoelectronic applications. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive overview of the energy alignments within these materials, offering a robust foundation for future experimental research. Furthermore, the methodology employed can be readily adapted to investigate other materials of interest. This article is categorized under 2.C. We provide a proof for the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ using the Standard Model. This study incorporates both photon radiation and photon radiation along with final-state rescattering. Our findings indicate that the combined effect of these two variables enhances the decay rate by approximately 1.5 times compared to the case without any radiation. Additionally, we calculate the total branching ratio, which is determined to be $\mathcal{B}(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-) = 1.1 \times 10^{-11}$. This value is consistent with the recent LHCb measurement of $\mathcal{B}(\Sigma^+ \to p e^+ e^-) = 1.99 \times 10^{-10}$, accounting for the expected ratio between the electron and muon channels of roughly 100:1. Finally, we provide a proof for the combined branching ratio of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \ell^+ \ell^-$ decay across the mass range $10~\mathrm{MeV} < q^2 < 1.5~\mathrm{GeV}^2$, which aligns with the LHCb result of $(1.12 \pm 0.04) \times 10^{-2}$. Furthermore, we compute the branching ratio as a function of the dilepton invariant mass $q^2$ and compare it with LHCb data. We investigate the formation of protoplanetary disks through the rupture of a prestellar nucleus, a process driven by the collapse of a dense core fragment. This scenario is motivated by the observation that young stars in Taurus often reside in dense stellar clusters, suggesting that disk formation may be influenced by the surrounding environment. Our findings indicate that the rupture of a prestellar nucleus generates a gas inflow toward the central star with mass and velocity distributions closely resembling those of actual protoplanetary disks. This mechanism offers a potential explanation for the common presence of gas in these disks and could account for the observed correlations between stellar and gas mass and velocity. Furthermore, the process of disk creation via nucleus rupture may be triggered by the dynamical interactions of nearby stars, such as close encounters or stellar flybys. These interactions can cause the prestellar core to become unstable against gravitational collapse, resulting in the formation of a central dense core fragment. This study demonstrates that disk formation through nucleus rupture is a natural consequence of core collapse initiated by stellar flybys, implying that stellar interactions and core fragmentation are intrinsically linked. Consequently, protoplanetary disks formed in this manner may exhibit unique characteristics, such as a higher frequency of binary systems and a greater abundance of massive planets. Our results underscore the necessity of studying the physical conditions of prestellar cores to fully understand disk formation and its relationship with the stellar environment. Ultimately, this research highlights the critical role of stellar interactions in the formation of protoplanetary disks. We introduce a multi-term temporal sequence modeling approach designed to capture diverse temporal dependencies within data. This method extends a recent technique called Temporal Sequence Modeling with Sparsity (TSSM), adapting it for Bayesian analysis. By employing a Bayesian perspective, we develop a novel Bayesian Variational Inference (BVIni) algorithm to efficiently approximate the posterior distribution of model parameters. This brief note aims to provide a more visual and intuitive understanding of Pontryagin dualism for groups with continuous topology, specifically focusing on locally compact Abelian groups. We will demonstrate that the dual group inherits the topology from its original group, ensuring that a locally compact Abelian group and its dual possess identical dimensions as topological groups. Furthermore, we will explore how this duality facilitates a more natural and continuous interpretation of Fourier transforms.

Finally, this work seeks to clarify and resolve various ambiguities and misconceptions that often arise when introducing Pontryagin dualism. We address common confusion regarding specific aspects of the theory and offer solutions to these issues. Additionally, we provide a list of references for readers interested in further exploration of the topic. Our approach is designed to be accessible to individuals with a basic understanding of harmonic analysis, group theory, and topology. Our goal is to assist readers in quickly grasping the fundamental concepts of Pontryagin dualism and to provide a solid foundation for future study in this area. We hope that readers will find our efforts valuable and that this note will contribute positively to their learning journey. Please do not hesitate to contact us if you have any questions. Federated learning (FL) is a widely adopted machine learning framework designed to safeguard user privacy by ensuring that neither clients nor the server can infer individual data. This paper introduces a new concept of differential confidentiality (DC) and demonstrates that DC, when combined with FL, constitutes a formal guarantee of such privacy. We illustrate the emergence of DC through specific gradient distributions and link it to statistical notions of independence and fairness. Furthermore, we prove that in binary classification tasks, training on independent Gaussian noise results in DC, whereas sampling from other distributions typically introduces bias. Additionally, we show that in federated learning scenarios, the non-IID nature of data and the freedom for clients to opt out of participation can establish independence between model updates and labels, thereby ensuring DC. These findings offer a novel perspective on privacy within FL and propose a new training strategy that leverages DC to enhance privacy. Experimental results confirm that this approach improves performance in federated binary classification while maintaining privacy guarantees. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi1997/FL-DC}.

We propose a supersymmetric minimal framework for embedding the Standard Model (SM) within a higher-energy $U(1)_X$ gauge theory, incorporating three right-handed neutrinos. This model extends the SM gauge group to $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y \times U(1)_X$, where the $U(1)_L$ component is a new symmetry associated with lepton number. The framework includes a complex scalar field carrying $U(1)_L$ charge, which serves as the dark energy candidate and remains stable due to its charge under the $U(1)_X$ symmetry. We demonstrate that all SM anomalies can be cancelled by assigning appropriate charges to the right-handed neutrinos, thereby resolving the issue of anomaly cancellation without requiring exotic matter fields. Furthermore, we analyze the phenomenology of this model, showing that it can accommodate a dark matter candidate and yield testable predictions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Finally, we discuss the implications for neutrino physics, noting that the model successfully accounts for neutrino oscillation data. Additionally, we derive constraints on the parameter space from LHC searches for supersymmetric particles and dark matter, as well as from LHCb investigations into lepton flavor violation. These analyses establish lower limits on the masses of gluinos and squarks, as well as the $W$ and $Z$ bosons, while also predicting the branching ratio for $B_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$. Our findings indicate that the proposed model remains consistent with current experimental data. We conclude that upcoming LHC searches for $Z'$ bosons and lepton flavor violation will provide further constraints on the model's parameter space. Additionally, we examine the potential for $Higgs$ collider experiments to detect a dark energy candidate, which would offer a promising avenue for exploring this model. Finally, we address the stability of the electroweak vacuum and the hierarchy problem within this framework. Overall, this study demonstrates that $U(1)_X$ extensions of the SM are viable and that the proposed model offers a comprehensive explanation for various physical phenomena. We anticipate that future searches for $Z'$ bosons and dark matter at the LHC will provide further constraints on the model's parameter space. In conclusion, $U(1)_X$ extensions of the SM are a promising avenue for future research, and the proposed model provides a unified explanation for a wide range of physical phenomena.

This paper introduces a new wireless communication framework designed to enhance throughput by integrating intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) with energy harvesting. The proposed system model assumes the IRS is mounted on a building's exterior wall, thereby enabling communication for both indoor and outdoor users. We examine a scenario where an indoor eavesdropper seeks to intercept the transmitted signal from an indoor source. To counter this threat, we consider a scenario where a portion of the IRS is coated with a light-absorbing material to disrupt the eavesdropper, while the remaining uncovered IRS assists a legitimate indoor user. The objective is to maximize the source's throughput under conditions of limited harvested energy at the indoor user. We derive the closed-form expression for optimal IRS coating depth and determine the optimal power splitting factor, which balances energy harvesting and information reception. Furthermore, we derive the optimal transmit power and optimal phase shift distribution. Our theoretical analysis and numerical results demonstrate that the proposed system can significantly improve throughput. Additionally, we prove that the achievable region for the coating depth is bounded, ensuring the problem remains solvable within a finite range. Finally, we show that the proposed system achieves a substantial throughput improvement.
