This study reports the first low-frequency radio observations of the binary system CR Draconis, a young, active T Tauri star in a 1.1-day orbit with a companion mass of 0.15 solar masses. The observations targeted the 10–100 MHz band, utilizing the LOFAR Low Band (10–25 MHz) and a custom setup combining the LOFAR Low Band with the Murchison Widefield Array (25–100 MHz). We identified a radio burst lasting 10.5 hours, characterized by a mean flux density of approximately 10 mJy, which is the most extended burst ever recorded from a T Tauri star. The burst's duration and morphology suggest it is driven by electron cyclotron maser (ECM) emission, a mechanism typically associated with magnetospheres of Jupiter and Saturn. The burst exhibits a complex structure, including a 1.5-hour event with a mean flux density of ~100 mJy, a single peak reaching ~1000 mJy, and a 2.5-hour event peaking at ~1000 mJy. We propose that the burst's longevity stems from a stable interaction between the stellar and companion magnetospheres, while the morphology is attributed to stochastic solar-like flares. The energy budget required to sustain this emission is estimated at ~10^31 erg s^-1, consistent with solar flare energy levels. These findings support the hypothesis that ECM emission is a primary mechanism for radio bursts from T Tauri stars. Furthermore, the burst's morphology and energy budget are comparable to those of solar flares, suggesting that the stellar flare companion is responsible for the prolonged ECM radiation. This event also demonstrates that low-frequency observations can detect radio emission from young stars over extended periods, offering a means to study stellar magnetic fields and magnetic activity in young stellar objects. Finally, the companion's influence on stellar magnetic fields and activity may be a critical factor in the formation of habitable planets. These observations underscore the necessity of future low-frequency facilities, such as the Square Kilometre Array, to continue investigating young stellar objects. The data are accessible at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.io/25q6a. Supplementary material is available at https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-4349/202144

This paper presents a method for creating a virtual articulated neural depiction of human figures in motion. Given a sequence of 3D joint positions, our approach learns a neural network that generates new views of the subject, specifically by sampling along rays defined by two directional parameters: view height and view yaw. We assess view synthesis performance using PSNR and SSIM metrics. Furthermore, we evaluate the method's real-time capabilities by measuring frames per second (FPS) across various hardware configurations. The system is trained via a single, straightforward objective function that combines these two factors. Experimental results demonstrate that, despite being constrained by a simple loss function, our algorithm successfully produces high-quality, real-time view synthesis. Additionally, the proposed approach yields a novel neural representation of human motion, which we validate through a single, direct application: virtual character creation for video games. In this context, we utilize the learned motion representation to train a neural network that renders virtual characters from any perspective. Our results indicate that the virtual characters generated from our articulated neural depiction are of high quality, visually realistic, and computationally efficient to render. Image intensification is a prevalent technique in digital image processing that alters image brightness and contrast. While human perception of intensively modified images differs from that of traditionally enhanced ones, automated systems often fail to detect these distinctions. This study introduces a novel dataset, IIM, comprising 10,000 pairs of images: one intensively modified and one traditionally enhanced. We conducted a user study involving 100 participants to evaluate their ability to differentiate between these two types of augmentations. Furthermore, we assessed the performance of 15 state-of-the-art image classification models on a new subset of the IIM data, revealing that their results vary significantly when handling intensively augmented images compared to traditional enhancements. These findings underscore the necessity for further research into image intensification from both human and machine perspectives. The IIM dataset will be made available for public use. The investigated systems consist of triangular units connected by either ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic links. Our analysis covers systems with coupling ratios $J'/J$ ranging from $-0.1$ to $0.9$, encompassing both weakly and strongly coupled regimes. We report numerical results for the specific heat, magnetic susceptibility, and uniform magnetic susceptibility susceptibility. Furthermore, we analyze the low-temperature behavior of these systems and compare our findings with existing theoretical predictions. Finally, we extend this analysis to a two-dimensional lattice featuring $J'$ ferromagnetic links connecting nearest-neighbor sites along one axis and $J$ antiferromagnetic links along the perpendicular axis. For this model, we provide specific heat and magnetic susceptibility data, contrasting the results with those of a two-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Based on our numerical findings, we conclude that the low-temperature phase of this model is characterized by a spin-glass-like state. This conclusion is supported by the absence of a sharp peak in the uniform magnetic susceptibility and the presence of a broad hump in the specific heat at low temperatures. Additionally, we demonstrate that the low-temperature specific heat exhibits a power-law temperature dependence, with an estimated exponent of $\alpha \approx 1.25 \pm 0.25$. This power-law behavior is attributed to the existence of an extensive number of nearly degenerate ground states. Finally, we show that the specific heat of this model can be accurately described by the specific heat of a one-dimensional Ising model. Consequently, the specific heat of this two-dimensional model is approximately equal to that of a one-dimensional Ising model. This study investigates the potential of GPT-3 for zero-shot educational tasks, focusing on two primary objectives: (1) assessing its capabilities in generating explanations for algebraic word problems, and (2) exploring strategies to enhance its performance. To address the first objective, we introduced a prompt engineering method that combines direct prompting with few-shot learning utilizing in-domain data. Results indicate that, without any modifications, GPT-3 achieves zero-shot performance comparable to state-of-the-art models on algebraic word problems. To improve upon this baseline, we developed meta-tuning techniques to refine both the model's parameters and prompts. Our experiments reveal that either modifying the prompt alone or applying meta-tuning to the prompt can yield significant performance gains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that simultaneously adjusting both the prompt and the model can achieve even more substantial improvements. Finally, we examine the impact of utilizing different training data sources and prompt combinations, finding that while specific choices affect outcomes, they do not exert a dominant influence. These findings highlight the critical role of prompt design in leveraging large language models for zero-shot learning. We also establish that Higgs inflation is achievable in this context, yielding a tensor-to-scalar ratio of $r \sim 0.01$. We introduce a new diagnostic tool designed to assess redshifts from (sub)millimeter observations, which we have applied to 12 sources previously identified at z>2 via ALMA spectroscopy. This tool is based on the high-redshift "Sudoku" effect—a phenomenon where emission lines are spaced at regular intervals on logarithmic frequency scales, creating a distinctive pattern in log-log spectra. We present a general method for estimating robust redshifts using this effect and demonstrate its utility in distinguishing robust from tentative identifications. This approach is particularly valuable for (sub)millimeter surveys, such as those conducted by the Atacama Large Aperture Millimetre/submillimetre Array (ALMA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array Precursor (ALPACA), where spectral data may be limited to continuum-only observations or sparse spectral coverage. Our findings indicate that the Sudoku effect remains detectable even with very sparse data, provided it includes at least one emission line. We illustrate this by analyzing 10 z>2 sources with prior ALMA spectroscopic redshifts, showing that the same robust redshifts can be recovered using ALPACA continuum data alone. This underscores the potential of future (sub)millimeter surveys to discover and characterize high-redshift galaxies without the need for spectroscopy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Sudoku effect can be employed to identify and filter out false positive redshifts in (sub)millimeter source catalogs. Finally, we provide a Python package, highz_sudoku, to facilitate the use of this diagnostic in (sub)millimeter source identification. This study investigates the topological and dynamical properties of both symmetry-disrupted and liquid states in a weakly frustrated $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice, utilizing the numerical renormalization group (NRG) method. We demonstrate that the NRG approach can accurately characterize the low-energy dynamics of long-range antiferromagnetic order in a frustrated system, a capability previously unexplored. Specifically, we determine the spin-stiffness exponent $\theta$ for a two-spin correlation function, yielding $\theta=0.60(1)$, which aligns with the long-range antiferromagnetic order expected from classical analysis. Additionally, we examine the liquid state arising from strong geometric frustration, which exhibits a non-zero spin-stiffness exponent $\theta=0.12(1)$. This $\theta$ value is significantly lower than the $\theta=1/3$ predicted by the spin-liquid fixed point of the $O(3)$ non-linear $\sigma$ model and represents the lowest estimate to date for a non-linear $\sigma$ model with $O(2)$ symmetry breaking. Finally, we analyze the spin-stiffness exponent for the singlet-doublet excitation energy gap, finding $\theta=0.25(1)$, a result that agrees with the $\theta=1/4$ prediction derived from the spin-liquid fixed point. These findings are supported by a detailed discussion of the NRG method's capabilities and limitations. Furthermore, we address the controversy regarding the critical behavior of the liquid state by comparing our results with those from other techniques, including Monte Carlo simulations, density matrix renormalization group, and variational cluster methods. We conclude that the NRG results are consistent with those from other approaches, which suggest that strong geometric frustration drives the system into a liquid state with long-range antiferromagnetic order, characterized by a quasi-long-range ordered correlation function with $\theta=1/3$. However, we note that the NRG estimates for both $\theta$ exponents are lower than the values predicted by other methods. We attribute this discrepancy to the NRG's inability to fully capture the long-range behavior of the correlation function. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for understanding the geometric frustration in triangular-lattice magnets. The antiferromagnetic phase transition in the metallic compound Cr$_2$Al was investigated using the muon spin rotation technique. Measurements across the temperature range of 2 to 300 K revealed that Cr$_2$Al undergoes a transition into an in-plane antiferromagnetic state at $T_{\rm N}=140$ K. The muon precession frequencies, derived from fitting the experimental data, indicate that the magnetic moments are arranged in a collinear antiferromagnetic configuration. Furthermore, the temperature dependence of the muon precession frequency was analyzed using a Heisenberg exchange model. This analysis suggests that the dominant exchange interactions are the nearest-neighbor interactions along the $c$-axis and in the $ab$-plane, as well as the next-nearest-neighbor interaction along the $c$-axis. Additionally, the temperature dependence of the muon precession frequency was compared with data from bulk magnetization measurements. This comparison demonstrates that the muon probes the same magnetic moments responsible for the bulk magnetization, confirming that the muon probes are not pinned to the surface. Finally, the muon precession frequency was compared with predictions from first-principles density functional theory calculations, which successfully reproduced the experimental findings. These results imply that the calculated magnetic moments align with the experimental arrangement and that the employed computational method is appropriate for studying this system. Finally, the magnetic properties of Cr$_2$Al were compared with those of the isostructural compound Cr$_2$Ga. This comparison shows that the antiferromagnetic ordering temperature is significantly lower in Cr$_2$Al than in Cr$_2$Ga, and that the muon precession frequency in Cr$_2$Al is smaller than in Cr$_2$Ga. These differences are attributed to variations in the electronic structure between the two materials. This work is part of a broader study on the magnetic properties of Cr$_2$Al and Cr$_2$Ga, which are both candidates for superconductivity. The observed in-plane antiferromagnetic ordering in Cr$_2$Al is consistent with the proposed spin-fluctuation mechanism for superconductivity in this class of materials. This study examines how the intermolecular potential influences rarefied gas flows through a kinetic model that incorporates a speed-dependent collision frequency. Utilizing the Hilbert expansion method, we derive an enhanced BGK-type model featuring a collision frequency that varies with molecular speed, alongside its corresponding slip boundary condition. By solving the resulting non-homogeneous linear Boltzmann equation, we demonstrate that this proposed frequency-dependent BGK model accurately captures effects such as thermal creep and normal shocks, including the creation of third-order normal shock profiles. Furthermore, numerical experiments confirm that the model successfully reproduces the potential-induced reduction in thermal creep velocity and slip lengths, as well as the observed increase in normal shock thickness. These findings indicate that a relatively straightforward modification to the standard BGK model is sufficient to account for potential effects in rarefied gas flows, a capability that the conventional BGK collision operator lacks. Finally, we outline the procedure for implementing this simplified model within the open-source framework OpenFOAM. Semantic grounding involves determining the natural language expressions that map to specific concepts within a target vocabulary. Current progress in this area has been constrained by a reliance on manually designed mappings, which are labor-intensive and restrict the method's scalability. This paper introduces an innovative approach to learning interpreters using a minimal dataset of examples. Our method trains semantic interpreters through self-supervised learning, leveraging both manual examples and automatically generated negative examples. We evaluate this technique on training data containing just one or two examples per concept, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches even when numerous examples are available. Furthermore, we establish the method's generalizability by applying it to learn semantic mappings for color terms across various languages and to neural network activation functions. The upcoming 24-TeV proton-ion Collider for Nuclear Science (CFNS) demands silicon sensors with exceptional spatial resolution, rapid data transmission, and low power consumption. To satisfy these requirements, we are investigating advanced sensor technologies, including thin silicon bulk material, specialized sensor designs, and novel sensor materials. This paper outlines our current research and development initiatives focused on these advanced silicon tracking sensors. Specifically, we are evaluating various sensor geometries and thicknesses using high-energy proton-ion collision data to identify the optimal configuration. Additionally, we are investigating high-resistivity silicon as a viable alternative sensor material. Our ongoing development aims to deliver a superior silicon tracking detector capable of meeting the stringent performance standards required for the next-generation CFNS. Furthermore, this work serves as a foundation for the CFNS R&D program, which will support the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC). We will also address the EIC's specific performance needs, such as handling high occupancy rates in heavy-ion collisions and ensuring precise vertex reconstruction in light-ion collisions. To achieve this, we are developing and testing ultra-thin sensors designed for high-precision vertex detection in high-energy heavy-ion environments. Additionally, we are exploring the application of flexible silicon sensors to the CFNS, leveraging their advantages in cost-effectiveness, lightweight design, and ease of integration. We report on the detection of pulsations in the low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (LLAGN) Mrk 3018, observed using the Transient Laser Interferometric Space Antenna (TISa). The data reveal a significant quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) with a period of 10.5 seconds, characterized by a root mean square (rms) amplitude of 0.15 mCrab. This finding confirms the presence of a QPO in Mrk 3018, which was previously identified in archival Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) data. We propose that these oscillations stem from pulsations within the accretion disk or corona, driven by a mechanism such as the global magneto-rotational instability (MRI). Furthermore, we demonstrate that the QPO frequency scales with the accretion disk's inner radius, a relationship consistent with LLAGN models. Additionally, we identified a new outburst in Mrk 3018, which we attribute to a magnetic reconnection event in the corona. This event caused a 3.5-fold increase in 0.3–3 keV flux and a 2.5-fold increase in 3–6 keV flux, with a notable softening of the X-ray spectrum. This outburst aligns with predictions from low-luminosity accretion disk-corona models. Finally, we note that the QPO frequency in Mrk 3018 is comparable to those of other LLAGNs, including NGC 4051, Mrk 335, and Mrk 33. These results underscore the necessity of conducting long-term, high-cadence, high-time-resolution observations of LLAGNs to better understand their fundamental physical processes. We conclude that TISa is uniquely capable of achieving this. The full dataset is accessible at http://www.tisa.org. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD 58260, a rapidly rotating, metal-poor star exhibiting strong magnetic fields. We conducted high-resolution spectropolarimetry using the FIES spectrograph at the Nordic Optical Telescope, targeting the Fe i lines at 6087 and 6174 Å. By analyzing Stokes V profiles of these lines, we derived line-of-sight magnetic field values at various heights above the stellar surface. Our results indicate that the magnetic field strength increases with altitude, rising from 1.2 kG at the photosphere to 2.5 kG at the chromosphere. This finding supports a radial dipole field configuration for HD 58260, consistent with similar conclusions drawn for other rapidly rotating, metal-poor stars. Additionally, we observed a shift in the center wavelength of the Fe i 6087 Å line, which we attribute to a gradient in the line-of-sight magnetic field. This suggests the presence of a toroidal magnetic field component, as the line formation region shifts outward with increasing rotational phase. These observations provide the first direct evidence of radial field variation in HD 58260 and offer the first confirmation of a toroidal field component in this metal-poor star. These results are crucial for understanding the magnetic field structure of rapidly rotating, metal-poor stars and the associated magnetic activity. Furthermore, the detected radial field variation in HD 58260 supports the dynamo theory, which posits that magnetic fields are generated by the differential rotation of the stellar interior. This aligns with the proposed link between the star's high rotation rate and its strong magnetic field. Ultimately, these findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between stellar rotation, magnetic fields, and activity. The data will also facilitate future investigations into the magnetic field structure of HD 58260 and its impact on the surrounding environment. We provide an explicit free boson representation of the Dunkl intertwining operator within the one-dimensional framework. In this formulation, the action of the operator on monomials yields Segal–Bargmann transforms of corresponding shifted monomials. As a direct consequence, we derive an explicit expression for the Laguerre propagator. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this free boson picture offers a valuable application in computing the Poisson kernel for the Laguerre domain. Additionally, we investigate the properties of the operator when acting on several important classes of functions, including complete elliptic integrals, Struve functions, and Struve $L$-functions. Finally, we examine the operator's behavior on the Fock space and on the space of polynomials, which naturally forms a module over the Laguerre–Hecke algebra. These findings contribute to the broader objective of developing a Laguerre version of holomorphic intertwining operators. To achieve this, we also investigate the properties of the generalized Appell–Lauricella $S$-function, which arises in the polynomial module context. Specifically, we establish that this function is entire in all its variables and derive an asymptotic expansion in a single complex variable using Laguerre polynomials. We further explore the operator's action on hypergeometric functions and establish an identity connecting Jacobi and Laguerre hypergeometric functions. Our work also introduces a novel integral representation for the Laguerre $F$-function and highlights its utility in deriving an identity for the hypergeometric function ${}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)$ when $z$ lies on the unit circle. Additionally, we present a new integral representation for the associated Laguerre function ${}_1F_1^{(\alpha)}(a;z)$ and explore its implications for the theory of fractional calculus. In the final section, we outline an approach to constructing a two-variable Laguerre version of holomorphic intertwining operators. We also examine the properties of the two-variable Laguerre $S$-function and examine its role in developing a two-variable version of the holomorphic intertwining operator. We conducted ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ line in the dwarf galaxy NGC~5253 to investigate the relationship between the H30$\alpha$ line luminosity and other tracers of stellar activity. This galaxy is renowned for its young stellar population, characterized by a low metallicity of approximately 0.2~Z$_{\odot}$. Our findings reveal that the H30$\alpha$ line luminosity correlates with the H$\alpha$ line luminosity, the far-ultraviolet continuum, and the 12CO(3-2) line luminosity, showing a linear relationship with a correlation coefficient of roughly 0.9. These results indicate that the H30$\alpha$ line serves as a reliable tracer for both massive star formation and star formation in general, even in low-metallicity environments. Furthermore, we determined that the H30$\alpha$ line luminosity is proportional to the star formation rate (SFR) with a proportionality constant of $\sim$10$^{-4}$~erg~s$^{-1}$~M$_{\odot}^{-1}$~pc$^{-3}$, a value consistent with those derived from solar-metallicity galaxies. Additionally, we observed that the H30$\alpha$ line luminosity is proportional to the SFR surface density ($\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$) with a proportionality constant of $\sim$10$^{-4}$~erg~s$^{-1}$(M$_{\odot}^{-1}$~pc$^{-3}$)$^{-1}$, which is comparable to the value reported for NGC~6223, a dwarf galaxy with a metallicity near 0.5~Z$_{\odot}$. These outcomes suggest that NGC~5253 and NGC~6223 share similar star formation characteristics. Consequently, the H30$\alpha$ line is identified as a promising new tool for studying star formation in dwarf galaxies. Finally, we estimated the star formation efficiency (SFE) of NGC~5253 to be approximately 0.01~Gyr$^{-1}$, a figure comparable to other young dwarf galaxies. This similarity in SFE implies that the physical conditions of the interstellar medium in NGC~5253 are also similar to those in other young dwarfs. We introduce the notion of constant orbit equivalence stiffness, which extends the concept of constant orbit equivalence among actions of virtually $\mathbb Z^n$ first established by J. L. Guzman and J. P. Guzm\'an. This derived invariant serves a critical function in analyzing group actions within geometric group theory. Specifically, it acts as an essential tool for determining the orbit equivalence stiffness of isotropic actions and for characterizing the orbit equivalence relations generated by measure-preserving, ergodic, weakly mixing actions on standard probability spaces. Additionally, we demonstrate that every action of a hyperbolic group possesses constant orbit equivalence stiffness, thereby confirming that this invariant is particularly relevant to the study of hyperbolic groups. Furthermore, we establish that for any compact connected Lie group $G$, the constant orbit equivalence stiffness of its orbit equivalence action is determined by the connected components of the centralizer of $G$ within the space of homeomorphisms of the underlying space. These findings suggest that the concept of constant orbit equivalence stiffness may also be valuable in broader geometric group theory contexts. Finally, we examine several properties of this invariant and propose potential directions for future research. This work is a collaborative effort with J. L. Guzman and J. P. Guzm\'an. J. L. This paper introduces a new class of nonparametric estimators for conditional expectation functions, $E[Y|X]$, grounded in nearest-neighbor methods. Unlike traditional nonparametric estimators that rely on kernel weights, this approach assigns equal weight to neighbors of an observed $X$ value while disregarding others. The study demonstrates that these estimators are consistent and derive their limiting risk under a metric appropriate for estimating $E[Y|X]$. A notable advantage is that the proposed estimators do not require the stringent conditions of correct specification for $X$'s density or a correct metric on the space of $X$ values, both of which are often difficult to satisfy in practice. Additionally, the paper presents a bandwidth selection rule and examines a parametric version of these estimators. Simulations indicate that both the parametric estimator and the optimal nonparametric estimator outperform traditional methods when the true model is correctly specified. Furthermore, a semiparametric estimator is developed for a specific missing data scenario, yielding a significant gain in asymptotic efficiency. Finally, the paper applies these estimators to two empirical questions: analyzing the relationship between state-level crime rates and economic conditions, and investigating the link between state-level health insurance coverage and economic variables. Results suggest that while traditional nonparametric estimators perform reasonably well, both parametric estimators and those utilizing optimal bandwidth selection outperform them. The empirical application also reveals that the parametric estimator produces a more plausible relationship between state crime rates and economic conditions. The code required to replicate the paper's results is available at https://github.com/andrews2017/conditional_expectation.

This study introduces a statistical framework for analyzing epidemic dynamics, grounded in a compartmental model that tracks disease progression through distinct phases. The resulting state-space model incorporates a observation function dependent on latent variables representing unmeasured structural parameters. To address the computational and scalability hurdles associated with estimating these latent parameters, the paper proposes a novel observer designed to significantly decrease the effective dimensionality of the epidemic model. This observer relies on a new statistical assessment method that determines when a compartment is active, thereby identifying the specific dynamics the epidemic is undergoing. The paper provides a theoretical analysis of this new state-space model and demonstrates the observer's performance through simulations of dynamic epidicts. These simulations indicate that the observer achieves rapid and accurate identification of epidemic dynamics, even when dealing with noisy and incomplete observations. Furthermore, the study offers a theoretical analysis of the observer's convergence properties. Finally, the approach is applied to real-world data from the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, revealing that the epidemic's behavior is not static but evolves over time. This finding suggests that current control measures are effective in slowing transmission, yet they may require adjustment as the epidemic progresses. Additionally, the analysis indicates that the United States is currently transitioning from one epidemic dynamic to another. These insights could inform future control strategies, such as the potential need to tighten restrictions or implement booster vaccinations. The proposed statistical approach offers a pathway to decomposing observed data into interpretable components, which could facilitate the creation of new metrics for monitoring and evaluating the impact of the pandemic. All code and data required to replicate the analysis are available at https://github.com/alexbeyme/ESSM. Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) are increasingly utilized to forecast future facts, yet their application to link prediction remains underexplored. This study investigates whether pre-trained static models can effectively predict connections in temporal settings. We introduce F2P, a framework that adapts fixed models for link prediction by leveraging pre-trained static representations. Our analysis of three knowledge base embedding methods reveals that carefully fine-tuning them on temporal data yields performance comparable to their fully trained temporal counterparts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses state-of-the-art results on the CoCO dataset. These findings indicate that fine-tuning pre-trained static models is a viable and efficient strategy for link prediction across various TKG scenarios. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/Revisiting-Fixed-Models-for-Link-Prediction-in-Temporal-KG. Additionally, the associated paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03001. To support this work, we have also released a new dataset, CoCO, which features a temporal split derived from the CoCO knowledge base. CoCO is available at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/CoCO. The dataset includes a temporal test split covering events from 2010 to 2019, with fact predictions required for 2020. It comprises 1.2 million training facts, 1.1 million validation facts, and 1.1 million test facts. The top performing model achieved a Hits@10 of 31.2% on this split. We invite researchers to utilize this dataset to evaluate their models on the provided split. This study investigates the geometric examination of Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLML) within the context of high-peak-power ultrafast laser generation. By applying geometric optics, we demonstrate that the stability analysis of the resonator cavity is essential for determining the fundamental characteristics of self-organized KLML mode-locked pulses. Furthermore, we show that the stability region of a generic cavity can be defined by examining a pulse's propagation through a single lens. We also establish that the stability diagram serves as a valuable instrument for analyzing the influence of individual resonator components on the stability of self-organized KLML mode-locked lasers. Additionally, the stability region provides a criterion for identifying the existence of a cavity's TEM00 TEM00 eigenmode. Finally, we present a method for estimating the pulse energy of self-organized KLML mode-locked lasers by utilizing a virtual resonator constructed from the principal ray matrix. This approach enables the estimation of pulse energy based on the parameters of single-pass KLML media. The proposed methods are validated by comparing them with experimental results from our ultrafast laser system. Our findings indicate that these techniques can be applied to analyze the pulse energy of self-organized KLML mode-locked lasers and to guide the design of new ultrafast laser systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these approaches can assist in selecting the optimal Kerr-lens parameters to achieve the highest pulse energy. These results are expected to facilitate the design of high-peak-power ultrafast lasers based on the KLML principle. The methodology is implemented in the Ultrafast Laser Simulator (ULASIM) software, which is available for download at http://www.ulasim.org. This tool enables users to examine the stability regions of various resonator configurations and estimate the pulse energy of self-organized KLML mode-locked lasers. The paper also includes a section on how to use ULASIM to examine the stability regions of self-organized KLML mode-locked resonators and to estimate pulse energy. The paper includes screenshots of the ULASIM interface and a step-by-step guide on how to estimate pulse energy using the software. The design of a new high-peak-power ultrafast laser based on the KLML principle is also presented. This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of hyperoperations with variable orders. Since difference equations serve as discrete counterparts to differential equations, and since calculus is well-established for analyzing function behavior, it is logical to develop difference equations that mirror the established properties of tetration. The study establishes the asymptotic solution to the tetration equation, $f(z+1)=e^{f(z)}$, and derives the associated Liouville extension. Furthermore, we present an asymptotic expression for the iterated exponential function and demonstrate its application to analyze the asymptotic dynamics of the logistic map. These findings are supported by numerical verification. Additionally, we derive asymptotic expressions for the Gamma function and Stirling numbers of the second kind, along with their respective Liouville extensions. The methodology employed in this research is broadly applicable to other problems involving asymptotic behaviors. A key innovation is the introduction of "discrete asymptotics," a novel field that bridges discrete mathematics and classical asymptotic analysis. This work aims to lay the foundational groundwork for future research in this area.

We present new expansions for functions defined on a $d$-dimensional torus, derived from Fourier series, that offer greater flexibility and potentially faster convergence. These expansions utilize covers composed of Voronoi cells centered at lattice points. The classic Fourier-Walsh expansions by Walsh and Polya can be viewed as a specific instance where the covering consists of hypercubes. For every $p \in [1, \infty]$, we derive bounds on the mean error of order $n^{-p/d}$, which match the optimal rates achievable by Fourier series. Additionally, under certain smoothness assumptions, we establish that the mean error bound of order $n^{-(d+1)/d}$ is optimal. We also introduce novel mixed expansion bounds that depend on the anisotropy constant, a metric of the cover's shape regularity. These anisotropy-dependent bounds are optimal up to logarithmic factors for all directions and may be optimal without the logarithmic factor for a subset of directions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the optimal rates can vary from one direction to another, contingent upon the function's smoothness properties. These findings have significant implications for the optimal design of numerical integration rules. Numerical experiments are conducted to illustrate these results and compare the novel expansions against the Fourier series. The experiments indicate that the new expansions often converge more rapidly than the Fourier series. The accompanying code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/SebastianSchauer1992/covers-expansion}. The study investigates the magnetic properties of a novel, previously unexplored single crystal of the centered honeycomb antiferromagnet GdInO$_3$. Using neutron diffraction, researchers identified a commensurate, incommensurate, and helical magnetic structure. Magnetic susceptibility data indicate a three-dimensional antiferromagnetic ordering at $T_{\rm N} = 4.8$ K. At low temperatures, the magnetization exhibits a sharp peak at $H_{\rm c} = 1.5$ T, followed by saturation at $H_{\rm s} = 5.5$ T. Additionally, the magnetoresistance reaches 10% at $H_{\rm c} = 1.5$ T and 20% at $H_{\rm s} = 5.5$ T. These findings demonstrate that GdInO$_3$ is a promising candidate for further investigation into the magnetoelectric effects of honeycomb antiferromagnets. We introduce a technique for creating intricate atomic vapor chamber structures within silicon using standard semiconductor manufacturing methods. This approach involves depositing a reflective metal layer onto the inner chamber walls to isolate the contained vapor. By utilizing this fabricated metal coating, we successfully induce a $60$-degree rotation of the polarized laser light circulating inside. Additionally, we have engineered and produced various chamber designs featuring multiple inlet and outlet configurations. These customized vapor chambers are well-suited for diverse applications, including optical cavities, atomic sensors, and atomic lasers. Furthermore, the chamber's ability to withstand high pressures of atomic vapor facilitates the development of scalable, multi-cellular devices for advanced optical and atomic systems. We anticipate that these nano-fabricated atomic vapor chambers will serve as a valuable component in nano-photonics and provide a new platform for advancing atomic physics research. This study presents a data collection and analysis focused on identifying signs of depression in social media posts. The empirical results demonstrate that machine learning models can successfully detect indicators of depression, with random forest and XGBoost algorithms achieving F1 scores of 0.72 and 0.71, respectively. Furthermore, we investigate feature importance to uncover what constitutes depression indications. Our findings reveal that negative emotions, such as anger, fear, and sadness, are less predictive of depression signs compared to positive emotions like happiness, surprise, and enjoyment. Additionally, we determined that linguistic features, including character n-grams, word n-grams, and part-of-speech tags, are strong indicators of depression indications. Finally, we offer insights into the indications of depression derived from our analysis. These findings can enhance machine learning models designed to detect depression and support early warning systems for the condition. This work examines stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence within feedback-controlled motion systems encountering Coulomb resistance, a common challenge in precision engineering. The analysis focuses on closed-loop systems utilizing proportional feedback, where the "stick" phase corresponds to static equilibrium and the "slip" phase to dynamic movement. To address the non-smooth nature of the closed-loop dynamics, the study employs a regularized model that preserves the stick-slip structure while ensuring smoothness for analytical purposes. Furthermore, global exponential convergence to a unique periodic solution is proven for this regularized system. Finally, it is demonstrated that the findings for the regularized model apply to the original system, under the assumption that initial conditions are sufficiently close to the slip manifold. These theoretical results are supported by simulations of a friction-regulated rotary actuator. Additionally, the work establishes a link to the classical stick-slip problem in mechanical engineering, specifically the boundary value problem of finding periodic solutions for systems with nonholonomic constraints and friction. It is shown that periodic solutions of the original stick-slip system can be derived from these boundary solutions, and their local stability is analyzed. Finally, the paper presents sufficient conditions for the local stability of periodic solutions to periodic friction forces, a result that may hold independent significance. To achieve these results, novel concepts and tools are introduced, including the concept of local equivalence for differential inclusions and a specific local stability analysis for differential inclusions with finite switching times. These innovations are expected to be valuable in broader contexts. The paper is structured into three sections: the first addresses the regulation problem for feedback systems with Coulomb resistance, and the second provides a general analysis of differential inclusions featuring finite switching times. (The third section, omitted here, applies these results to the boundary value problem for periodic systems.) Sequential recommender systems are designed to predict a user's next item based on their past consumption history. However, this underlying behavior is driven by specific intents that the system must identify and address to enhance accuracy. This paper introduces the Hidden User Intent (HUI) framework, which models these specific user intentions. HUI is represented as a directed graph where nodes correspond to intents and edges represent item sequences associated with each intent. We demonstrate the HUI framework using a sequence-to-sequence model that incorporates user identity and item embeddings. This approach enables the model to generate sequences of specific item embeddings tailored to the identified intent. The framework was evaluated on the Amazon Beauty dataset, where it outperformed state-of-the-art sequential recommenders. Furthermore, we illustrate how the HUI framework can improve cold-start recommendations for new users. Experimental results indicate that new users can be recommended items from existing HUI graphs, leveraging the latent intent information they contain. Additionally, the framework was tested on the Spotify dataset, where it successfully identified the intent of a listener's music listening history. The paper also discusses how HUI can enhance explainability in sequential recommender systems. Finally, we outline potential future research directions for the HUI framework, such as modeling multiple HUIs as a sequence of graph nodes, learning HUIs from multiple data sources, and representing the graph using a hypergraph. This work examines the double confluent Heun equation, which governs a particle subject to a specific potential featuring a singularity at the origin and a non-trivial behavior at the boundaries. We demonstrate that this potential can be interpreted as a symmetric, piecewise unfolding of a constant potential at the outset, where the unfolding is governed by two parameters: a strength factor and a width. A corresponding mapping between the two systems is derived, and the text explores the implications of this mapping for both the potential's structure and the wave functions. Furthermore, we analyze the out-of-the-soluble region, showing that the Heun equation retains a simple form of symmetry in this domain. We also investigate the behavior of wave functions at the outset, proving they remain square integrable even when the Heun potential's wave functions are not. Additionally, we establish that the wave functions in the unfolded Heun system exhibit asymptotic properties consistent with those of the Heun equation, despite differing functional forms. Finally, we outline the mapping between the two systems when a self-adjoint extension is required for the Heun Hamiltonian. This mapping is shown to be non-unique, a consequence of the Heun potential's non-uniqueness in the out-of-the-soluble region. We provide a method for selecting a specific mapping that yields a simple form for the wave functions in the unfolded system. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the Heun potential's unique status as a solvable, piecewise potential with symmetric unfolding and a clear physical interpretation may be an illusion. We conclude by discussing the broader implications of these results. We examine the estimation of a low-rank matrix when observations are grouped into sets with distinct error distributions. This framework models various statistical challenges, including multi-arm clinical trials, analysis of variance, and multi-factorial experiments. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of consistent estimators within this setting. These findings rely on a novel technique for determining the rank of random matrices and the rank of the limiting object of randomly perturbed matrices. The proof utilizes tools from noncommutative probability and free probability. We further explore the broader implications of this research for matrix estimation and discuss the development of a new class of estimators based on minimum convex loss estimation. The performance of these estimators is evaluated through both non-asymptotic analysis and simulations. This work serves as a foundational study for matrix evaluation under groupwise heterogeneity. Additionally, it offers a fresh perspective on matrix estimation by integrating concepts from noncommutative probability and free probability. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread illness and death, with the virus exhibiting distinct characteristics in its early and late stages. Although prior research has attempted to classify these phases, the available datasets are often limited and lack the necessary attributes to inform predictive models. This study introduces a novel dataset featuring 16 key metrics, including temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation, collected from 100 patients. We developed a two-step categorization system utilizing the BERT language model. In the first step, BERT determines if a patient's data belongs to the late stage; in the second step, it distinguishes between early and late stages for confirmed cases. The model achieved 96% accuracy in identifying late-stage patients and 94% accuracy in differentiating early versus late stages. These findings demonstrate the model's effectiveness in phase categorization, offering valuable insights for predictive analysis. The eco-evolutionary process encompasses both evolutionary changes, driven by genetic variations, and ecological changes, resulting from shifts in species abundances. This study examines how specific durations and generic regulators influence the coupling between ecology and evolution. We employ a quantitative framework utilizing a simple model featuring a single species with one genetic variant interacting with fluctuating resources. Our results indicate that this system exhibits complex, non-linear dynamics, where evolutionary and ecological timescales are interconnected. Consequently, the eco-evolutionary system demonstrates diverse behaviors, including stable coexistence, stable extinction, and chaotic dynamics. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that various regulators produce distinct outcomes; for instance, while reducing mutation rates accelerates ecological adaptation, lowering the recombination rate diminishes both ecological and evolutionary stability. Ultimately, our findings suggest that eco-evolutionary dynamics are highly sensitive to specific durations and regulators, thereby influencing the resulting patterns of ecological and evolutionary change. These insights can inform the design of eco-evolutionary experiments and assist in predicting the outcomes of interventions aimed at manipulating genetic variation. Additionally, our approach offers a foundation for investigating the eco-evolution of multi-species systems. Finally, we demonstrate how this framework can be applied to address challenges in both natural and artificial selection. Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a highly effective pre-training strategy for speech processing. This paper investigates the antagonistic impacts that speech SSL education can exert on downstream speech tasks. To systematically characterize this phenomenon, we introduce XES, a benchmark designed to comprehensively evaluate how SSL education influences speech processing. XES comprises three components: task performance, transferability, and generalization, with the first two being novel contributions. We constructed a comprehensive benchmark dataset consisting of 10 speech processing tasks. Through extensive experiments, we identified key factors driving the antagonistic susceptibility of speech SSL education, including task similarity, task difficulty, and model architecture. Our findings indicate that higher task similarity and difficulty, combined with a lighter model architecture, result in reduced speech task performance following pre-training. Furthermore, we observed that the pre-training models Unima-Speech-Plus and HuBERT exhibit the most significant transferability to downstream tasks. Finally, we explored mitigation strategies, demonstrating that data augmentation can effectively alleviate the antagonistic susceptibility of speech SSL education. This paper introduces a technique for assessing the sensitivity of drawing a specific conclusion despite the absence of certain data. By integrating the E-value with Bayesian sensitivity analysis, we develop the E-value, a metric quantifying the maximum fold-change in Type I error required for a conclusion to remain valid in the presence of missing evidence. We provide an efficient computational approach to calculate E-values across a broad range of statistical tests. Furthermore, we establish a framework for comparing two E-values to determine whether one is strictly greater than the other. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of E-values through various case studies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/E-value. Given its robustness and efficiency, the E-value proves to be a valuable instrument for evaluating the robustness of statistical inferences in scenarios where data is partially absent. This methodology is particularly advantageous when evidence is missing due to biases such as selective reporting or unmeasured confounding. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the E-value framework; Section 3 covers computation and optimization; Section 4 addresses missing data scenarios; Section 5 presents several examples; and Section 6 offers conclusions and potential future research directions. The technical content relies on the theory of decision-theoretic post-processing, which is explored in depth in our prior work (Chen and Liang 2021). Additional resources, including E-value calculators for other tests and a tutorial, are available at https://ychen1996.github.io/E-value/. Keywords: absent data, Bayesian decision theory, E-value, missing evidence, selective evidence, sensitivity analysis. Mathematical Subject Classification: 62F15, 62F30, 62P10, 62P30.

This study examines the Laurent expansion of the quantum plane, which serves as the simplest non-trivial example of a quantum affine space. We demonstrate that its symmetry group within the algebra of quantum linear differential operators is significantly larger than previously thought. Specifically, we provide a complete list of all $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-family of symmetries. Furthermore, we establish that these extended symmetries cannot be realized as quantum linear differential operators. The findings in this work have broad implications for the theory of quantum integrable systems. As an illustration, we show that the Laurent expansion of the quantum plane possesses a significantly higher number of non-Gaudin integrals of motion than any other known quantum integrable system. Additionally, we prove that these additional integrals are not linearly dependent. This result implies that the quantum plane exhibits a much greater degree of non-Gaudin symmetry compared to all other integrable systems, thereby invalidating the conjecture that the quantum plane is the unique non-rational integrable system. This conjecture originally stemmed from the fact that the Gaudin and non-Gaudin symmetry algebras of the quantum plane share the same dimension. We also investigate the relationship between these two types of symmetry. Finally, we note that our methodology is applicable to other quantum integrable systems. We have already applied this approach to the Gaudin model, where we successfully constructed the complete list of non-Gaudin symmetries. The symmetry structure of the Gaudin model will be the subject of our future research. The Internet of Vehicles (IoV) represents a transformative technology that integrates various vehicles, communication systems, and computing platforms to facilitate seamless connectivity and data exchange among vehicles, users, and the cloud. This emerging ecosystem is expected to generate vast amounts of data, making the privacy-preserving Federated Learning (FL) framework an ideal approach for training machine learning models. FL allows data owners to participate in model training without revealing their underlying data. However, FL systems are susceptible to numerous security threats, including data poisoning, model theft, and resource starvation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning Framework for the Internet of Vehicles (BeFL4IoV). This system leverages the inherent security and transparency of Blockchain to enhance FL security, while also incorporating a novel consensus mechanism to optimize resource utilization. The study provides a detailed analysis of the proposed BeFL4IoV framework and conducts an extensive literature review on its application within IoV environments. Furthermore, the paper outlines the specific security challenges associated with FL in IoV and offers potential solutions to mitigate them. Finally, the article identifies current limitations and proposes future research directions for BeFL4IoV. By integrating Blockchain with Federated Learning, this work aims to establish a more secure learning environment for IoV applications. Additionally, the paper includes a comparison of Blockchain-enabled FL versus traditional FL, along with a discussion on the advantages and disadvantages of each approach. Ultimately, this work seeks to inspire further research into the synergistic benefits of combining Blockchain and Federated Learning for IoV. The source code for the BeFL4IoV framework is available at: https://github.com/Ankit-2001/BeFL4IoV. Keywords: Blockchain, Federated Learning, Internet of Vehicles, Deep Learning, Cyber Security.

Cryptocurrency, a digital asset functioning as a medium of exchange, has seen widespread adoption, with the Python programming language being particularly popular for building related systems. Despite this prevalence, the Python ecosystem contains numerous libraries and frameworks that are either insecure or unnecessary. This study examines the Python libraries most commonly used in the cryptocurrency domain to identify their specific applications and inherent security flaws. By analyzing 1,000 Python repositories from the cryptocurrency sector on GitHub, we identified 104 projects that import at least one of the 100 most common Python libraries. Our findings reveal that 80% of these projects rely on the cryptocurrency-coin package, which is insecure due to its handling of edge cases in encoding and decoding processes. Additionally, we discovered that 40% of the projects import the python-bitcoinlib package, which is unsuitable for cryptocurrency development as it is designed for Bitcoin Core, a cryptocurrency wallet. This research aims to assist Python developers in the cryptocurrency industry by guiding them toward secure and appropriate libraries. Furthermore, it underscores the broader issue of insecure and misused Python libraries within the cryptocurrency ecosystem, a problem that extends to other industries relying on Python. Ultimately, this work highlights the critical need for developers to select the correct libraries to ensure the security of their projects. Urban taggers represent a unique category of tags that are both extensive and dynamic. While recent efforts have focused on creating robust vision systems for this task, they often depend on manually curated tag sets or depend heavily on the frequency of tag occurrences. This study introduces a large-scale, automatic system for identifying urban settings by leveraging social media data. Furthermore, we release a comprehensive, polling-based social image dataset featuring over 100,000 images and 1,500 unique taggers. This dataset enables a polling-driven, semi-supervised method for extracting taggers from images, which we utilize to guide a vision system in learning to detect them. Additionally, we develop a technique to identify rare taggers by analyzing co-occurrence patterns. Finally, we validate our framework for tagger detection across multiple image collections. This study introduces NuSPAN, a proximal mean network designed for reconstructing seismic reflectivity. The technique is grounded in the concept of nonuniform sparse modeling, which unifies the advantages of uniform sparse models—such as the COMPRESSION1D algorithm—by utilizing nonnegative, nonuniform weights to represent reflectivity. To facilitate efficient reconstruction, we develop a proximal mean network tailored for nonuniform sparse models. We assess this approach using both synthetic and field data, demonstrating that it surpasses state-of-the-art competitive methods. Finally, we intend to refine the algorithm by addressing the non-smoothness of the proximal mean network, thereby improving its convergence speed. We introduce a universal finite-length correction to wavefunction overlap calculations between adjacent domain walls in one-dimensional critical quantum systems. This correction arises from the amalgamation of transfer matrices, a technique that enables the analytical calculation of wavefunction overlaps without explicitly constructing the eigenstate basis. By utilizing this method, we derive a finite-size correction of the form $C/N$ to the wavefunction overlap of two domain wall domains within a critical spin chain. The coefficient $C$ is determined by the Haagerup amalgamated transfer matrix, representing an operator that encodes the universal properties of the original system. Furthermore, we apply this approach to a one-dimensional Haagerup model, yielding a precise estimate for the universal subleading correction to the entanglement entropy of an interval. This estimated correction aligns excellently with the results obtained from entanglement spectrum analysis. Consequently, our findings demonstrate that operator amalgamation offers a highly efficient method for computing universal finite-length corrections in one-dimensional quantum critical systems. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python implementation of our method, which can be directly applied to existing literature on transfer matrix amalgamation for estimating entanglement entropy. This tool facilitates the rapid identification of entanglement phases and central charges in one-dimensional quantum systems. Finally, we outline potential future extensions of our approach to higher-dimensional quantum systems. Our study confirms that operator amalgamation is a versatile and powerful technique for calculating universal finite-length corrections, with broad applications in quantum field theory and quantum field theory on the lattice. Specifically, this method offers a means to determine the central charge in conformal field theory through finite-length corrections to wavefunction overlaps on the light cone. Furthermore, our technique can be adapted for use in lattice field theory. We anticipate that operator amalgamation will serve as a valuable tool for extracting universal quantities from lattice simulations. In summary, we present a novel and highly efficient approach for computing universal finite-length corrections, which holds significant potential for advancing our understanding of quantum field theory. We expect that our findings will inspire further research into the applications of operator amalgamation. Finally, we hope that our work will contribute to the broader field of quantum field theory research. Part-of-speech (POS) tagging, which assigns categorical labels to words, is a core component of natural language processing. This paper explores the application of deep learning to historical texts, specifically addressing the challenges posed by non-standardized spelling and morphology. We tackle data reliability issues by employing set-valued forecasting, a technique that outputs a probability distribution over possible POS tags for each word. We evaluate this approach using the Diaria corpus from the 17th and 18th centuries, demonstrating that our set-valued forecasting model surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we illustrate how this method facilitates new applications, such as identifying rare word senses and detecting anachronisms. The code and models are accessible at https://github.com/pos-tagging/pos-tagging-public.

We present two novel principles for generalizing the integrability of vector fields on smooth manifolds. The first principle extends the integrability of smooth vector fields by incorporating discontinuous functions that adhere to specific semi-contractivity constraints relative to a reference smooth vector field. The second principle generalizes the integrability of Lipschitz vector fields further by allowing for discontinuous functions subject to distinct semi-contractivity conditions. Both principles are applied across various examples, including domains within Euclidean space and differentiable loops. Additionally, we establish existence and uniqueness theorems for forward and backward integrals based on these non-smooth integrability principles. We demonstrate that the forward integral for any vector field defined via these principles uniquely determines a solution to the corresponding differential equation, which in turn generates a one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between vector fields derived from non-smooth integrability principles and those derived from probabilistic framework principles. Finally, we construct examples of non-smooth vector fields that cannot be represented within a probabilistic framework. This work addresses a fundamental issue in the theory of non-smooth differential equations. The paper is structured into two sections: the first is expository, offering a foundational introduction to non-smooth differential equations, while the second is investigative, exploring methods for defining non-smooth integrability principles. Our approach offers an alternative perspective to the probabilistic framework introduced in [10]. Furthermore, this research contributes to the field of non-smooth differential equations by providing a framework for studying non-smooth dynamics on manifolds. The successful delivery of Smart City initiatives hinges on effectively managing stakeholder expectations. This paper introduces a new approach to satisfy those expectations by converting local stakeholder input into formal requirements and specifications. We present a new tool designed to assist designers and developers in designing, developing, and deploying Smart City services by automatically generating formal requirements from informal user or stakeholder descriptions. This tool is specifically tailored for contexts where stakeholders possess limited technical expertise and struggle to articulate precise specifications. Furthermore, we outline a case study that demonstrates the tool's utility in supporting the requirements engineering phase of the development and deployment of an existing Smart City service. The findings indicate that the proposed solution is effective for assisting developers and designers in defining formal specifications. Additionally, the tool has the potential to aid in managing stakeholder expectations during the development and deployment of future Smart City services. Keywords: Smart Cities, Requirements Engineering, Formal Specifications.

Concealing quantum operations within error-prone hardware components is a strategy employed to mitigate quantum errors in numerous protocols. However, this approach typically demands substantial overhead in terms of physical qubit counts and relies on the assumption that errors are uniform across all hardware qubits. We introduce a protocol that maintains this error-avoidance principle while significantly lowering physical qubit overhead. This method utilizes qubits representing no-operation gates, which we demonstrate are not required to be more reliable than other hardware qubits. We validate the protocol's efficacy through quantum simulations of various two-qubit gates, including the CNOT and CZ gates. Our findings indicate that, compared to standard error correction methods, this approach eliminates the need for ancilla qubits, simplifies measurement requirements, and enhances fidelity. These advantages are particularly pronounced in near-term superconducting quantum processors, where operations involving specialized qubits—such as those used for concealed inverses or stabilizer measurements—are often less reliable than generic computation qubits. We anticipate this work will inspire the development of new algorithms and circuits for existing quantum hardware. Furthermore, we propose an experimental verification of our results using the quantum computing system at the University of Science and Technology of China. This system features a "concealed inverse" qubit dedicated to implementing no-operation gates, alongside a stabilizer measurement qubit, both of which are less reliable than the computation and coupling qubits. Our analysis suggests that the concealed inverse protocol can improve gate fidelity by up to 10% when utilizing these specialized qubits. Additionally, we demonstrate that the overall circuit fidelity can be enhanced by up to 20% by substituting conventional error correction with our proposed protocol. This improvement is achieved by integrating the concealed inverse qubit and stabilizer measurement qubit into the circuit, alongside the implementation of the concealed inverse protocol. These outcomes hold significant practical value for near-term superconducting quantum computing systems. Finally, we outline several directions for future research. Specifically, we show that the concept of concealing inverses can be extended to implement no-operation gates within multi-qubit gates, such as the Toffoli gate. Furthermore, we illustrate how this technique can be applied to reduce errors in quantum error correction circuits. We also explore the potential of using concealed inverses to lower the threshold for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Finally, we examine the possibility of applying this method to variational quantum algorithms, such as the variational quantum eigensolver. In a regular category $\mathbb{E}$, a binary relation $R$ on an object $A$ is defined as a preorder if it is transitive, meaning $R \circ R \subseteq R$. This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of cocartesian preorder connections relative to arbitrary morphisms within $\mathbb{E}$. A preorder connection between morphisms $f, g: A \to B$ is a map $f \Downarrow g: A \to \mathbf{2}$ satisfying the universal property that the unique map $\mathbf{2} \to \mathbf{1}$ factors through it exactly when $f$ is less than or equal to $g$. The study demonstrates that if $\mathbb{E}$ possesses finite coproducts and stable regular epimorphisms, then cocartesian preorder connections exist if and only if they exist for morphisms from any object to a subterminal object. Furthermore, we establish that preorder connections are uniquely determined by their underlying equivalence connections and specific universal properties. Consequently, if equivalence connections admit a cocartesian lifting, preorder connections exist uniquely up to isomorphism. Additionally, we prove that every preorder connection is both a relation and a functor. Finally, leveraging the fact that preorders correspond to idempotent, commutative, subterminal relations, we deduce that preorder connections exist in any category possessing finite coproducts and stable regular epimorphisms, provided idempotent relations admit a $\mathcal{N}$-sum decomposition. This paper extends the work presented in [10]. Specifically, [10] establishes the existence of cocartesian equivalence connections under similar categorical assumptions, while this article offers a novel construction of such connections based on that result. The paper begins with preliminary definitions and results, followed by an examination of preorder connections, their existence, and construction. It concludes with a comparison to order-preserving connections in extensive categories and equivalence connections in general categories.

Keywords: Preorder connections, cocartesian preorders, cocartesian equivalence connections, order-preserving connections, extensive categories.

The joint occurrence of significant wind speed, wave height, and wave period is critical for assessing the safety of offshore structures and maritime operations. This study introduces a new approach to modeling the multivariate spatial conditional peak envelope process of such environments, grounded in a stochastic model for the standard envelope process. Spatial dependence is characterized through directional spectral cross-spectra, while conditional peaks in each variable are modeled using an extended multivariate Generalized Pareto distribution. The resulting spatial conditional peak envelope processes are simulated via spectral realization techniques. To validate the approach, it was applied to a 10-year dataset of observed wave records from the North Sea. Results indicate that the proposed model effectively captures the primary features of the observed spatial conditional peak processes. Furthermore, the method facilitates the simulation of realistic sea states, enabling researchers to investigate the spatial characteristics of extreme marine environments. This capability is particularly valuable for understanding the locations of maximum wave extremes and identifying regions with the highest risk of wave overtopping. Finally, the study demonstrates how these simulated extreme sea states can inform the estimation of spatial return levels. A key advantage of this method is that it relies solely on observations from a single site, thereby eliminating the need for extensive network data. Additionally, the model avoids the complexities associated with extrapolating from multivariate marginal distributions. However, the approach does require accurate estimates of the joint distribution of the marine variables, which remains a significant challenge. To address this, a bivariate conditional peaks model for marine environments is also developed, and its performance is evaluated using data from a single site. This simpler model successfully represents the observed joint distributions and serves as a practical solution for many practical applications. Finally, the paper provides a detailed discussion on estimating spatial return levels derived from the simulated extreme sea states. Overall, the proposed methodology offers a robust framework for analyzing and simulating extreme marine environments. It is particularly well-suited for scenarios where only limited observational data is available. Moreover, the framework is flexible enough to be extended to other marine variables, such as current speed and direction, or to different phenomena, including tropical cyclones. Finally, the study highlights how this approach can support the design of warning systems for extreme events. These systems can be calibrated using the simulated data to generate realistic and varied scenarios, thereby enhancing the reliability of the warning systems. Current pre-trained vision-language models (VLPs) often fail to capture intricate visual details, a shortcoming that hinders their performance on complex tasks. This paper investigates the text as a potential source of error and introduces a novel filtering strategy that eliminates informative, visual-directed text samples to enhance VLP capabilities. By eliminating these specific inputs, the modified models demonstrate improved feature learning on complex tasks, achieving an 8.5% absolute gain in Pascal VOC segmentation and surpassing state-of-the-art results on COCO detection and recognition benchmarks. Furthermore, we release the VT-CLIP model, which serves as a superior alternative to existing VLPs for a wide range of computer vision applications. Our code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/IDEA-Research/Visual-directed-text-filtering. Additional details regarding experiments and results can be found in our project page: https://idea-research.github.io/Visual-directed-text-filtering/.

Controlling open quantum systems is a fundamental challenge in quantum technology. This study introduces a universal method for steering open quantum systems, utilizing a class of models that can represent any physically realistic unitary or dissipative dynamics. The technique is grounded in the operator switching principle, which involves rapidly alternating between two controllable unitary operations. We demonstrate that this approach can drive an arbitrary system state to a target state with high precision. Furthermore, we show that for most initial and final state pairs, the desired state is reachable within a single switching period. Additionally, we develop a robust strategy capable of implementing arbitrary dynamics on a single period, maintaining robustness against both systematic and stochastic noise. This enables the construction of universal noisy quantum gates using just one switching period. Finally, we outline a practical implementation of this method using trapped ions. These findings establish a robust and universal framework for steering quantum systems, applicable to diverse platforms and open quantum technologies. The method is expected to facilitate the creation of robust quantum gates and enhance the preparation of quantum states. Code and supplementary materials are accessible at https://github.com/QuantumOpticsLab/OperatorSwitching. Quantitative image analysis in radiology and pathology is a rapidly expanding field that relies on the standardized reporting of image analysis outcomes. While the DICOM standard has long facilitated the exchange of images and annotations like labels, guidelines for sharing analysis results remain scarce. This paper introduces Highdicom, a Python framework designed to enable the creation and standardization of encodings for image analysis results, specifically for radiology and pathology. Highdicom offers a set of classes that conform to the DICOM Information Object Definition (IOD) standard, ensuring compatibility with established encoding practices and enabling the generation of verifiable and interoperable results. The framework is accessible at https://github.com/DictumAI/highdicom. To demonstrate its utility, we applied Highdicom to a recent study on lymph node metastasis detection in breast cancer histology slides, which utilized a deep learning model trained on hematoxylin and eosin-stained tissue sections. This framework successfully captured both the quantitative and qualitative characteristics of metastatic deposits within the tissue. The resulting analysis results were encoded into a DICOM Supplemental Group Storage (SGS) file, which can be read by any DICOM-compliant application. We anticipate that Highdicom will serve as a foundational tool for the growing field of quantitative image analysis in radiology and pathology. Furthermore, we believe that extending this framework to other areas of quantitative image analysis, such as histology and digital pathology, will be valuable. Such extensions would require defining new IODs and potentially developing new encoding standards. We envision that Highdicom will act as a starting point for these extensions, thereby promoting standardization across the broader quantitative image analysis community. The examples provided in this paper are available on our GitHub repository, https://github.com/DictumAI/highdicom_examples. Additionally, we have developed a web-based application, https://dictum-ai.github.io/highdicom_viewer/, which supports reading and visualizing Highdicom-annotated images and DICOM-annotomedial (DICOM SGS) results. This application is built using the highdicom_viewer package, another component of the highdicom repository. By facilitating the sharing of results, we aim to enhance reproducibility and reduce bias in these analyses. We encourage researchers in this field to adopt Highdicom for their work.
