This paper introduces and analyzes the Randomized Newton Method (RNM) for solving large-scale stochastic convex optimization problems. In this framework, decision variables are determined by minimizing the expected value of a sum of convex functions, a setting prevalent in machine learning and control. The method is designed to handle scenarios where the number of terms in the objective function far exceeds the dimension of the decision variables. We develop a distributed implementation of RNM and demonstrate that this parallelized version maintains the same convergence rate as a centralized algorithm. Furthermore, we provide numerical evidence confirming the substantial computational gains achieved through this distributed approach. Additionally, we extend RNM into a stochastic variant, offering convergence guarantees for both smooth and nonsmooth cases. Finally, we illustrate the application of this distributed stochastic RNM through a specific power system problem. The key contributions of this work are: (i) the proposal of a distributed RNM for large-scale stochastic convex optimization; (ii) convergence analysis for both distributed and stochastic versions of the method; and (iii) a numerical study applying the distributed stochastic RNM to a power system context. High-resolution triple-coincidence gas time projection chambers (TPCs) are capable of measuring nuclear and molecular recoil spectra with sensitivity exceeding $10^{-11}$, offering a promising avenue for detecting dark matter and neutrinos. These devices utilize three independent signals to identify recoils, typically comprising ionization charge, ioninduced fluorescence, and acoustic waveforms generated by the expansion front of ionized gas. By combining these measurables, researchers can effectively suppress electronic and environmental backgrounds, as well as distinguish nuclear recoils from beta events. This study details fluorescence and acoustic measurements from a tetrode-based TPC filled with 95% isobutane and 5% CO$_2$, which recorded ionization, acoustic, and fluorescence signals from 1.1 MeV electron recoils. The data demonstrate that these three signals are tightly correlated, allowing for the reconstruction of ionization energy with a resolution better than 10%. Furthermore, we compare the acoustic and fluorescence signals to identify optimal coincidence cuts that enable the discrimination of nuclear recoils. These findings facilitate future investigations into the correlation between ionization energy and nuclear recoil energy. Ultimately, this work aims to establish a framework for the design and optimization of tetrode TPCs for dark matter detection. The experimental techniques and data analysis methods described here are also applicable to other nuclear recoil detectors, such as those designed for neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. The experimental apparatus is currently being upgraded to enhance sensitivity for dark matter and neutrino research. This paper was submitted to the 2018 Snowmass Cosmic Frontier Committee. Commercial driving serves as a vital driver of economic growth and social advancement, yet it is severely hindered by the lack of sufficient data. This scarcity is particularly acute for underrepresented groups, such as women, who often lack the necessary information to make informed decisions. To address this disparity, we introduce a novel approach to moderating commercial machine outputs that leverages specialist knowledge to generate context-aware recommendations for choices regarding employment and career advancement. By utilizing a dataset of 100 successful female drivers, we developed a collection of heuristics to guide AI-based decision-making. Our results demonstrate that these contextual choices can enhance the utility of AI for specific populations. Furthermore, our evaluation of various moderation techniques reveals that specialist-based output offers the most equitable and beneficial means of employing AI to support individuals in commercial driving careers. This represents the first application of contextual choices to this domain. We conclude that AI should be employed to facilitate informed decisions within commercial driving, and we have made our code and data available to assist researchers in advancing this field. This work is grounded in the principles of Participatory Design and AI for Social Good. (This research is supported by the UKRI DTP: DTP-AI4SG). This paper serves as a technical report for the Out-of-Lexicon Challenge, which investigates word-form generalization. Specifically, it examines the capacity of neural network models to identify and generate novel words that are absent from their training vocabularies. Acting as a "stress test" for neural networks, this challenge probes their internal word representation mechanisms. The stress test comprises two tasks: the First-Time Seeing (FTS) task, requiring models to recognize unseen word forms, and the First-Time Seeing Production (FTSP) task, which demands the generation of novel, previously unseen word forms. This report examines model performance across various architectures and hyperparameter configurations. The primary objective of these experiments is to determine the conditions under which models excel at the FTS and FTSP tasks. Our findings indicate that while certain models demonstrate strong performance on these tasks, achieving high results consistently across both tasks simultaneously remains difficult. Furthermore, we have established a publicly accessible leaderboard at https://tldr.io/challenges/oolc. We anticipate that the insights gained from this report and the leaderboard will facilitate the development of even more robust models for handling out-of-vocabulary words in the future. Additionally, we plan to release a dedicated repository for this challenge, which will include a tutorial on performing FTS and FTSP evaluations with PyTorch and various popular models. This resource will enable researchers to easily replicate our experiments and assess the vocabulary generalization capabilities of their own models. The repository can be accessed at https://github.com/tldr-io/challenges-oolc. Finally, we acknowledge the contributions of the challenge organizers, the review team, and all participants. We introduce a novel approach for identifying geodesic routes within Gaussian-based field theory frameworks. This method relies on the principle of geodesic action minimization, where the action is defined through the intrinsic metric of field configurations. We demonstrate that this technique successfully recovers established results from both statistical mechanics and quantum field theory, yielding novel insights into interacting scalar field models. Furthermore, we apply our formalism to a stochastic setting to derive a stochastic geodesic equation, which can be utilized to explore field configuration landscapes. Finally, we present initial numerical findings regarding these stochastic geodesics. These findings indicate that stochastic geodesics exhibit a mean-field trajectory consistent with deterministic geodesics, while also displaying significant fluctuations around this mean path. We conclude that stochastic geodesics offer valuable new perspectives on field space, potentially advancing our understanding of field theory landscapes. Additionally, we demonstrate the method's applicability to a broad range of actions, including those derived from machine learning. This work is supported by grant no. 1610219. The primary objective of this study is to determine whether the sporadic nature of box office revenue collection impacts the validity of standard econometric methodologies used to forecast total earnings. To address this, we examine the time intervals between distinct revenue bursts and their cumulative effect on prediction accuracy. Our analysis indicates that both traditional and recently proposed approaches to estimating "To Be Announced" (TBA) outcomes experience reduced precision when applied to films with irregular revenue streams. Consequently, we introduce a straightforward yet effective correction to enhance the accuracy of these techniques. Our findings are robust, and we conclude that the proposed adjustment is both simple and effective. While our methodology is designed for cross-sectional data, it is also applicable to panel datasets. Furthermore, we note that although our framework was developed for the film industry, it can be adapted to other sectors where revenue is collected intermittently. Finally, we demonstrate that these corrections yield significant economic benefits. To our knowledge, this represents the first time that both economic gains and losses associated with such corrections have been quantified. This study examines how zigzag edges and external fields influence electron transport through narrow armchair graphene regions connected to broad electrodes. The edges are modeled as sources of spin-dependent electron scattering. By analyzing the dependence of current on the edge scattering parameters, we identify a regimatable regime where the Datta and Das spin transistor achieves high efficiency within the narrow segment. Furthermore, we show that applying a transverse magnetic field can suppress this spin sensitivity, a finding that aligns with experimental data. These results offer a pathway for developing spin transistors based on nanostructures featuring zigzag edge sources of spin-dependent scattering. Additionally, we observe that while the Landau-Zener formula accurately predicts spin polarization in broad graphene areas, it fails to do so for narrow sections. These findings are derived using the nonequilibrium Green's function method. Finally, we discuss the potential for achieving high-efficiency spin transistors using existing graphene nanostructures. This research was conducted within the framework of the Russian Science Foundation grant No. 19-13-00058.

This study establishes analogues of Korovkin's theorem for the weak convergence of sequences of functions mapping from a compact Hausdorff space to a Banach lattice. The theorem addresses nonlinear operators characterized by a specific type of monotonicity relative to a cone, alongside scenarios involving nonlinear operators and weak convergence within Banach spaces. Additionally, we provide applications of these results to spaces of continuous functions and investigate convergence types for nonlinear operators with mildly nonlinear modulations mapping into Banach lattices. Furthermore, we examine applications concerning vector-valued measures and functionals, as well as vector measures and multivalued functions. This work serves as a generalization of the first author's previous publications. All cited results are novel. The concept of pancyclicity in graphs is extended to linear operators acting on coordinate spaces. By defining the Hamiltonian of a graph as the independence quantity of its adjacency operator, we demonstrate that this parameter is equivalent to that of its cycle coverage quantity. Leveraging these equivalences, we establish sufficient conditions under which the Hamiltonian becomes pancyclic. Furthermore, we present a partial characterization of the Hamiltonian for coordinate operators defined on orthogonal matrices. The discussion concludes with an analysis of the significance of the Hamiltonian in the context of quantum computing. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive review of graph invariants derived from the independence quantity of a graph's adjacency operator. Notably, the Hamiltonian on orthogonal matrices emerges as a novel invariant in this classification. The paper also examines the relationship between the independence quantity and the dimension of a coordinate space defined over an orthogonal matrix. Finally, we establish a lower bound for the independence quantity of a graph's adjacency operator and provide a characterization for the minimum value when this quantity equals the graph's dimension. These findings are achieved through an analysis of binary adjacency matrices. Additionally, we characterize binary adjacency matrices whose associated graphs possess an independence quantity equal to their dimension, and we characterize those matrices for which the maximum independence quantity is achieved. All characterizations concerning binary adjacency matrices are formulated using binary vectors. The study of these characterizations gives rise to a binary vector space equipped with a binary operation termed the "independence product." We demonstrate that this space constitutes a commutative monoid and provide a characterization of its zero element. Furthermore, we characterize monoids formed by vectors of identical length and explore the relationship between this construction and binary vector spaces of various lengths. The paper also investigates the relationship between the independence product and the tensor product of matrices. Finally, we characterize binary vectors based on the length of their binary representation and characterize the binary independence product through these binary representation lengths. Additionally, we characterize vectors within the binary monoid based on their lengths. The study also characterizes vectors in the set $\{0,1\}^n$ according to their positions within the lexicographically ordered set $\{0,1\}^n$. Finally, we characterize the binary independence product using vector lengths and binary representation lengths, and we characterize vectors in the binary monoid based on their lengths and binary representation lengths. This study presents a new method for characterizing hadron production in heavy-ion collisions by analyzing the directed flow ($v_1$) of positively and negatively charged particles. Utilizing data from the ALICE experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) across Pb+Pb and Xe+Xe collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}= 200$ GeV, we observe that the $p$/$\bar{p}$ ratio and the charge-sign dependent $v_1$ exhibit a correlated behavior. Specifically, as the p/$\bar{p}$ ratio approaches unity, the flow of positively charged particles surpasses that of negatively charged ones. This phenomenon is also evident in Xe+Xe collisions, where the p/$\bar{p}$ ratio is lower than in Pb+Pb collisions, yet the $v_1$ of positive particles remains higher. Furthermore, the data indicate that this effect is more pronounced in the midrapidity region, suggesting a potential link to the local baryon chemical potential. These findings offer a novel perspective on the baryon asymmetry within the quark-gluon plasma and its influence on hadron production. This study introduces a new approach to estimating the linear Koopman operator for dynamical systems, termed the Sparse-Grid-Driven Adaptive Spectral Koopman (SGDAS) method. By integrating sparse grid sampling with adaptive spectral basis selection, SGDAS optimizes the balance between computational efficiency and estimation accuracy. The algorithm begins by generating an initial estimate of the spectral representation of the Koopman operator using data from a sparse grid within the state space. Subsequently, it calculates the mean squared error (MSE) across the entire state space to identify a reduced set of states that ensures a specific accuracy threshold. These selected states are then sampled at a higher resolution to refine the initial estimate. To enhance accuracy, the SGDAS method incorporates adaptive spectral truncation, which dynamically adjusts the number of retained eigenfunctions to mitigate overfitting. Numerical experiments conducted on three nonlinear systems demonstrate that SGDAS achieves superior accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art algorithms while maintaining high computational efficiency. Furthermore, the method's practical utility is highlighted by its application in estimating the spectral representation of a nonlinear dynamical system derived from a chaotic time series. This case study enables accurate prediction of the chaotic system's future trajectory and the identification of its unstable periodic orbits. Overall, the findings indicate that SGDAS serves as a robust and versatile framework for estimating the spectral representation of the Koopman operator, with significant potential for advancing various applications in dynamical systems. Keywords: Koopman operator, spectral representation, nonlinear dynamical systems, chaotic time series, prediction, unstable periodic orbits. The Sinkhorn-Byzagov algorithm is a well-known iterative method for solving the Schrödinger problem, an optimization task designed to determine a joint distribution for two random variables that maintains their specified conditional marginals while minimizing relative entropy against a given joint distribution. Originally formulated by Schrödinger in 1949 as an alternative to the principle of least action, this problem was later adapted by Peierls and Howard for applications in nuclear physics. The theoretical foundations of the Sinkhorn-Bayezov algorithm were established by Fortet and Koenig, with subsequent refinements by others. By 2010, the method was applied to image processing by Maume-Beurrier and Hachem. More recently, Goldman, Ma, and Ma introduced a variant of the Schrödinger problem that yields the Sinkhorn algorithm as the solution; this version accommodates asymmetric penalties and relaxes strict constraints on the input joint distribution. This paper investigates the convergence of the Sinkhorn algorithm when the corresponding Schrödinger problem admits no solution. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the Sinkhorn iterations converge to a solution that minimizes one of the two relative entropies. Furthermore, we provide a geometric interpretation of these iterates, linking them to projections onto convex cones and illustrating their application in matrix scaling. Finally, we extend these findings to a generalized framework applicable to networks with multiple sources and sinks. The results presented here offer a complement to existing literature, which primarily addresses scenarios where the Sinkhorn problem does have a solution. Additionally, we propose a conjecture regarding the behavior of Sinkhorn iterates in cases lacking a solution, a hypothesis that could prove valuable for applications such as matrix balancing and network optimization. This conjecture posits that the iterates converge to a rank-deficient matrix, a phenomenon that may also occur in regular solution cases. We support this with numerical evidence, including an example of slow convergence in a matrix-balancing scenario. The methodology employed in this study draws upon techniques from recent research by Fortet, Fortet and Koenig, and Ma and Ma. Our work also introduces novel concepts, such as analyzing the asymptotic behavior of iterates within the space of couplings and utilizing a specific type of coupling to establish convergence. The paper is structured into three sections, with the first providing an overview of the problem and its applications, the second detailing our main results, and the third offering a geometric perspective on the problem. This study details the measurement of the $t\bar{t}$ production cross-section in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis focuses on events where at least one top quark decays leptonically. A dataset of $200\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ was examined, covering three distinct event categories defined by the leptonic decay of the remaining top quark: electrons, muons, or both. To mitigate the substantial background from non-top quark events, the analysis employs multivariate discriminants. The resulting cross-section is determined to be $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 692 \pm 10 \text{ (stat) } \pm 14 \text{ (syst) } \pm 10 \text{ (lumi) } \mathrm{pb}$, which aligns with the Standard Model prediction. Additionally, the top quark pair production cross-section is derived as a function of the invariant mass of the top quark pair. The measured differential cross-sections are compared against next-to-leading order QCD predictions and various Monte Carlo event generator simulations. The analysis also examines the production of electroweak top quark pairs, finding that their differential cross-sections are consistent with predictions from electroweak and QCD mixed production. Furthermore, the top quark polarization is investigated, with the spin asymmetry measured as $A_\mathrm{spin} = 0.69 \pm 0.05 \text{ (stat) } \pm 0.04 \text{ (syst) }$, a value that agrees with QCD predictions. Finally, the cross-sections for the production of $T\bar{T}$ and $S\bar{S}$ di-new-physics particles are assessed, where $T$ and $S$ represent vector-like top and scalar partners, respectively. These findings are compared with various beyond-Standard-Model scenarios, including simplified models and those based on Little Higgs and supersymmetry frameworks. All results are consistent with the standard model production of top quark pairs. The paper concludes with a discussion on the statistical power of the ATLAS data and the methodology used to derive these measurements. This work is based on the ATLAS Collaboration paper: Eur. Phys. This study examines the localization dynamics of a central site within a ring of $N$ classically chaotic sites connected to a classically linear chain. Our numerical findings indicate that when chain transport is localized, energy reaching the central site remains trapped, whereas global diffusion within the ring enables the system to equilibrate through the chain. Consequently, the system's evolution is governed by a competition between chain and ring diffusion. Furthermore, we explore how initial conditions influence this competitive process. Finally, we extend our analysis to a ring of $N$ sites linked to multiple linear chains. We demonstrate that systems with symmetric configurations exhibit symmetric evolution, while those with asymmetric conditions display asymmetric behavior. Additionally, we observe that even in asymmetric setups, the system can reach equilibrium if all chains are coupled to central sites. These outcomes are supported by statistical analysis. Ultimately, our results underscore the critical role of all system components in facilitating energy transfer. This insight is particularly significant for understanding energy dissipation in nanostructures and could inform the future design of efficient energy transfer mechanisms. Finally, we outline potential future research directions. Specifically, we propose that future investigations should examine the effects of weak coupling between the chain and the chaotic system, as well as the impact of weak nonlinearity within the chain. Furthermore, it is essential to explore whether a similar phenomenon occurs in other configurations, such as systems featuring a central classically chaotic site or multiple classically chaotic sites arranged in a ring. This could be achieved by substituting the current central or ring sites with different structures, such as molecules or nanoparticles. Additionally, we suggest that future work should address whether the observed behavior persists in quantum systems, thereby offering a comprehensive approach to advancing this field. Finally, we note that our statistical analysis indicates that the probability of a system achieving equilibrium increases with the number of sites in the ring. This trend is intuitive, as a larger ring provides more pathways for energy to reach the chain, thereby enhancing the likelihood of equilibration. However, it is important to recognize that this statistical insight is derived from a specific model and may not apply universally to all systems. Therefore, further research is necessary to determine whether this behavior is a unique characteristic of the present model or a general phenomenon. To address this, we recommend extending the analysis to other models, such as those with different coupling schemes or with all sites being chaotic. This could be accomplished by implementing various coupling methods or by considering a configuration where all sites are classically chaotic. The paper addresses the inclusion of generalized Bessel functions within the Janowski category. A key outcome is derived from establishing the convexity of the function $z\mapsto \frac{f(z)}{g(z)}$ defined on the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$. Furthermore, the Bessel-type function $B_{\lambda}(z)$ is demonstrated to be strongly starlike of order $\frac{1}{2}-\lambda$ for the case where $0\leq \lambda<\frac{1}{2}$. This result extends the finding of Bulboaca (2009), who proved that $B_{\lambda}(z)$ is starlike of order $1-\lambda$ under the condition $0\leq \lambda<1$. Additionally, it is established that $B_{\lambda}(z)$ is $\alpha$-convex for any $0\leq \alpha<1-\lambda$. The work also explores related topics, including the inclusion of $B_{\lambda}(z)$ in the Janowski class, subordination between two generalized Bessel functions, and the properties of these functions within the Janowski category. Finally, the inclusion of the function $f(z)=z+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}na_nz^n$ in the Janowski class is derived using the established results. This paper aims to stimulate further research into the properties of Bessel-type functions. Urban interaction intensity is a defining characteristic of city life, and the pandemic has profoundly altered interaction patterns, thereby impacting urban sustainability. This study examines how variations in daily mobility and social distancing compliance influenced the intensity of urban interactions across different income levels during the pandemic. We analyzed the mobility and panel data of 1,000 U.S. cities from 2019 to 2020 using fixed effects models. The results indicate that while increased remote work reduced income inequality in urban interactions, adherence to social distancing measures exacerbated the gap. This adverse effect is more pronounced in cities with high pre-pandemic mobility and low population density. Furthermore, the inequality-amplifying role of social distancing was driven by the decline in social interaction among lower-income groups, whereas higher-income groups maintained relatively stable interaction levels. These findings highlight the critical need to safeguard social interactions for all income groups amidst public health crises. Finally, we propose that implementing public health measures in a targeted manner, rather than uniformly, could mitigate their negative impact on income disparity within urban interactions. Additionally, we explore the potential of big data-driven approaches to sustain urban social connections during future epidemics. This research offers valuable insights into the complex relationship between public health interventions and urban income inequality. By elucidating the mechanisms through which pandemic-related policies affect interactions across income groups, it provides a foundation for designing more equitable public health strategies. Ultimately, this study advances our understanding of urban social dynamics and their significance for sustainable urban development. Furthermore, it underscores the necessity of developing public health policies that ensure social connectivity remains accessible to every income level during future outbreaks. This aligns with the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goal 10, which aims to reduce inequality worldwide. By promoting more equitable public health measures, this research contributes to achieving the UN's broader goal of making societies more inclusive and cohesive. This study evaluates the performance of a nonlinear black-oil field-separated preconditioner applied to a two-phase flow problem within a heterogeneous porous medium, utilizing flow simulations from the open-source software OGS. We contrast this approach with a nonlinear fully coupled formulation and two other field-separated methods: the classical Schur complement and a recently introduced approximate Schur complement that employs a linearized interface problem. Results indicate that both the classical and approximate complement operators outperform the fully coupled system, with the approximate variant offering superior performance by reducing complexity. Furthermore, the approximate complement operator is less sensitive to the permeability contrast between phases compared to the classical version. Finally, the use of a multigrid method to solve the resulting interface problem enhances the overall efficiency of the field-separated strategy. Overall, these findings suggest that the proposed approximate complement operator is a highly effective choice for field-separated strategies. Additionally, the paper examines the multigrid approach employed to resolve interface equations, which is essential for achieving the described efficiency gains. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed operator remains robust in simulating cross-flow in uneven porous media, a scenario where the classical black-oil complement operator previously failed. All simulations were conducted using OGS, an open-source software for subsurface flow and transport. The source code for the proposed operator is available in the OGS repository under the tag `ogsv2.1.0-100-g00272207`. We anticipate that this work will facilitate the development of more efficient and robust strategies for two-phase flow simulation. Additionally, we aim to encourage the research community to adopt field-separated strategies, which are currently underutilized in the field. To support this, we have developed a general framework for implementing such strategies, which is also accessible via the OGS repository. This work serves as a foundation for future research into field-separated strategies. Our goal is to enable the field to replicate our results and to foster the development of increasingly efficient and robust field-separated methods. We believe this will lead to a significant increase in the application of these strategies in the near future. To facilitate this, we have provided the code for our general field-separated strategy implementation, which can be accessed through the OGS repository. This will serve as a starting point for future research. Additionally, we have included a detailed description of the code implementation to assist readers in understanding the approach. This detailed description is also available through the OGS repository. We hope this will assist readers in replicating our results and in developing increasingly efficient and robust field-separated strategies

This study introduces a theoretical framework for achieving chiral light propagation within an "optical chamber" by utilizing a planar, unilateral metasurface at one of the bilateral walls. This device functions as a one-way mirror, permitting transmission in only a single direction while maintaining a specific phase and impedance. We demonstrate that within a such a chamber, certain wave modes can become confined and directed solely along the chamber's axis, exhibiting both handedness and unilateralness. These unilateral chiral modes offer potential applications in chiral sensing and energy storage. Furthermore, we illustrate that these unique properties emerge from the interference between standing waves and the partial images of the source produced by the mirrors; this phenomenon is closely linked to the Fresnel drag effect and the motion of the virtual mirrors associated with the metasurface wall. The proposed unilateral chiral optical chambers may serve as versatile platforms for investigating fundamental physical principles, including those related to light's unilateral behavior, motion, and reflection. Additionally, this framework can be extended to other systems involving unilateral metasurfaces and bilateral mirrors. Finally, we outline potential applications for these chambers in energy storage and harvesting. This research was conducted within the framework of the Russian Science Foundation grant No. 19-12-00031. The corresponding author is A. V. Zayats. Finally, we examine the matrix model representation of the Liouville CFT bound. In the classical regime, the matrix model for the CFT on the complex plane is defined by a trace of a product of two $N \times N$ random Hermitian matrices, $H_1$ and $H_2$, where the probability distribution for each is determined by the two-point function. It demonstrates that within the Minkowski space-time framework, the cosmological constant must be zero. Cities are increasingly adopting digital technologies to enhance urban living, boost productivity, and mitigate climate change. Central to this transformation is the development of a unified digital infrastructure, which relies fundamentally on comprehensive, high-resolution geospatial data. To support this, we present GUIDES (Geospatial Metropolitan Infrastructure Data Engineering Resolutions), a data model designed for large-scale, multi-resolution city information systems. This model integrates diverse geographic and thematic datasets across three primary levels: street, block, and administrative boundaries. We have applied GUIDES to model a digital infrastructure for the city of Turin, Italy, and have validated its utility through a case study in data integration. The framework is also well-suited for integration with emerging global digital infrastructure initiatives, such as the European Union's INSPIRE. To facilitate broader adoption, the GUIDES model is available as a ready-to-use ontology within the Resource Description Framework (RDF) and the World Wide Web Consortium's Conceptual Modeling language (OWL). The complete project can be accessed at http://www.digi-turin.eu. Supplementary material is provided in additional file 1. We report on heating dynamics and temperature distributions within a two-dimensional Coulomb lattice of $^{40}\mathrm{Ca^+}$ ions, where the lattice temperature is established by the thermalized collective vibrational modes. The temperature is determined by analyzing the spin dynamics of a single probe ion. The temperature distributions align with the Boltzmann distribution, while spin dynamics match the prethermalization model. The derived heating velocity, $0.015~\mathrm{K/ns}$, is consistent with heating rates observed in other ion traps. These findings demonstrate that collective vibrational modes thermalize quickly, enabling the creation of ion lattices with controlled temperatures. Furthermore, the probe ion serves as an effective method for measuring the heating speed of the lattice. The proposed technique is applicable to other ion lattices and offers a pathway to achieve lattices with lower temperatures. Additionally, we outline the potential for lattices with tunable heating speeds, which could facilitate the study of non-equilibrium thermodynamics. This approach is compatible with existing tools for lattice manipulation, such as optical dipole forces and electric fields. The experimental platform is also suitable for investigating quantum simulation and thermodynamics in two-dimensional systems. The ability to precisely control vibrational mode temperatures in ion lattices may advance the development of quantum simulators and support the creation of quantum technologies, including quantum memories and heat engines. We present a fully quantum mechanical approach grounded in time-dependent density functional theory to simulate the nonlinear terahertz response of molecules within a tip-sample junction, specifically for application in tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS). This response is driven by a local terahertz field that modulates both the electronic and vibrational states of the molecule. Our study examines how factors such as molecular position relative to the tip and the oscillation of the tip under terahertz excitation influence the resulting nonlinear response. Furthermore, we explore how combining these nonlinear effects with optical excitation can advance high-contrast, chiral tip-enhanced spectroscopy. Finally, we address the computational demands of this method and outline potential strategies to mitigate them. These findings establish a foundation for future theoretical and experimental efforts aimed at achieving high-energy terahertz spectroscopy using the nanometer-scale spatial resolution characteristic of TERS. Additionally, our approach is applicable to a broad spectrum of surface-enhanced spectroscopic techniques. The code is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7100000.

This study reports microwave observations of 25 nearby galaxies conducted using the Sardinia Radio Telescope (SRT) as part of a survey designed to detect non-thermal emission and potential microwave background components. The SRT's 10-meter dish, operating at frequencies between 1 and 26 GHz, was employed to image these galaxies in the K band. The selected sample comprises 25 galaxies previously observed in the Green Bank Multi-frequency Survey (GAMMOS) at 1.4 GHz, selected to ensure a wide range of star formation rates and morphologies. We present the first detailed analysis of these observations, comparing our GAMMOS data with the new K-band results. Our primary findings include: (1) All 25 galaxies were successfully imaged, with most showing consistent morphologies across both frequencies; (2) The SRT images reveal a strong correlation between radio emission and H$\alpha$ emission, suggesting that the observed radio signal is primarily thermal in nature; (3) A significant scatter exists between radio luminosity and H$\alpha$ luminosity, which we attribute to variations in the electron-to-proton ratio and the thermal-to-non-thermal emission ratio; (4) The SRT data indicate a linear relationship between radio luminosity and H$\alpha$ luminosity, with a slope of approximately 0.5, aligning with theoretical predictions for thermal emission. These results suggest that the SRT is highly effective at detecting thermal emission, a capability that could be leveraged to search for non-thermal components in future observations. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the search of the Microwave Background Radiation (MBR) components.

This study investigates the origins of entropy changes in caloric materials, utilizing ammonium sulfate as a representative molecular ferroelectric. We demonstrate that entropy variations stem from multiple contributors, including alterations in short-range hydrogen-bonding structures, long-range ordering, and configurational entropy. By combining calorimetric data with molecular dynamics simulations, we quantify the magnitude of each factor. Our findings indicate that entropy changes are primarily driven by short-range ordering, which is partially offset by long-range ordering. These results offer a quantitative framework for comprehending entropy alterations in molecular ferroelectrics and establish a methodology for identifying high-performance caloric materials. Specifically, we propose that materials exhibiting large caloric effects should display distinct caloric responses in their high- and low-temperature specific heats. Furthermore, we predict that ammonium sulfate possesses significant magnetic caloric potential, a hypothesis supported by a substantial magnetic entropy change observed near its caloric transition temperature. These conclusions are corroborated by a strong correlation between the entropy change and the magnitude of the caloric response in ammonium sulfate. Finally, we identify several existing caloric materials that align with our proposed criteria. Collectively, this work provides a quantitative approach for unraveling the sources of entropy changes in caloric materials and establishes a new criterion for the discovery of superior caloric substances. The accompanying Python code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-ASU/Caloric-Entropy-Source. Additional details regarding the sources of entropy changes in caloric materials can be found in our supplementary materials. Reinforcement learning (RL) models are frequently employed to analyze decision-making processes, yet it remains unclear whether neural activity genuinely reflects the optimal computations these models entail. This study addresses this issue by applying two distinct RL frameworks to experimental data gathered from participants performing a probabilistic learning task. The participants were instructed to select between two options to maximize rewards, acquiring the underlying probabilities through experience. The two RL models utilized were the Rescorla-Wagner (RW) model and the Q-learning (QL) model. Both were fitted to the participants' choices using a Bayesian hierarchical approach. Subsequently, the posterior distributions of the participants' latent parameters were sampled to simulate new trial outcomes using both the RW and QL models. These simulated outcomes were then used to calculate trial-specific temporal difference (TD) errors. We then examined the correlation between these TD errors and the trial-by-trial BOLD signal in the ventral striatum, a core region of the brain's reward system. The QL model yielded a superior fit to the observed data compared to the RW model. Furthermore, TD errors derived from the suboptimal RW model showed a significantly stronger correlation with BOLD signals than those from the optimal QL model. These findings suggest that RL models merely approximate actual brain computations, and that neural encoding of TD errors indicates that learning is driven by a process more sensitive to outcome characteristics than optimality. This research underscores the necessity of integrating neuroimaging data when employing RL models to analyze behavior and decision-making. Additionally, it offers a framework for investigating how the brain's encoding of prediction errors influences decision-making. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for theories of consciousness and free will. We introduce root structures derived from the complexification of the $E_8$ lattice, which arise from root systems linked to affine Dynkin diagrams. These structures are constructed using an orthonormal basis of 24 vectors within the 24-dimensional space spanned by the complexified basis vectors of the simple roots of the affine Dynkin diagram for $E_8$. These basis vectors correspond to the vertices of the 4-dimensional regular simplex. Our analysis demonstrates that these root structures support quantum entanglement, as evidenced by the existence of both maximally and partially entangled states. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these root structures for Bell's theorem, specifically in relation to quantum contextuality. We define a set of 120 hyperplanes, noting that any three linearly independent vectors from our root system lie on at least one of these hyperplanes. This arrangement creates a configuration where any vector can be expressed as the sum of exactly three others, forming triangles. These triangles are categorized into three distinct types based on the specific root vectors they contain. We illustrate how these categories of triangles can be utilized to construct Kochen-Specker sets, thereby demonstrating quantum contextuality. Additionally, we provide an outline of the relationship between our proposed root structures and the Leech lattice. Finally, we explore the construction of root structures with analogous properties by applying the same methodology to the other 19 Dynkin diagrams. This process yields 19 further root structures, each possessing at least one family of hyperplanes with the property that any two linearly independent vectors are contained within at least one such hyperplane. Collectively, these 20 structures (the original $E_8$ case plus the 19 additional ones) constitute the solution to the $E_8$ case of the $K_4$-design problem. This paper investigates the approximate close neighbor search problem for time series under the Fréchet distance. We establish the first narrow limits for this problem within the one-dimensional Euclidean model. Specifically, for any parameter $\epsilon > 0$, we demonstrate that no algorithm can achieve a $(1-\epsilon)$-approximation within sublinear query time, assuming the Orthogonal Range Reporting (ORR) conjecture. Furthermore, under the stronger assumption of the Stronger Orthogonal Range Reporting (SORR) conjecture, we prove that no algorithm can attain an approximation factor better than $1 + n^{o(1)}$ in sublinear query time. These findings represent the first negative results concerning the achievable approximation factors for this problem. Additionally, we show that the first-order necessary conditions for the optimality of the discrete Fréchet distance are both necessary and sufficient. Our proofs rely on a novel reduction from the Fréchet distance to the Euclidean Shortest Path problem. Our primary technical contribution is a new lower bound for the Euclidean Shortest Path problem, which is of independent interest. We also present a general framework for establishing conditional lower bounds in geometric algorithms that achieve query times approaching linear time. Finally, our work introduces the first general framework for analyzing the trade-off between approximation factors and query time for Fréchet distance problems. Our framework is broadly applicable to a wide class of problems involving Fréchet distance. We demonstrate that the first-order necessary conditions for the optimality of the Fréchet distance approximation are sufficient for establishing narrow limits in this class of problems. This result follows from a novel extension of the Fréchet distance to metric spaces, which we term the metric path problem. The metric path problem is a generalization of the Euclidean Shortest Path problem and is closely related to the Fréchet distance. Our lower bounds for the Euclidean Shortest Path problem are derived from this metric path problem. We also provide a general framework for establishing conditional lower bounds for geometric problems with query times nearly linear in the query size. This framework is applicable to a wide class of geometric problems. A primary challenge in large-scale educational testing is the inherent uncertainty in scoring, which stems from the subjective nature of evaluating complex tasks, particularly in open-ended items. This uncertainty is typically quantified using a binary Asker Agreement (AA) matrix, where a '1' indicates consensus between two askers on a correct response and a '0' signifies disagreement. While Asker Disagreement (AD) is commonly used to identify responses requiring further review, it often leads to the unnecessary re-scoring of clearly correct or incorrect answers, thereby wasting resources. To address this, we introduce an Iterative Bayesian Reconstruction (IBR) approach designed to minimize assessment errors in large-scale tests. By integrating AD information with response characteristics, IBR calculates the probability that a specific response is misclassified by askers. This method is grounded in a latent variable model that incorporates item parameters and student ability estimates derived from standard item response theory. We validate IBR's effectiveness through a case study using data from the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), which is widely recognized as the most comprehensive educational assessment system globally. Our findings demonstrate that IBR significantly reduces misclassification rates, offering a more efficient alternative to current methods for identifying responses needing re-scoring. Additionally, we explore how to leverage AD data to enhance the accuracy of initial asker ratings. These results hold significant implications for the design of large-scale assessments, especially regarding the development of open-ended questions. Finally, we outline the advantages of IBR for scalable assessment and propose a novel framework for the automated correction of student responses. This framework enables the automatic identification of potentially misrated responses, facilitating the application of correction techniques to historical datasets. Ultimately, this research aims to advance the understanding of assessment error mitigation and provide a foundation for future large-scale assessment design. We introduce HiTMap, a Hierarchical Topological Map designed for navigation in unfamiliar settings. This system constructs a tree-structured hierarchical topological diagram from sensor data, utilizing subgraphs to compress knowledge about the environment. The process involves two main components: 1) a topological diagram generator that builds and maintains the diagram's structure, and 2) a topological diagram navigator that guides the vehicle to a target location. Furthermore, we present a novel topological diagram generator inspired by the hierarchical object detection method MDDNet, which constructs the diagram's architecture, identifies adjacent nodes, and assigns weights to represent distances between locations. Additionally, we develop a method to acquire global topology by connecting nodes across different subgraphs, thereby integrating information from multiple locations and establishing the initial tree structure. Finally, we implement a local metric navigation module to complete path planning and execution. Experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully navigates to target points in unfamiliar settings and effectively handles unseen environments. This paper introduces the S2 array code set, which is derived from the Z-array code set by applying multivariable functions. Within the S2 code set, there exists a specific subcode set, referred to as the Z-supplementary array code set, that maintains the same size and orthogonality as the original Z-array code set. The primary benefit of the Z-supplementary array code set is its ability to enhance the capacity of an existing array code set without altering its fundamental structure. This capability is particularly valuable for applications requiring array processing. Furthermore, the Z-supplementary array code set offers the advantage of generating a wide variety of diverse code sets. To demonstrate this, the paper also presents an inter-group supplementary code set, developed by extending the Z-supplementary array code set using multivariable functions. This new code set provides diversity while preserving the structural properties of the original Z-array code set. The study includes examples of code sets generated using multivariable functions to illustrate these concepts. Additionally, the paper explores the application of S2 array code sets in array processing, specifically for direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation. It is shown that employing S2 array code sets can significantly improve the performance of array processing systems. Finally, the paper compares the performance of multivariable functions with other extension methods, such as direct product and Kronecker product, in the context of array processing. The results indicate that multivariable functions outperform these other methods in terms of processing efficiency. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive approach to designing array code sets that can be utilized for array processing. The proposed method offers a flexible and efficient way to generate code sets with specific properties, such as orthogonality and diversity, which are essential for various array processing applications. The paper also discusses the potential applications of these array code sets in areas like channel estimation, data transmission, and signal detection. By utilizing multivariable functions, the proposed method can generate a wide range of code sets with diverse properties, thereby enhancing the performance of array processing systems. The paper concludes by outlining several directions for future research, including the development of new code sets with unique properties, the investigation of array code sets for other applications, and the exploration of new extension methods for array code sets. The authors believe that multivariable functions hold significant potential for generating a wide variety of array code sets with specific properties, making them a valuable tool for advancing array processing technology. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both medical and industrial settings for visualizing internal structures. However, obtaining high-quality images necessitates prolonged data acquisition, which significantly restricts its utility in dynamic scenarios. This study introduces a joint reconstruction framework designed to simultaneously address the polyenergetic issue, sensor noise, and material breakdown within industrial CT. By integrating total variation (TV) regularization with variational splitting techniques, the proposed method effectively reduces noise and artifacts stemming from polyenergetic effects. The approach is validated using synthetic and real-world industrial CT datasets. Numerical results demonstrate that the method achieves state-of-the-art performance, producing highly accurate and sharp images with minimal noise. Furthermore, the method successfully recovers material breakdown with exceptional precision. The entire procedure is fully automated, eliminating the need for manual data preprocessing. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness against sensor noise, maintaining stable performance even under severe noise conditions. The proposed approach is implemented using the open-source PyTorch library. The corresponding Python code is accessible at: https://github.com/abdelrahimh/CT. The PyTorch library utilized in this work is available at: https://pytorch.org. The method is built upon a novel total variation regularizer, which is detailed in our paper: Abdelrahim, H., & Katsaggelos, A. K. (2020). A new total variation regularizer for image reconstruction. IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, 29, 6200-6213. The Python code for this regularizer can be found at: https://github.com/abdelrahimh/TV-regularizer. Gap surface plasmons (GSPs) are supported by the collective oscillation of electrons within the nanoscale space separating two metallic structures. This phenomenon is heavily influenced by the system's geometry and the inherent nonlocality of the metal's dielectric response. In this study, we employ a local dielectric function to model the metal, incorporating an exponential decay term that mimics the nonlocal effect of electron spill-out. This approach enables us to analyze the impact of electron spill-out on how plasmon resonances vary with the metal-electrode separation. Our results demonstrate that the exponential decay term can either enhance or diminish the metal-plasmon coupling, depending on the specific resonance mode and the rate of electron spill-out. Furthermore, we establish that an electron layer emerging from one of the metals can induce the sudden appearance of a new plasmon resonance as the interval width decreases. This finding underscores the critical role of electron spill-out in plasmonics and suggests that this mode could be harnessed for sensing applications. Additionally, we show that this effect can be accurately replicated using a nonlocal dielectric function. Finally, we examine the influence of the electron-electron interaction strength within the spilled electron layer and its effects on the plasmon resonance. These insights provide a foundation for designing novel electron transport devices and plasmonic sensors. Our findings indicate that these structures can operate in the terahertz frequency range, offering a pathway to achieve high sensitivity in plasmonic sensing. Specifically, we observe a significant enhancement in sensitivity when the spilled electron layer is present. This enhancement is further improved by increasing the electron-electron interaction strength within the layer. Consequently, this suggests the potential for developing new types of plasmonic sensors that leverage electron spill-out. We also explore the possibility of detecting the presence of the spilled electron layer through plasmonic resonance measurements. This is achieved by analyzing the shift in resonance frequency as a function of the electrode interval width. We demonstrate that the resonance frequency exhibits a distinct kink as the electron layer crosses the gap between the electrodes, providing a clear signature for detecting the spill-out electron layer. These results highlight the potential for plasmonic sensing applications that exploit electron spill-out. Finally, we discuss the potential for plasmonic devices that can manipulate electron flow by tuning the plasmon resonance frequency through adjustments to the electrode width. This capability is enabled by the strong dependence of the resonance frequency on the electrode interval width, which is caused by the accumulation of spilled-out electrons within the gap. This study addresses the Named Entity Recovery (NER) challenge, which involves identifying all entities within a given sentence and annotating them with a specific label set. Unlike traditional NER, NER with Recovery (NERwR) necessitates the detection of previously unseen entities. While most existing recovery methods rely on ensembling multiple NER predictions, these approaches often incur high computational costs and lack robustness. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel framework that leverages term importance scores (TIS) derived from a language model to facilitate NERwR. Our method employs a straightforward procedure to integrate NER predictions with TIS, enabling the recovery of novel entities. We validate our approach across eight NER datasets spanning diverse domains, demonstrating that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we present an analysis of the impact of various hyperparameters and provide illustrative examples to highlight the effectiveness of our proposed framework. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/NERwithRecovery.

Temporal data is ubiquitous in contemporary society, manifesting in diverse formats ranging from complex time series to simpler sequences. While data visualization is a well-established field, the specific challenge of visualizing time sequences remains underexplored. This paper introduces a survey of existing techniques for visualizing multivariate time series and time sequences, with a primary focus on multivariate and multi-attribute sequences. The study categorizes these methods by their data encoding strategies and highlights key design considerations. Furthermore, the paper outlines potential application domains and proposes several directions for future research. Given the growing prevalence of temporal data, this work aims to stimulate interest in visualization techniques that facilitate user interaction with time sequences. Additionally, it offers a foundation for developing visualization methods tailored to less explored data types, such as temporal networks and tabular data. Finally, the survey identifies specific design aspects that require further investigation. Overall, this research contributes to the visualization community by addressing a previously neglected area of temporal data visualization. Specifically, it examines how visual encodings for time sequences can be enhanced to promote engagement and interaction, thereby aiding data comprehension. The paper concludes with a list of potential future directions for the field. Finally, it presents the authors' original contributions, which include: (1) a comprehensive survey of visualization techniques for time sequences, (2) an analysis of visual encodings designed to improve interaction and understanding, and (3) a set of proposed future directions for temporal data visualization. The work is supported by the following grant: 1R01MH116003-01A1. Keywords: Time Sequence Visualization, Multi-Attribute Time Sequence Visualization, Time Series Visualization, Temporal Data Visualization, Engagement.

Digital health records (DHRs) encompass a wide array of diverse data formats, including text, time series, and structured fields. While existing methods for tasks like disease prediction have focused on specific data types, this paper introduces DSwingGraph, a novel framework designed to process heterogeneous DHRs. DSwingGraph employs a unified, unsupervised similarity learning approach to capture data characteristics without requiring labels, thereby enhancing generalizability. This process generates similarity graphs that preserve relationships among diverse records. Furthermore, a SWIN transformer-based encoder is utilized to extract features from these graphs, while a graph neural network (GNN) decoder aggregates and aggregates information across the records. The method is evaluated on a multi-label disease prediction task using data from the MIMIC-IV clinical database. Experimental results demonstrate that DSwingGraph surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/DSwingGraph. Given its robust performance, the model holds significant potential for application in other domains involving digital health records. The authors hope this model will inspire future research in this field. Additionally, the paper seeks to inspire researchers to explore diverse data sources to develop more generalizable models. This study examines the electric double layer (EDL) adjacent to an uncharged or charged soft interface within an electrolyte solution, incorporating solvent polarization effects. A novel closed-form analytical solution for the Poisson-Boltzmann equation is developed, applicable to both nonpolarizable and polarizable scenarios. Using this solution, we compute the electrostatic potential, Gouy-Chapman length, and surface capacitance, analyzing their dependencies on physical parameters. Results indicate that solvent polarization can substantially alter the characteristics of the electric double layer. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the surface capacitance of the charged soft interface follows a saturation behavior at high salt concentrations, a feature that distinguishes it from the capacitance of an uncharged soft interface. These findings may prove significant for modeling soft matter systems containing charged membranes or biomolecules in electrolyte environments. Additionally, the derived analytical solution is expected to be a valuable resource for researchers in this field. Finally, this work introduces a new perspective on the interaction between solvent polarization and soft interfaces, a subject of growing interest in soft matter physics. The methodology employed here is also broadly applicable to other areas of physics. To facilitate future research, all relevant source code is provided in the supplementary materials. The Python script used to generate the plots is available at: https://github.com/abhishekbhagwat/EDL_with_polarization. One promising strategy to mitigate these issues involves automatically generating software specifications from unstructured source materials like emails, meeting notes, and project documents. This paper introduces a collaborative network encoding approach designed to minimize total energy consumption across a wireless network by jointly optimizing relay timetabling, power distribution, and energy trade-offs between a base station (BS) and its relays. The objective is to reduce the BS's total energy usage, which encompasses both electrical consumption and signaling costs, relative to a scenario without collaborative encoding. To achieve this, the study proposes a low-complexity scheme where the BS and relays simultaneously determine their own encoding strategies and power levels to optimize the collaborative encoding gain. Relay timetabling is managed by having relays transmit data only when they can contribute to the encoding gain, thereby reducing their total power usage. The proposed scheme is proven to converge to a solution that optimizes the sum of the BS's electrical energy usage and the savings from reduced signal power. Furthermore, the design ensures the BS operates within its power constraints while remaining below a specified signaling rate. Finally, the paper demonstrates the scheme's performance in a two-relay setup through simulations. Results indicate that, compared to a non-collaborative scenario, the proposed method can achieve up to a 40% reduction in total energy usage. Additionally, the scheme is shown to be robust against variations in channel conditions and noise levels. Robustness is assessed by varying the noise power spectral density and the number of relay nodes, with the latter specifically testing the scheme in a multi-relay environment. Simulation outcomes confirm that the scheme maintains its performance in such settings. Finally, the computational complexity of the proposed solution is analyzed. The paper concludes that the scheme is suitable for practical implementation due to its low computational complexity. This is evidenced by the fact that the encoding strategy computation time scales linearly with the number of relay nodes, making the approach feasible for real-world deployment. In summary, the proposed scheme effectively minimizes total energy usage in collaborative network encoding, offering an energy-efficient solution for wireless communication systems. It is applicable to various scenarios, including point-to-point point-to-multipoint, and can be extended to other collaborative encoding schemes. The scheme is also compatible with different modulation techniques, such as QPSK and 16-QAM. Additionally, it can be adapted for use in both line-of-sight and non-line-of-sight communication channels. These filters are essential for reducing bias in 1D representations used for 1D to 1D scan alignment, as well as for 1D data annotation and modeling. While prior research has introduced 1D filters for alignment tasks, they often struggle with 1D data of limited size and diversity. Furthermore, existing 1D filters for 1D to 1D scan alignment have not been evaluated. To address these gaps, this paper introduces a robust and diverse filter designed to mitigate prejudicial biases. Non-linear high-intensity X-ray absorption near-edge structure (N-Linear HIXANES) represents a recently introduced technique for probing electron groups within solids under extreme conditions. This method involves irradiating samples with high-intensity, tunable X-ray pulses to generate non-linear electron groups, which are subsequently analyzed via time-resolved diffraction. The resulting N-Linear HIXANES data reveals the temporal evolution of these electron groups. However, a formalism to describe the electron groups and their changes over time is currently lacking. This paper introduces a rate framework for N-Linear HIXANES, defining the rate of the electron group as a vector composed of the photon rate, electron group lifetime, and electron group size. This framework enables the characterization of the electron group's formation rate, size, and lifetime. Furthermore, the paper provides a mathematical model for the evolution of electron groups and their associated rate, offering a tool to interpret N-Linear HIXANES data. Finally, a proof-of-principle experiment is presented to demonstrate the applicability of this framework. The results indicate that the electron group size is proportional to the photon rate but independent of the X-ray pulse duration. Additionally, the group lifetime is found to be independent of both the photon rate and group size, suggesting that the group evolves through internal degrees of freedom. These findings offer a foundation for future research into the dynamics of electron groups. Ultimately, this work establishes a formalism for N-Linear HIXANES, facilitating the interpretation of experimental results and the design of upcoming experiments. The proposed framework can be readily applied to existing N-Linear HIXANES datasets. Additionally, the paper includes a tutorial on utilizing the N-Linear HIXANES rate to interpret data, with a specific example provided. This example illustrates how the rate framework can be used to identify the specific X-ray pulse responsible for creating the electron group. Such insights are crucial for advancing the field and for the continued development of N-Linear HIXANES as a research tool. The work is intended to guide future experiments and enhance the utility of N-Linear HIXANES for investigating electron groups in solids. The paper also offers a roadmap for advancing the field, including a discussion of the challenges and opportunities ahead. The roadmap highlights the need for new theoretical models to interpret N-Linear HIXANES data, as well as new experimental techniques to generate and study electron groups with greater precision. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved significant advancements in automatic modulation classification (AMC), yet their susceptibility to adversarial attacks remains a critical challenge. This paper introduces a robust GAN-based approach designed to ensure resilience against both transferability and reconstruction noise within the GAN framework during adversarial attacks on modulations. The proposed method employs a dual-generator architecture: the first generator creates adversarial samples by injecting perturbations into the input waveform, while the second generator synthesizes samples from both the original and the first generated adversarial inputs. Additionally, the system integrates both original and generated inputs into a classifier for modulation recognition. Experimental findings demonstrate that this dual-generator configuration effectively counters adversarial attacks on modulations, yielding superior performance compared to single-generator systems. Furthermore, the use of both original and generated samples in the recognition process significantly enhances overall accuracy. The results indicate that the proposed dual-generator architecture provides robustness against adversarial attacks on modulations, surpassing the accuracy levels achieved by the single-generator system. Keywords: Automatic Modulation Classification, Generative Adversarial Networks, Deep Learning, Adversarial Attacks.

We introduce dCM, a novel method for contrastive representation learning that enhances standard contrastive learning through domain adaptation. While traditional contrastive learning leverages augmentation to identify representation learning objectives, our approach utilizes this strategy for domain adaptation. We demonstrate that this form of adaptation strengthens contrastive learning, particularly in scenarios involving significant domain shifts caused by substantial domain gaps or restrictive objectives. Furthermore, we show that our method achieves competitive or superior results compared to existing self-supervised methods on image representation learning and pretraining tasks. Additionally, in supervised learning scenarios, our method surpasses related techniques like transfer learning and fine-tuning, especially when dealing with large domain shifts. Finally, we validate the method's effectiveness in natural language processing through experiments on text classification and sentiment analysis. This paper introduces a framework for modeling machine intelligence regarding dynamics and model error. Within this approach, the model error is represented as the sum of a stable, unstable subspace component, and a fully connected deep neural network. We establish both existence and uniqueness results for model error dynamics that possess a machine intelligence structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of model error solutions exhibiting chaotic behavior and possessing a deep learning structure. Additionally, we investigate the existence of invariant manifolds within the space of models possessing deep learning structures. The implications of this work extend to establishing criteria for the existence of invariant manifolds and chaotic solutions in model error solutions, thereby offering insights into the limitations of model-based control and machine learning. Finally, numerical examples are provided to validate the existence and uniqueness theorems and to illustrate deep learning structures in model error solutions. These structures may inform the design of neural networks intended to learn model error dynamics.

We present high-resolution (0.15 arcsec) 12CO J=1-0 and 13CO J=1-0 observations of the Dragon infrared dark nebula (G035.19+00.30), revealing a core structure with a mean width of 0.6 pc and a mass of 1.2×10^5 solar masses. Core expansion is indicated by the 13CO emission, which is brighter at the center and exhibits a blue-shifted velocity offset of 1.5 km/s relative to the 12CO emission. This expansion is likely driven by the formation of a massive star cluster, supported by the detection of 100 Class 0/I protostars and 10 protostars in the advanced Class II/III stage. Furthermore, we identified a compact HII region (0.01 pc) coinciding with the brightest 13CO emission, which we attribute to the protostars in the advanced stage. The presence of this compact HII region suggests that the Dragon core is expanding due to the prior formation of massive stars. Additionally, we detected a 1.3mm continuum source with a luminosity of 1.2×10^38 erg/s, consistent with the emission from this compact HII region. This star formation scenario in the Dragon core aligns with the theory of massive star formation occurring in expanding cores. We also observed a large-scale filamentary structure in the Dragon core, with a mean width of 0.05 pc and a length of 0.6 pc, which is likely a remnant of the original cloud. The density of this structure is approximately 10^4 cm^-3, indicating that it is insufficient to trigger further star formation. Overall, our findings suggest that the Dragon core is currently in an advanced stage of massive star formation. This tool enables researchers to investigate the statistical distribution of these shadows, the likelihood of a planet being fully obscured, and variations in shadow length caused by the PBH's altitude. We examine a two-dimensional system of interpenetrating rigid wedges constructed from spheres, where each branch consists of multiple spheres and the wedge angle is defined by the variation in branch splay. This interpenetrating architecture prevents any translational motion, restricting the system to collective bending modes. We demonstrate that this system exhibits two distinct stages with opposite splay variations, which can be interpreted as a chiral phase transition. Furthermore, we show that phases characterized by identical splay variations correspond to nonchiral phase transitions, resulting in either first or second order depending on the splay fingerprint power. Finally, we establish that increasing the number of spheres per branch raises the system's rigidity, thereby lowering the second-order transition from the critical temperature to the absolute zero. These findings suggest that a system of interpenetrating wedges serves as a model for materials displaying chiral properties, such as liquid crystals, which can be engineered through the interpenetrating structure. Additionally, we note that the physical mechanisms driving phase transitions in this system are analogous to those observed in the Frank elastic theory of liquid crystals. Consequently, our theoretical framework may prove valuable for designing functional materials and devices that leverage chiral characteristics. Additionally, we explore the potential to control the splay variation in these wedges through external fields. Specifically, we show that an electric field can be utilized to manipulate the system's chiral nature. These results indicate that our theoretical model can guide the design of functional materials and devices, with external fields serving as a means to regulate the system's chiral properties. Parameter-efficient methods have emerged as a viable alternative to full fine-tuning for adapting pre-trained models to downstream tasks. This paper introduces a novel approach that employs a single, uninitialised token to adjust pre-trained models for specific tasks. We demonstrate that this unique token can replicate the performance of full fine-tuning across various tasks. Furthermore, we show that employing multiple such tokens allows the model to accommodate multiple tasks concurrently without necessitating any form of model merging. Finally, our experimental results indicate that employing two tokens yields complementary benefits. The code is accessible at https://github.com/roymz12/Unique-Token-Adjustment. Keywords: parameter-efficient adjustment, pre-trained models, full fine-tuning, model merging, multi-task learning.

This paper investigates the preference ordering of subsets, a concept introduced by Barbera (1989) and later expanded by Barbera and Monge (1998). These frameworks involve a finite collection of subsets paired with a finite set of agents, where each agent holds a strict linear preference relation over the subsets. A central challenge in this area is identifying subsets that are preferred by a majority of the agents. This study specifically targets issues in set augmentation, a topic initiated by Barbera and Monge (1998) and recently addressed by Barbera and Barberà (2020). The latter work examines two distinct social choice problems: first, determining an initial subset when agents have strict linear preferences over subsets; and second, selecting an appropriate additional agent for an existing group when agents hold strict linear preferences over individuals. We analyze these problems within both non-contextual and contextual frameworks, comparing the two to derive new findings. Our results indicate that the choice between adding an element to a subset or recruiting a new member to an existing team can yield different social choice properties. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between these issues and majority voting on individual objects, demonstrating that while the rules for team selection may differ from those of majority voting, they can still be derived from it. Finally, we establish conditions under which the issues reduce to majority voting and propose axiomatic characterizations for each scenario. The paper concludes with a discussion on computability issues.
