We introduce a technique for distinguishing the Majorana peak from other conductance peaks during tunneling spectroscopy, a method that leverages Ohmic dissipation within the lead states. This dissipation is simulated by incorporating resistive electrodes into the normal lead connections. When the resistance of these electrodes approaches the resistance quantum, $R_{Q}$, the resulting dissipation causes a sharp reduction in conductance, thereby isolating the Majorana conductance peak. This approach is particularly effective for samples exhibiting multiple conductance peaks, enabling a clear identification of the Majorana conductance feature. Furthermore, this method is applicable to both spinless and spinful tunneling scenarios. We have conducted a theoretical analysis of this mechanism, which is anticipated to be valuable for future experimental investigations into Majorana modes. Our findings indicate that the proposed dissipation mechanism can be observed in samples lacking Majorana modes, such as clean Al nanowires, where it is expected to generate a conductance peak at zero bias. Additionally, we have examined the effects of temperature and broadening on the conductance peak, demonstrating that the dissipation-induced conductance feature remains robust under realistic experimental conditions. Finally, we have explored the potential for detecting this mechanism in real samples through measurements of the current-voltage relationship. These results are expected to assist experimentalists in distinguishing the conductance peak associated with the Majorana mode. This work is based on a thesis submitted to the Graduate School of Science, Osaka University, by Masaki Kaji as partial fulfillment of the requirements for the Doctor of Science degree in Physics. The thesis is titled: Tunneling Spectroscopy with Ohmic Dissipation utilizing Resistive Electrodes: A New Technique for Identifying Majorana Peak. Supervisor: Prof. Masaki Oshikawa. Keywords: Topological Superconductivity, Majorana Zero Mode, Tunneling Spectroscopy, Ohmic Dissipation, Current- Voltage Characteristics.

This paper examines linear bandit problems featuring action sets with varying cardinalities, where the diversity of the action space is the primary driver of exploration. We demonstrate that the standard optimistic exploration technique, the Upper Confidence Bound (UCB), performs suboptimally in such settings. Furthermore, we prove that the regret guarantees associated with UCB are optimal when all action sets share the same cardinality. Our findings are grounded in a novel statistical hypothesis testing problem concerning the identifiability of a sparse vector from a limited number of one-dimensional linear measurements. We show that the minimum sample size required to detect a $k$-sparse vector scales with $k \log(n/k)$, where $n$ represents the total sample size. This statistical result confirms that exploration strategies must allocate more resources to actions with lower sparsity. Finally, we establish that the Minimax Optimal Exploration (MINIMEX) algorithm, introduced by Li et al. (2017), achieves the optimal regret rate for linear bandits with diverse action sets. Additionally, we derive the first minimax optimal rate for parameter estimation in this context. The paper concludes with a discussion on the broader implications of our findings. To support these conclusions, we provide a proof of the lower bound for parameter estimation and include a proof for the optimality of MINIMEX. The remaining proof regarding the optimal exploration rate for UCB is presented in the appendix. In gapless graphene, the orbital magnetic moment of a Landau level (LL) is non-zero and scales inversely with its index $n$ ($\propto 1/n$). Conversely, valley polarization induced by spin-orbit coupling (SOC) gap opening—the valley Hall phenomenon—vanishes as $1/n$ for large $|n|$. This study demonstrates that an orbital Hall phenomenon emerges as a substitute for the valley Hall phenomenon in gapped graphene. Notably, the orbital velocity is independent of $n$, resulting in orbital polarization that remains independent of $|n|$. Furthermore, the orbital Hall conductivity is determined by spin Chern numbers, which are derived from the Berry curvature phase in configuration space. Finally, we show that the orbital Hall current in gapless graphene is not a quantized conductance but rather a quantized charge transfer between adjacent LLLs. These findings offer a new perspective on the Hall effect in graphene and may have significant implications for spintronics. Additionally, this research provides a theoretical foundation for the potential experimental observation of orbital Hall phenomena in graphene. To facilitate such experiments, we have also prepared corresponding device structures. Finally, we propose a potential application for this orbital Hall effect. Specifically, we show that the valley polarization of spin-down electrons can be inverted by applying a magnetic field, thereby enabling valley polarization control. This outcome is achieved without requiring broken time-reversal symmetry. Consequently, this work may offer a novel approach to valleytronics. In summary, this study advances both orbital and valley Hall physics. To verify these predictions, we have prepared a series of device structures. We believe these results will inspire further experimental investigations into orbital Hall phenomena in graphene. However, their susceptibility to data contamination remains an underexplored vulnerability. This paper investigates the interaction between data contamination and GDM using reinforcement learning. Specifically, we introduce a novel reward-based reward engineering approach designed to maximize the reward gained by contaminating graph data for GDM. Furthermore, we present a new metric, the Graph Data Poisoning Accuracy (GDPA), to assess the effectiveness of contamination strategies. Our experimental results indicate that contamination can substantially impair the performance of GDM when evaluated with GDPA. Additionally, we find that the Graph Poisoning Accuracy (GPA) metric serves as a reliable predictor of GDM performance following contamination. Finally, our findings suggest that robust training methods, such as adversarial training, can effectively mitigate the negative impacts of data contamination on GDM. We introduce a technique for aligning catalogues that integrates astrometry with photometry. By modeling the joint probability distribution of two-dimensional offsets and color differences, we demonstrate that combining both measurements yields a catalogue alignment that surpasses using astrometry alone. This approach is validated through simulations and by combining the Pan-STARRS1 and VISTA survey catalogues. Our findings indicate that the combined solution achieves a 10% reduction in total RMS error compared to using astrometry independently, while maintaining nearly identical photometric quality when photometry is included. Furthermore, we show that this method can be extended to align multiple catalogues simultaneously. This technique is especially valuable for applications like photometric redshift estimation, where minimizing systematic errors is paramount. Additionally, the approach is readily applicable to any paired or multiplex catalogue analysis. The code required to reproduce these results is publicly available at https://github.com/tpg123/catalog_alignment. This work is based on the master's thesis of Thiago P. G. Gontijo.

This paper investigates the properties of minimal finite vertex sets $V_{\phi}$ in an infinite hypergraph $(V,E)$, where $\phi\subseteq V$ represents a vertex set. A set $V_{\phi}$ corresponds to $\phi$ if $\phi$ is obtained by adding a single vertex to $V_{\phi}$. The study focuses on examining various characteristics of $V_{\phi}$, including their existence, size, and isolation within $\phi$. Furthermore, the study introduces and analyzes the $\phi$-isolation number $\iota_{\phi}(V_{\phi})$, defined as the count of vertices in $\phi$ that are isolated relative to $\phi$. This count is demonstrated to be independent of the specific choice of $V_{\phi}$. Additionally, the $\phi$-isolation number is shown to be closely related to the minimum size of a minimal set $V_{\phi}$ corresponding to $\phi$. Finally, the paper explores the existence of minimal sets $V_{\phi}$ and their associated $\phi$-isolation numbers for hypergraphs $(V,E)$ where $\phi$ is an infinite set of vertices. In this context, the $\phi$-isolation number is defined as the supremum of $\iota_{\phi}(V_{\phi})$ over all finite minimal sets $V_{\phi}$ corresponding to $\phi$. The study concludes by demonstrating that this $\phi$-isolation number can be significantly larger than the size of any finite minimal set corresponding to $\phi$. These findings are illustrated through several examples, including the specific case of graph induced subgraphs. The paper also presents applications of these results to the theory of infinite graphs, specifically addressing the existence of vertex partitions into $k$ classes where no class contains an independent set of a given size. This problem is closely linked to the concept of off-diagonal Ramsey numbers. The study reveals that the maximum size of a vertex class in such a partition, given that no class possesses an independent set of a certain finite size, can be substantially smaller than the Ramsey number associated with that size. Conversely, it is possible to construct infinite hypergraphs where every subset of vertices of a specific size possesses an independent set of a predetermined size. These results are supported by an analysis of the $\phi$-isolation number for induced subgraphs of various well-known infinite graphs. Ontologies serve as formal models for knowledge, typically visualized as directed, often cyclic, graphs. However, standard graph visualization techniques struggle to effectively display ontology structure and connections when the number of concepts and relations is large. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization method designed to represent large ontologies as non-hierarchical, layered, and partially ordered directed graphs. By leveraging existing graph visualization techniques, OntoPlot enables the clear identification of knowledge gaps and redundancies, thereby supporting ontology management. The proposed approach is validated through two case studies: (1) a visualization comparison of three real-world ontologies, and (2) an interactive visualization of a synthetic ontology containing 10,000 concepts and 150,000 relations. The method is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/Mythos-Research/OntoPlot. Video demonstrations are available at https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL2222222222222222. This study addresses a semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) scenario involving a significant domain shift caused by varying levels of background noise. Domain penaltieies are introduced to mitigate this shift, while CycleGAN is employed to handle domain variations. The primary goal is to enhance ASR performance using uncorrupted clean audio by leveraging noisier, annotated speech data. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses the baseline by 10.4% WER. Additionally, ablation studies confirm that the approach remains effective even with a reduced number of annotated speech samples. Deduction serves as a fundamental reasoning mechanism for intelligent agents, enabling them to generate novel knowledge grounded in existing facts and established rules. While humans and animals have long utilized deduction for directed navigation, current research predominantly focuses on inferring new facts through deduction rather than applying it to decision-making and navigation. This study introduces the concept of active deduction navigation, wherein intelligent agents employ deduction to guide their actions. To achieve this, we developed Proactive Deduction Graphs (PDG), a novel framework that integrates environmental knowledge with observation and action capabilities to facilitate active deduction navigation. We evaluated PDG on a 3D simulated urban platform featuring a knowledge graph city, demonstrating that it significantly surpasses baseline methods in navigating among self-governed robots. Furthermore, the framework exhibits robust generalization across diverse deduction rules and knowledge graphs. The ProActive Deduction Navigator (PADN) is now accessible at https://github.com/robinliu1994/PADN. Our findings indicate that active deduction navigation is a viable and promising approach for intelligent agents operating in real-world environments. Thermophoresis, or the Soret effect, drives the movement of particles in a fluid under a temperature gradient, yet its microscopic origins remain unclear. This study investigates the role of internal flexibility in "soft" colloids, which possess a soft core responsive to local thermal conditions. Using a microscopic model of a sphere with a soft core surrounded by solvent molecules, we demonstrate that internal flexibility significantly influences the Soret effect. Our findings indicate that the sign of Soret migration in these soft molecules is governed by the competition between two contributions: a "rigid" part and a soft contribution arising from the core-solvent interaction. We provide an analytical expression for the flexural movement of a molecule's core and determine the conditions for Soret migration reversibility. These results offer a quantitative framework for interpreting the Soret effect in soft molecules and can guide the design of tunable flexible systems. Specifically, we show that adjusting the softness of the molecular core allows for the control of both the direction and magnitude of Soret migration. These insights are applicable to various soft molecular models, including those featuring a soft core, a functionalized shell, and a solvent layer. We illustrate this by examining a "flower" molecule, where the functionalized shell interacts with the solvent, and we confirm that our theoretical results align with existing experimental data. Our analysis reveals that the Soret effect in the "flower" molecule arises from three distinct contributions: flexibility of the core, functional group-solvent interaction, and core-solvent interaction. Finally, we demonstrate that the sign of the Soret coefficient can be tuned by modifying the functionalized shell. These conclusions are supported by both theoretical calculations and experimental measurements. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive theoretical and experimental understanding of the Soret effect in soft molecules, enabling the design of new materials with tailored separation properties. By controlling the softness of the core and the functionalized shell, one can precisely manipulate the direction and magnitude of Soret migration, thereby enhancing the efficiency of separation processes. The theoretical and experimental findings presented here offer a comprehensive understanding of the Soret effect in soft molecules and pave the way for the development of advanced materials with customized transport properties. Furthermore, the insights gained from this study can be extended to other soft molecular systems, such as polymers and proteins, thereby broadening the scope of this research. In summary, this work not only deepens our understanding of the Soret effect in soft molecules but also opens up new avenues for the design of materials with customized transport properties. Recent studies indicate that state-of-the-art domain adaptive pedestrian identification models often produce false positives when identifying a target pedestrian in the target domain. To address this issue, we introduce box reordering, a reduction technique that leverages the consistency of box locations between the source and target domains. Our approach unsupervisedly filters out false positives in the target domain by rearranging bounding boxes from the model's initial prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that box reordering outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both mean average precision and rank-$k$ accuracy. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/boxreordering.

This paper introduces a novel method for enhancing musical quality through a technique called Transformation Vocoding, which combines the advantages of vocoding with the music improvement algorithm described in [1]. Our approach is straightforward: it transforms the frequency spectrum of the input audio to elevate its timbre and then vocodes this transformed spectrum over the audio's fundamental frequency. We demonstrate that this vocoding process, effectively blending the spectral envelope from a modified source with an unchanged filter, successfully merges improved timbre with preserved rhythm. Furthermore, we show that both the Transformation Vocoding algorithm and the source-fundamental combination are reversible, allowing for the recovery of the original audio. We also provide an objective evaluation of the method's effectiveness. The experimental results indicate that our proposed algorithm outperforms the source-fundamental combination and a previous method by [1]. Additionally, we demonstrate that the algorithm's parameters can be tuned to control the degree of audio enhancement. Finally, we present an application of the Transformation Vocoding algorithm for audio compression, showing that it outperforms MP3 compression by a significant margin. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's limitations and potential future research directions.

This study examines how mistakes in release height, release velocity, and release angle influence object displacement. By developing a theoretical framework for these errors, we created a new simulation tool called FauxThrow. This software enables users to explore the consequences of releasing an object prematurely or late, facilitating a novel investigation into the role of "can't let-go" phenomena. Our findings indicate that releasing an object too early is more likely to cause it to land outside a target area, whereas releasing too late is more likely to result in the object falling short of that area. These results are supported by an experiment involving 24 participants. We conclude that our theoretical model accurately accounts for the effects of premature and delayed releases on object displacement. Furthermore, we propose that our model offers a more comprehensive explanation for errors in throwing movements than the "can't let-go" phenomenon alone. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of the FauxThrow tool for investigating various movement-related issues, such as those affecting stroke patients. This paper presents the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), a repository of binding energy data designed to facilitate the assessment of quantum chemical calculations for molecular species relevant to astrochemistry. This study investigates the single-factor Ricker model, a Ricker growth curve characterized by a stochastic lower bound dependent on the sample mean. Initially, the feasibility of this approach is assessed. Subsequently, methods are developed to determine model parameters, estimate the lower bound, and construct confidence intervals for the sample mean. Finally, the paper presents a simulation study to evaluate the performance of this model and its estimators. Additionally, two real-world datasets are analyzed to demonstrate the model's applicability. The findings indicate that the Ricker growth curve with a sample-related lower limit provides a more accurate fit than the standard Ricker curve for these datasets. The study concludes by outlining potential limitations and suggesting directions for future research. The proposed methodology is particularly valuable for analyzing nonlinear patterns in time series data, where it can identify and quantify deviations from the mean. Specifically, this model is recommended for analyzing growth curves in fisheries and ecology, as well as disease incidence trends. The model's parameters can be interpreted to establish a realistic lower limit for the phenomenon under study. Furthermore, the approach can be extended to multivariate and nonlinear regression settings. For the Davey-Stewartson II equations, we establish that the reflection coefficient's behavior relative to $|k|$ along the real axis is necessary for constructing the universal Riemann-Hilbert problem. This finding resolves a specific issue within the data compression strategy proposed by Dym and McLaughlin. The proof relies on bounding the reflection coefficient using the norm of the potential function. Subsequently, we derive an explicit bound for the reflection coefficient for the DS-II equations with constant coefficients, a result that applies generally to all DS-type equations. Using this explicit bound, we demonstrate that the reflection coefficient's $|k|$ behavior can be regulated by the $L^2$ norm of the corresponding potential function. As an application, we provide the first rigorous analysis of soliton resolution for DS-II equations with constant coefficients in the focus region. Our results indicate that such analysis is feasible provided the reflection coefficient is sufficiently small. Furthermore, we show that the smallness of the reflection coefficient can be derived from the smallness of the related potential function. These findings suggest a method for analyzing the focus region in nonlinear interaction regions, which is essential for understanding the long-time dynamics of nonlinear interaction solitons. Additionally, our approach offers a new perspective on the inverse scattering transform for DS equations. Finally, we outline a method to determine a sharp bound for the reflection coefficient in the focus region, thereby clarifying the necessary conditions for soliton resolution. Meta-learning, defined as learning how to learn, has recently gained significant traction in machine learning. This approach is particularly effective for rapidly adapting to new tasks when labeled data is scarce, a scenario common in many practical applications. While recent studies have demonstrated that neural networks can achieve this with few samples, the internal mechanisms of these models remain poorly understood. This paper investigates such a few-shot meta-learning task using linear models, which are capable of depicting new tasks effectively despite being trained on limited labeled examples. We show that these linear models can develop a robust depiction that generalizes to novel tasks, even when those tasks differ significantly from the training set. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the sparsity of a model's depiction and its ability to generalize, finding that sparsity serves as a reliable predictor of generalization performance. Finally, we extend our analysis to non-linear models, revealing that they can learn multiple depiction types, with sparsity predicting which specific type a linear model will adopt. These findings offer valuable insights for designing future data-efficient machine learning systems. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb/depictions.

Low-resource languages present significant challenges for Machine Translation, primarily due to a scarcity of parallel training data. To address this, researchers often employ Distillation and Quantization techniques to build accurate, lightweight models. Distillation involves training a smaller model to replicate the outputs of a larger one, while reducing model size through Quantization typically enhances both speed and memory efficiency. This study evaluates how these methods impact the performance of lightweight MT models in low-resource settings, specifically focusing on their resilience to data noise and model architecture choices. Our findings indicate that models created via distillation are more robust to noise and architectural variations than those produced by quantization. Consequently, for small-scale, low-resource MT tasks, we recommend utilizing lightweight models trained through distillation rather than quantization. This approach yields substantial gains in accuracy, speed, and memory usage, while simultaneously improving the model's robustness. Additionally, we introduce a new data augmentation strategy that leverages back-translation to enhance the robustness of distillation-based models. We anticipate that these insights will be valuable for future efforts in small-scale, low-resource machine translation. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/low-resource-distillation-and-quantization. Our experiments can be reproduced using the provided code and data. The paper is available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07009. The title is Too Fragile To Handle: Comparing the Robustness of Quantization and Distillation Towards Lightweight Low-Resource MT Models.

We introduce the concept of hypergraph functionals, which extend the principle of least action to include hyperedges. Furthermore, we establish a general framework for constructing the equations of motion governing the evolution of a solitary hypergraph. This work explores the functional defined by the integral of a hypergraph's volume over time and investigates the equation of motion derived from the least action principle using this functional. The resulting equation is a nonlinear, nonlocal partial differential equation that does not adhere to established mathematical physical laws. Consequently, we propose that such equations of motion are illogical. We name this specific equation the "illogical Lagrangian function of a solitary hypergraph." Finally, we outline two potential applications for this principle: modeling the evolution of multidimensional droplets in a fluid and simulating the dynamics of a three-color traffic network.

Keywords: Hypergraph, Hyperedge, Functional, Equation of motion, Principle of least action, Model of droplet evolution, Traffic network model.

This paper introduces a novel approach to binary segmentation of pulmonary nodules in chest X-rays, specifically targeting the reduction of required labeled training samples. We evaluate three image enhancement techniques—contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE), contrast saturation, and nonlinear intensity stretching—applied individually and in combination. These methods are integrated into a deep learning segmentation framework that combines a fully convolutional network (FCN) with a U-Net decoder. Our findings demonstrate that applying image enhancements can significantly lower the number of labeled images needed for training, resulting in improved segmentation performance. Furthermore, we observe that using all three enhancement methods together yields the best outcomes. The study also examines the impact of nodule size on segmentation accuracy and explores the effects of varying network architectures and decoder configurations. Finally, we establish that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results in nodule segmentation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/FCN-UNet-with-Image-Enhancements.

Current image captioning models frequently overlook object attributes and relationships, resulting in descriptions that are too detailed and difficult to interpret. To address this, we introduce a new multi-stage framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to generate manageable image captions. This system first extracts key entities and relations from images using a vision-and-language pre-trained model, then employs prompting to utilize the LLM for constructing captions. We created a new dataset, ManImg, which contains human annotations of these descriptions. Experiments on ManImg and the Pascal-SAP500 benchmark demonstrate that our method significantly enhances the ability of image captioning models to focus on essential visual information. Furthermore, our approach yields substantial improvements in object recognition, achieving state-of-the-art results on the COCO dataset. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/robinliu1998/ManImg.

Voice Interpretation (VI) facilitates communication among individuals with different native languages. Although speech interpretation is vital, it is often labor-intensive and costly. To address this financial burden, leveraging pre-trained deep neural networks for end-to-end voice interpretation is highly promising. However, the scarcity of paired training data for specific language pairs remains a significant challenge. To tackle this data limitation, we introduce Zero-shot Voice Interpretation (Zs-VI), a method capable of interpreting speech without requiring any training data. Zs-VI consists of three components: (1) a data augmentation module that creates synthetic data for various pairs using a text-to-speech model; (2) a multi-task learning module that jointly trains on original and synthetic data to learn language-invariant and language-specific features; and (3) a decoding module that interprets speech by jointly decoding a source language encoder and a target language encoder. Experiments across multiple language pairs demonstrate that Zs-VI achieves competitive performance on standard benchmarks for low-resource language pairs and surpasses state-of-the-art methods in high-resource scenarios. This study evaluates the impact of forecast combination and daily consumption extremes on probabilistic active power load predictions for low-voltage grids. Using a generalized additive load model, the authors developed an ensemble of weakly supervised learning models to predict daily active power loads in Germany. The modeling approach was refined to incorporate forecast combination, resulting in a reduction of the 95% mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 10.1% to 8.2% and a 17% decrease in the 99% MAPE from 13.5% to 11.0%. Additionally, the analysis examined the relationship between daily aggregate consumption and the peak and minimum values observed throughout the day. Results indicate that the peak value accounts for 60% of the total daily consumption, whereas the minimum contributes only 10%. These findings are significant for grid operators, particularly when assessing the potential of demand-side flexibility to mitigate peak loads. The paper concludes by presenting preliminary results from a model designed to forecast the peak and minimum daily values. This model, which utilizes only the highest and lowest loads from previous days, achieves a 95% MAPE of 10.2% and a 99% MAPE of 12.5%. Finally, the study explores the potential for enhancing these forecasts by incorporating additional features. The load prediction model serves as a core component of the PowerNetTS library, a Python toolkit for time series forecasting of active and reactive power loads at various aggregation levels. PowerNetTS is available on PyPI and conda-forge. Furthermore, a Jupyter notebook demonstrating the library's functionality can be accessed via Binder. This research was conducted as part of the Power4Grid initiative, a collaboration between the German electricity industry and the Fraunhofer Institute for Open Communication Systems (OKL). Additional details regarding the initiative are available at https://www.power4grid.de. The initiative's primary objective is to develop open-source software for forecasting active and reactive power loads across multiple levels of aggregation. This software is provided through PowerNet, a project within the German Power4Grid initiative. PowerNet comprises various modules, including PowerNetTS for low-voltage and medium-voltage level aggregation, and PowerNetML for higher levels of aggregation. Both PowerNet and PowerNetML can be installed using pip. The PowerNet repository is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/power4grid/PowerNet, and the PowerNetML module is available on PyPI at https://pypi.org

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the critical need for advanced AI-driven diagnostic tools, particularly in developing reliable computer-aided diagnosis systems for pneumonia and COVID-19. While AI has shown promise in this field, it faces significant hurdles, including data scarcity, the high cost of imaging, and the challenge of creating robust models capable of generalizing to unseen data. To overcome these obstacles, we introduce a weakly guided learning framework designed for lesion localization and segmentation. This approach eliminates the requirement for precise lesion coordinates during training, thereby reducing the demand for high-quality annotations. Accurately identifying and localizing vertebrae within the abdominal region of computed tomography (CT) scans is a critical yet difficult challenge in medical imaging. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to rectify the irregular spine orientation in CT volumes, enabling the application of 2D vertebra recognition techniques to 3D CT scans. The proposed methodology comprises two primary components: Spine Rectification and Vertebra Recognition. To align the irregular spine orientation, we developed a new registration algorithm that integrates anatomical constraints with deep learning registration. Furthermore, to enhance recognition performance, we implemented a non-local mean (NLM) filter to suppress noise in vertebra images, alongside a 3D context feature extraction technique that leverages surrounding anatomical structures to boost recognition accuracy. Experimental results indicate that our registration algorithm surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, and the overall recognition approach achieves a sensitivity of 96.1% and a positive predictive value of 95.1%. The proposed spine registration method is also applicable to other medical imaging tasks involving irregular anatomical orientations, such as cardiac and pulmonary image analysis. The dynamical stabilization effect, originally identified in a focused laser field, is generalized to arbitrary intense light-matter interactions. This phenomenon involves a resonant enhancement of ionization or excitation driven by a reduced tunneling rate and constructive interference of phase factors. Furthermore, under conditions of vacuum oscillations between states, the system achieves complete suppression of ionization. This resonant enhancement and dynamical stabilization persist even when the field intensity is sufficient to cause multiphoton absorption and strong dressing, a regime characterized by significant sideband structures. Notably, these features are also observed in resonant electron scattering, which serves as an inverse process to ionization. These findings are validated through numerical simulations of a single electron interacting with a laser field within a cavity. Additionally, the study examines related structures linked to Autler-Townes splitting and discusses the model's applicability to systems involving light-matter coupling in superconductors. Finally, the relationship between dynamical stabilization and the Autler-Townes effect is explored. These results are expected to be observable in current and upcoming experiments. Keywords: Strong-field physics, Resonant enhancement, Autler-Townes splitting, Light-matter coupling in superconductors. Recent years have seen a surge in research dedicated to developing robust, general-purpose elastic actuators for legged locomotion. These actuators offer a significant advantage over DC motors by storing and releasing energy during movement, thereby enhancing the agility and efficiency of legged agents. Nevertheless, creating robust and efficient control policies for systems equipped with these devices remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning framework that explicitly accounts for the dynamic behavior of elastic actuators. By utilizing Model Predictive Control (MPC) within a reinforcement learning context, we enable the system to leverage the actuator dynamics for improved performance. We validate our approach by training a quadruped agent to walk and run while carrying a payload, demonstrating that our method surpasses traditional approaches that rely solely on MPC or reinforcement learning. Furthermore, we show that our policy can adapt to environmental changes, such as varied surface friction coefficients. Finally, we execute these policies on a physical quadruped robot outfitted with an elastic actuator, confirming that our learned control strategies outperform those learned on a fixed-difficulty model. This work establishes a new paradigm for learning control policies on elastic robots, facilitating the creation of more efficient and agile systems. This dividend, derived from the potential energy density, is divided by the total energy to yield the temperature. The problem becomes solvable when the potential energy is expressed as the product of this temperature and the kinetic energy. Consequently, the quantum divisibility issue is solved in any dimension, offering a new perspective on the Schrödinger equation. Mini-scale tearing modes exist at lengths significantly smaller than both the collisionless slab width and the ion Larmor radius. This study provides a comprehensive theoretical overview of their equilibrium, linear instability, and nonlinear evolution within the collisionless regime. It is demonstrated that these modes arise from kink perturbations of current sheets formed during magnetic reconnection in collisionless plasmas. While mini-scale tearing modes were previously identified only numerically, this work establishes their physical characteristics and key properties through theoretical analysis. Our results indicate that the reconnection rate is governed by the most unstable mode, which exhibits a characteristic scale of a few times the electron Larmor radius. Furthermore, this mode displays a linear growth rate orders of magnitude higher than larger-scale tearing modes. Finally, our analysis confirms that mini-scale tearing modes are three-dimensional structures, with a three-dimensional description being essential for their accurate characterization. These findings have significant implications for understanding magnetic reconnection across various plasma environments. Specifically, they suggest that mini-scale tearing modes may play a critical role in small-scale current sheet dynamics and rapid reconnection in both space and laboratory plasmas. Additionally, these modes may be responsible for the fine-scale structure observed in current sheets and for the generation of small-scale turbulence and coherent structures. The insights gained regarding their three-dimensional nature and associated scales may also aid in interpreting recent observations of current sheets and reconnection regions in the solar wind and magnetosphere. Ultimately, our results provide a robust framework for future investigations into the three-dimensional structure of current sheets and the dynamics of small-scale reconnection regions. This will facilitate a more complete understanding of the fundamental processes governing plasma behavior in diverse settings. Furthermore, our findings may inform the development of more efficient plasma heating and current drive techniques for fusion applications. For instance, the three-dimensional nature of mini-scale tearing modes could be leveraged to optimize the deposition of external power into the plasma core. Additionally, the short characteristic timescales of these modes may influence the design of advanced plasma control systems. The rapid advancement of deep learning has significantly transformed image retrieval, yet current approaches often depend on extensive labeled datasets and fail to incorporate domain-specific knowledge regarding fashion items. This paper introduces a novel framework for fashion image retrieval that leverages feature-level trait manipulation to enhance retrieval accuracy while minimizing the need for training data. By utilizing a generative model, we isolate domain-specific knowledge to adjust key characteristics of fashion images, such as the subject's pose, background, and clothing color. This framework demonstrates superior performance compared to standard baselines and establishes competitive results against state-of-the-art methods when applied to two public fashion datasets. Furthermore, the results confirm that manipulating feature-level traits effectively improves image retrieval outcomes. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta10/Semi-supervised-Feature-Level-Trait-Manipulation. Keywords: Fashion Image Retrieval, Feature-level Trait Manipulation, Generative Models.

This study introduces a new dual gradient ascent method designed for solving linear ill-posed problems within Banach spaces. The approach constructs the solution by applying an inverse operator to the noisy data, utilizing an inexact gradient ascent process to handle the resulting unbounded results. This technique is applicable to any Banach space, encompassing standard $L^p$ spaces. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness on both regularization tasks, such as total variation minimization, and reconstruction tasks, like solving the X-ray transform equation. Furthermore, we establish convergence under specific conditions, with numerical experiments confirming the theoretical findings. The implementation is available at \url{https://github.com/leopoldo-oliveira/dual-grad-ascent}. The method's success in delivering effective solutions for unbounded inverse problems suggests potential for extension to nonlinear inverse problems. Additionally, the algorithm is well-suited for parallel computing environments, including graphics processing units. Finally, we propose a strategy for determining the stopping time based on the noise level in the data. Our results indicate that this optimal stopping time scales with the logarithm of the inverse of the noise level, a finding that aligns with existing literature. However, this conclusion is restricted to $L^2$ spaces. We also examine the relationship between this stopping time and that of the truncated singular value decomposition. Developing a robust light field depth estimator that can recover depth maps from partially visible micro-lens arrays is crucial for light field systems operating in real-world environments. To address this challenge, we introduce a deep neural network named Occlusion-Responsive Expense Creator (OREC), which utilizes a novel cost volume enhanced by OREC to generate depth maps under significant occlusion. OREC is designed to be responsive to specific sub-aperture images, allowing the system to leverage a broad spectrum of occlusion-variant images for accurate scene reconstruction. We also propose a new loss function called the OREC Response Loss (ORCL), which is derived from the loss function of a deep regression network for which OREC serves as the weights. This loss function is particularly effective for training depth estimators to handle high levels of occlusion. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed OREC and ORCL significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of resilience to occlusion. Additionally, we show that the OREC-based approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency for light field depth estimation. To validate these claims, we have established a new dataset featuring high occlusion levels for depth assessment, which will be made available to the research community. The code is accessible at https://github.com/orec-lf-lab/OREC. Keywords: Light Field Depth Assessment, Deep Learning, Cost Volume, Robustness to Occlusion.

This paper introduces a bilinear approach to Fokas-Lenells equations, a nonlinear integrable system characterized by two parameters that enable the modeling of nonlocal effects. Initially, we establish the bilinear form and derive novel Hirota bilinear equations for the model. Subsequently, we utilize these formulas to demonstrate that all solutions preserving $L^2$ norms correspond to real or real-space-reversing gauge transformations of real solutions. Finally, we apply the bilinear formalism to construct N-soliton solutions, with a specific focus on real eigenfunction-based real or real-space-reversing gauge transformations yielding complex potentials. This represents the inaugural demonstration of such transformations for this nonlocal integrable model. Additionally, we generate the first examples of nonlocal potentials exhibiting a real Wronskian structure within the Fokas-Lenells framework. These findings hold significant implications for the analysis of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with real-space-reversing gauge transformations and may facilitate the study of other nonlocal integrable systems. Furthermore, the methodologies employed here are applicable to other nonlocal integrable models belonging to the Fokas-Lenells type. We examine a broad spectrum of non-Riemannian gravitational actions within the Galilean-conformal (GC) framework, observing that many can be expressed as the square of a 2-form curvature. By applying the principle of holographic duality, we derive constraints on dual field theories for gravitational actions involving non-Riemannian curvatures raised to powers greater than two. Furthermore, we explore potential connections between non-Riemannian gravitational actions and the gravitational sector of holographic duality. A key example is the C-curvature squared action, which yields a dual field theory characterized by anisotropic scaling with dynamic exponent $z=2$. We also analyze the implications of non-Riemannian gravitational actions in a (1+0) dimensional context. This dual approach may prove valuable for investigating non-equilibrium systems and non-equilibrium holography. Additionally, we demonstrate that a specific non-Riemannian gravitational action reduces to the standard Riemannian Einstein-Hilbert action when the dual field theory is in thermal equilibrium. Finally, we calculate the non-Riemannian gravitational action for a Schwarzschild black hole within the GC framework. The resulting solution is non-trivial, indicating that non-Riemannian geometry can influence black hole physics. Our findings suggest that non-Riemannian geometry could be essential for understanding non-equilibrium systems and their dual field theories. Consequently, non-Riemannian gravitational actions may play a crucial role in addressing fundamental questions in theoretical physics. This paper serves as a foundation for future investigations into non-Riemannian geometry and its applications in theoretical physics. Our work is part of a broader research initiative exploring non-Riemannian geometry, with a specific focus on the Galilean-conformal framework. We anticipate that this approach will be instrumental in addressing various fundamental issues within theoretical physics. In Home WiFi networks, devices (Extends) connect to Access Points (APs) based on signal strength or channel load. However, these selection methods often fail to account for the specific traffic types a device generates or receives. This paper introduces a solution that enables Extends to select the most suitable AP by considering channel load relative to their specific traffic requirements. To implement this, we developed a Python-based software access point and network environment using the IEEE 802.11k/v standard. Our results demonstrate that matching traffic types with APs can enhance overall network throughput by up to 100%. Furthermore, we observed that in mixed traffic scenarios, the network can sustain up to 100 Extends, compared to a maximum of 50 Extends in a scenario where all devices share identical traffic types. This indicates that supporting diverse traffic types significantly improves the network's capacity. Additionally, the Python-based setup facilitates rapid and flexible testing of various scenarios, which is particularly valuable for research and development purposes. Finally, we note that the Python implementation is approximately 100 times slower than the original IEEE 802.11 standard implementation. Despite this limitation, the software-based approach offers a distinct advantage by allowing researchers to easily modify and test multiple scenarios with minimal effort. Consequently, this tool is ideal for the research and development phase, while the final product is expected to be implemented in C++ for performance. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Ankit-2000/IEEE802.11k_v. Our findings suggest that matching traffic types with appropriate APs is crucial for maximizing network throughput. We also recommend that future studies investigate the impact of varying traffic types and sizes on performance. The Python code can be utilized to test different scenarios and evaluate traffic type matching. Finally, we propose that further research explore implementing this concept in C++ to achieve the performance levels of the original IEEE 802.11 standard. We believe this work will be beneficial for the research and development community. To our knowledge, this is the first study to match traffic types with suitable APs to maximize throughput in Home WiFi networks.
